By the middle of the 16th century resistance in the Greater Antilles was largely quashed. In the Lesser Antilles the Kalinago kept their independence against the Spanish and later the French and English, helped by the lack of gold and the heavy Spanish casualties.

In the 17th century they regularly attacked English and French plantations in the Leeward Islands. In 1660 France and England signed the Treaty of Saint Charles with the Island Caribs, which left only Dominica and Saint Vincent as reserves, but the English ignored it. By 1763 the British had annexed Saint Lucia, Tobago, Dominica and Saint Vincent. On Saint Vincent the Kalinago intermarried with free West African captives, forming the Black Caribs, or Garifuna, who were expelled to Honduras in 1797.

Stories of cannibalism come from Spanish accounts, and there is no hard evidence for it. Historians such as Hilary McD. Beckles suggest the stories were an ideological campaign to justify violent expeditions against the Kalinago. The English word cannibal comes from karibna, an Island Carib word that meant person.

The Kalinago and their descendants live in the Antilles, notably in Dominica, where the Kalinago Territory on the east coast was granted by the British government in 1903. The people elect their own chief, and the name Carib was officially changed to Kalinago in Dominica in 2015. Canoes are important in their material culture and economy. The Garifuna, who share common ancestry with the Kalinago, live mainly in Central America.
kaliningrad-oblast: Kaliningrad Oblast covers 15,125 square kilometres and is bordered by Poland to the south, Lithuania to the north and east, and the Baltic Sea to the west. It has sea access, so it is described as a semi-exclave. It is mainly flat, with its highest point, Gora Dozor, at 230 metres. The river Pregolya, its largest, drains through the Vistula Lagoon into the Baltic, and the Curonian Lagoon is shared with Lithuania. The port of Baltiysk is Russia's only Baltic port that remains ice-free all year. The oblast also holds amber, and many Russians call it the Amber Land.

The area was inhabited by the Old Prussians and other Western Balts before the Teutonic conquest in the 13th century, after which Germans settled it extensively. The Teutonic Order founded Königsberg in 1255 on the site of a destroyed Sambian settlement called Tvanksta, naming it for Ottokar II of Bohemia. The Lithuanian-inhabited areas of the Teutonic State were known as Lithuania Minor, which covered all of the modern oblast until the 18th century, and the Old Prussians died out through Germanisation in the first half of the 18th century. In 1525 Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg secularised the Order's Prussian branch and made himself ruler of the Duchy of Prussia, the first Protestant state in Europe, with Königsberg as its residence.

Königsberg was a place of Polish and Lithuanian printing, including the first Lithuanian grammar and the first Polish translation of the New Testament, and its Albertina University received a royal privilege from King Sigismund II Augustus in 1560. In 1807, after the defeat at Jena–Auerstedt, the Prussian court fled to Königsberg, and the battles of Eylau and Friedland were followed by the Treaties of Tilsit.

The territory was the northern part of East Prussia and overwhelmingly German. After the defeat of Nazi Germany in the Second World War the Soviet Union annexed it into the Russian SFSR. The flight and expulsion of the Germans left it largely empty until Soviet citizens, mostly ethnic Russians, were settled there. When Lithuania became independent in 1990 and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, the oblast was cut off from the rest of Russia, and land links now cross neighbouring states. Königsberg Cathedral was restored in the 1990s.

Kaliningrad Oblast is a federal subject of Russia, with its largest city and administrative centre at Kaliningrad, formerly Königsberg. Its population is roughly one million, and Russians form the large majority. Before 1945 the region was overwhelmingly Lutheran.
kalisz: Kalisz lies on the Prosna river in the south-east of Greater Poland, the region regarded as the cradle of the Polish state, and with Poznań is one of its two traditional capitals. Its name is thought to come from the archaic word kal, meaning swamp or marsh. Roman-era finds in the area suggest a stop on the Amber Trail to the Baltic Sea.

Excavations show an early medieval settlement of the Piast period, and the modern town was most likely founded in the 9th century as a castellany and minor fort. In 1106 Bolesław III Wrymouth captured it for his domain. Between 1253 and 1260 it was incorporated under the German town law of Środa Śląska, a variant of Magdeburg law, and during the fragmentation of Poland it formed a separate duchy under a local branch of the Piast dynasty.

The Statute of Kalisz of 1264, issued by Bolesław the Pious, protected Jews at a time of persecution in Western Europe, and in later centuries Poland became a destination for Jewish migration.  In 1314 Ladislaus the Short made it capital of the Kalisz Voivodeship. Casimir III the Great signed a peace treaty with the Order there in 1343.

Kalisz was annexed by Prussia in the Second Partition of 1793, regained by Poles after the Greater Poland uprising of 1806 and, after Napoleon's fall, became a provincial capital of Congress Poland. In August 1914 German forces shelled the city and burned it to the ground, although the Russian troops had left without a fight; of about 68,000 inhabitants only 5,000 remained a year later, and much of the centre was rebuilt by the war's end.

After the German invasion of 1939 the city was annexed by Germany. The Wehrmacht executed Polish defenders in the city and at Winiary, and the Intelligenzaktion targeted the Polish intelligentsia. The Germans set up a Germanisation camp for Polish children taken from their parents. About 30,000 local Jews were murdered by the end of the war, and 20,000 local Catholics were murdered or expelled. The population in 1945 was 43,000, about half the pre-war figure.

Kalisz is the second-largest city of the Greater Poland Voivodeship, with 97,905 residents in December 2021, and is the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Kalisz, created in 1992. It is a historical burial site of Piast dukes and medieval Polish monarchs.
kalka-shimla-railway: The idea of connecting Shimla by rail was first raised by a correspondent to the Delhi Gazette in November 1847. Shimla became the summer capital of British India in 1864 and the headquarters of the Indian army, so twice a year the entire government had to be moved between Calcutta and Shimla by horse- and ox-drawn carts. The opening of the broad-gauge Delhi–Kalka line in 1891 made a branch to Shimla feasible. Surveys were made in 1884, 1885, 1892, 1893 and 1895, and after much debate an adhesion line was chosen in preference to a rack system.

Construction was begun by the privately funded Delhi-Ambala-Kalka Railway Company after a contract with the secretary of state on 29 June 1898. The government gave the land free but no financial aid. Herbert Septimus Harington was chief engineer and Sujan Singh Hadaliwale chief contractor. The line opened on 9 November 1903 and was dedicated by Viceroy Lord Curzon. The estimated cost of 8,678,500 rupees had doubled by the opening. The Indian Army thought the 2 ft gauge too narrow, so the contract was revised on 15 November 1901 and the line was regauged to 2 ft 6 in.

The route climbs from 656 metres at Kalka to 2,075 metres at Shimla, through 20 stations and more than a hundred tunnels, the longest at Barog. The first locomotives were two small engines from the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, replaced from 1902 by ten 0-4-2T engines built by Sharp, Stewart and Company. Thirty larger 2-6-2T engines followed between 1904 and 1910. In 1908 the coaches were rebuilt with aluminium roofs, an early use of aluminium in coach construction, so that locomotives could haul six coaches instead of four. Regular steam operation ended in 1971, and diesel locomotives began running in 1955.

The company had spent 16,525,000 rupees by 1904 with no sign of profit, and the government bought the line on 1 January 1906 for 17,107,748 rupees. In 2007 the Himachal Pradesh government declared the railway a heritage property, and on 8 July 2008 UNESCO added it to the mountain railways of India World Heritage Site, alongside the Darjeeling Himalayan and Nilgiri Mountain Railways. The BBC Four series Indian Hill Railways featured it in 2010. Several sections were washed out by landslides during the 2023 North India floods.
kalkar: Kalkar was founded by Dirk VI of Cleves in 1230 and received city rights in 1242. It was one of the seven capitals of Cleves until the line of the Duchy of Cleves died out in 1609, whereupon the town passed to the Margraviate of Brandenburg.

Marie of Burgundy, Duchess of Cleves, retired to Monreberg castle in Kalkar and founded a Dominican convent there in 1455. Under her influence the town flourished and artists were drawn to its favourable climate for cultural investment. She died at Monreberg in 1463. The Catholic church of St Nicolai has preserved one of the most significant church inventories of the late Middle Ages in Germany.

Between 1957 and 1991, West Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands pursued a plan for a fast breeder reactor, and a 300-megawatt prototype, the SNR-300, was begun near Kalkar in April 1973. Demonstrations against it grew in the mid-1970s after large protests at Wyhl and Brokdorf. A large demonstration in September 1977 involved a police operation that closed autobahns in northern Germany and checked the identity of almost 150,000 people.

Construction was completed in the middle of 1985, but a new state government was against the project, and opposition increased after the Chernobyl disaster in April 1986. In March 1991 the German federal government announced that the SNR-300 would not be put into operation. Its costs had risen from an estimated 150 to 200 million dollars to about 4 billion. The plant has since become an amusement park, Kern-Wasser Wunderland.

Kalkar is a municipality in the district of Kleve, in North Rhine-Westphalia, about 10 kilometres south-east of Cleves and near the Rhine. Notable natives include the theologian Henry of Kalkar (1328–1408), the painter Jan van Calcar (1499–1546) and the Prussian general Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz (1721–1773). The science fiction writer Edgar Rice Burroughs borrowed the name for the Kalkars, a hostile race on the Moon in his novel The Moon Maid.
kalmar: Kalmar lies in the south-east of Sweden by the Baltic Sea, in the province and cultural region of Småland. It is the seat of Kalmar Municipality and the capital of Kalmar County, and the main route to the island of Öland crosses the Öland Bridge beside it. From the thirteenth to the seventeenth centuries it was one of Sweden's most important cities. The oldest evidence of a town dates from the 11th century. Kalmar's oldest city seal, from between 1255 and 1267, is the oldest known city seal in Scandinavia.

The first foundations of a castle were laid in the 12th century with a round tower for guard and lookout, and the tower was expanded in the 13th century. There Queen Margaret called an assembly of the heads of state of Sweden and Norway, and on 13 July 1397 the Kalmar Union treaty was signed, creating a union that lasted until 1523. At the time the Scanian lands, the provinces of Blekinge, Halland and Scania, belonged to Denmark, so Kalmar's position near the border, together with its harbour and trade, drew it into several feuds.

Two events are independently called the Kalmar Bloodbath: in 1505, when King John had the mayor and city council executed, and in 1599, by order of Duke Charles, later King Charles IX of Sweden. In the 1540s King Gustav Vasa and later his sons Erik XIV and John III rebuilt the castle as the Renaissance castle seen today. Kalmar became a diocese of the Church of Sweden in 1603 and the capital of the newly founded Kalmar County in 1634. The city suffered in the Kalmar War of 1611–1613, which began with a Danish siege of the castle, and counted 22 sieges in all, the last during the Scanian War in the 1670s; the castle was never taken.

After the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658 the borders of Sweden moved further south and Kalmar's strategic importance faded. In 1689 the king set up his main naval base at Karlskrona, and Kalmar lost its place as one of the main military outposts. A new fortified town was built on Kvarnholmen around the mid-1600s on baroque lines. Kalmar Cathedral, designed by Nicodemus Tessin the Elder and begun in 1660, was interrupted several times, including during the Scanian War, and finished in 1703.

Kalmar had 41,388 inhabitants in 2020 and is the third largest urban area in Småland. The city has a university, parts of Linnaeus University, and its cathedral is a leading example of baroque classicism in Sweden.
kalmar-union: The union was the work of Scandinavian aristocrats who wanted to counter the influence of the Hanseatic League, a northern German trade league centred on the Baltic and North Seas. Denmark had recently suffered a humiliating defeat in the Danish-Hanseatic War of 1361 to 1370. On the personal level it was achieved by Queen Margaret I of Denmark, daughter of King Valdemar IV of Denmark and wife of King Haakon VI of Norway and Sweden. Her son Olaf inherited the Danish crown in 1376 and the Norwegian crown in 1380.

When Olaf died in 1387 Margaret became regent of Denmark and Norway and adopted her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania. After she defeated King Albert in 1389, with the help Swedish nobles had asked of her, Eric was proclaimed King of Norway and was elected King of Denmark and Sweden in 1396. The union joined under one monarch the three kingdoms and Norway's maritime possessions, which included Iceland, Greenland, the Faroe Islands, Orkney and Shetland.

The union was never continuous. The Engelbrekt rebellion, which began in 1434, led to the overthrow of King Eric in Denmark and Sweden in 1439 and in Norway in 1442. The three kingdoms had been united without a break for a long time until the death of Christopher of Bavaria in 1448. Christian of Oldenburg then became king of Denmark, and of Norway from 1450, and Karl Knutsson Bonde ruled in Sweden. After Karl's death, Christian was defeated by Sten Sture the Elder at the Battle of Brunkeberg in 1471, and Sweden was mostly governed by protectors of the realm.

In 1520 Christian II invaded Sweden, killed Sten Sture the Younger at the Battle of Bogesund and was crowned king, and supporters of Sture were executed in the Stockholm Bloodbath. Gustav Vasa, whose father was among those executed, raised a rebellion in Dalarna and allied with Lübeck. His election as King of Sweden on 6 June 1523 ended the union for Sweden, and Frederick I renounced his claim in 1524 at the Treaty of Malmö.

A remnant lasted until 1536 or 1537, when the Danish Privy Council declared Norway a Danish province, though it kept its own laws. The union of Denmark and Norway lasted nearly three centuries, until Norway was ceded to Sweden in 1814. The historian Sverre Bagge explains the union's instability by the power of the national aristocracies, the different effects of its foreign policy on each kingdom, and the difficulty of controlling so large a territory.
kalmar-war: Denmark–Norway controlled the strait between the Baltic Sea and the North Sea, and the Sound Dues it collected there were its main source of income. Sweden sought an alternative trade route through sparsely populated Lapland to avoid paying them. In 1607 Charles IX of Sweden declared himself King of the Lapps in Nordland and began collecting taxes in Norwegian territory, even south of Tromsø. Christian IV of Denmark and Norway protested, and Charles ignored him. In April 1611 Denmark–Norway declared war and invaded.

The Swedes were ill-prepared, since their main field army was engaged in the Ingrian War. The Danish and Norwegian plan was to attack on three fronts: from Kristianopel towards Kalmar, from Halmstad towards Jönköping, and from the Norwegian side towards the fortress of Älvsborg. A force of 5,200 Danish troops besieged and took Kalmar, and the Swedes had to scuttle some 20 ships in the harbour to keep them from capture. On 26 June a Swedish force carried out the storming of Kristianopel. In the summer Swedish forces under Baltzar Bäck took Jämtland and Härjedalen with little fighting, but excesses against the population led to a rising, and the troops were forced out in the autumn of 1612.

Charles IX died on 20 October 1611 and his son Gustavus Adolphus sued for peace. Christian IV saw a chance of larger gains and strengthened his armies in southern Sweden. In February 1612 Gustavus nearly drowned at the Battle of Vittsjö after a Danish army surprised him. In early 1612 Denmark–Norway took Älvsborg and Gullberg, in present-day Gothenburg, leaving Sweden without access to the sea in the west. A thrust towards Stockholm failed against scorched earth and guerrilla warfare, and many unpaid mercenaries deserted. Christian's naval expedition to Stockholm in August and September 1612 also failed, and he left the archipelago by 10 September.

England and the Dutch Republic, invested in Baltic trade, pressed for an end before a decisive victory could curtail Denmark–Norway's power. Christian, short of funds and reliant on mercenaries, agreed to talks, and with the intercession of James I of England the Treaty of Knäred was signed on 20 January 1613. Lapland was incorporated into Norway, and Sweden had to pay a high ransom for Älvsborg and Gullberg, two towns and six surrounding hundreds. Sweden won exemption from the Sound toll, with the right of free trade through the strait. Sweden recovered under Gustavus Adolphus, and in the Torstenson War Denmark–Norway lost and ceded control of the Baltic to the Swedish king.
kalmyks: The Kalmyks are the only Mongolic people in Europe. They are a branch of the Oirat Mongols, whose grazing-lands spanned parts of present-day Kazakhstan, Russia, Mongolia and China. After the fall of the Yuan dynasty in 1368 the Oirats struggled for 400 years against the Khalkha Mongols, the Ming and the Qing for control of Mongolia; the struggle ended in 1757 with the defeat of the Dzungar Khanate by the Qing. The Kalmyks descend chiefly from the Torghut, with smaller groups of Dörbets, Khoshuts and Dzungars. The name is of Turkic origin and means remnant or to remain.

In the early 17th century the First Altan Khan drove the Oirats west to eastern Kazakhstan, where the Torghuts were blocked by the Kazakhs from trading with towns on the Syr Darya and turned to the new Russian outposts. In 1618 the Torghuts and a contingent of Dörbets, 200,000 to 250,000 people under their taishi Kho Orluk, chose to migrate to the lower Volga. They reached the region in 1630 and encamped on land that had belonged to the Astrakhan Khanate and was claimed by Russia. The Kalmyks became Russian allies, and a treaty to protect the southern Russian border was signed with the Kalmyk Khanate. The Oirats expelled most of the Nogai Horde and made the remaining nomadic tribes their vassals.

After the exodus of 1771 the Kalmyks who stayed in the Russian Empire continued their nomadic life between the Don and the Volga. The Soviet government set up the Kalmyk Autonomous Oblast in November 1920, with Elista as its capital, and in October 1935 it became an autonomous republic. On 28 December 1943 the Soviet government accused them of collaborating with the Germans and deported the entire population to Central Asia and Siberia within 24 hours, at night in winter, in unheated cattle cars. In 1957 Khrushchev permitted the Kalmyks to return, and Kalmykia again became an autonomous republic in 1958.

The Kalmyks embraced Tibetan Buddhism in the early 17th century and belong to the Gelug school, the Yellow Hat sect. Their clergy trained either in monasteries on the steppe, many of which were felt tents that moved with the tribes, or in Tibet. In the 17th century the Khoshut monk Zaya Pandita devised Clear Script, based on the vertical Mongol script, to write Oirat. They live mainly in the Republic of Kalmykia between the Volga and the Don, and small communities live in the United States, France, Germany and the Czech Republic.
kalocsa: Kalocsa is a town in Bács-Kiskun county, Hungary, about 142 kilometres south of Budapest, near the left bank of the Danube. It lies in a marshy but highly productive district. Historically it had greater political and economic importance than it has now. Its residents and the people of its wide communal lands have mostly worked in growing paprika, fruit, flax, hemp and cereals, in catching waterfowl and in fishing.

The town is almost as old as the Hungarian state. After the Conquest, the tribe of Prince Árpád settled there, and later, along with Esztergom, Kalocsa became an archdiocese founded by King Stephen in the early years of the state. Its first archbishop, Asztrik, is said to have brought the crown to Stephen from the Pope, and the first church was built in the first decade of the 11th century. Some medieval archbishops served as generals: Ugrin Csák led the Hungarian forces against the Tatars at the Battle of Mohi on 11 April 1241, and Pál Tomori, archbishop from 1523 to 1526, led the army against the Ottomans and was killed at Mohács.

The Turks entered Kalocsa on 15 August 1529, the people dispersed and the archbishopric lost its importance. In 1602 Hungarian Calvinistic Haiduk burned the town. The Turks burned the castle and withdrew on 13 October 1686, after 148 years of rule. Returning archbishops attracted new residents, and Cardinal Imre Csáki, archbishop from 1710 to 1732, recovered the lands. The railway came late, in 1882, and in 1886 the town lost its rank, which it regained in 1921. In the summer of 1944 the Jews of Kalocsa were deported, and most were murdered.

The town is the seat of one of Hungary's Catholic archbishops. Its Italian-baroque cathedral, the fourth on the site, was begun with a foundation stone laid in 1735 to a design by András Mayerhoffer and stands on Holy Trinity Square beside the baroque archbishop's palace of the 1760s. The Archbishop's Library holds 150,000 volumes. The Jesuit building carries an observatory founded as the eighteenth in the world. Kalocsa has a Paprika Museum, since the town is, with Szeged, among the best-known places for producing paprika, and it is known for its women folk painters.
kaloyan-of-bulgaria: Kaloyan was born around 1170, the younger brother of Theodor and Asen, who led the uprising of Bulgarians and Vlachs against the Byzantine Empire in 1185. The uprising restored Bulgaria as an independent state, with the help of Cuman warriors. Baptised Ivan, he was called Ioannitsa, little Ivan, because his elder brother had the same name; his Greek enemies called him Skyloioannes, John the Dog. In the spring of 1188 he was sent to Constantinople as a hostage in exchange for Asen's wife. After Asen was murdered in 1196, Theodor, crowned as Peter II, made him co-ruler, and when Peter was murdered in 1197 Kaloyan became sole ruler.

Kaloyan attacked Thrace and captured fortresses from the Byzantines, among them Braničevo, Skopje and Prizren. He wrote to Pope Innocent III offering to recognise papal primacy in return for an imperial crown. The pope refused an imperial crown, and on 8 November 1204 the papal legate crowned him king of the Bulgarians and Vlachs, though Kaloyan kept styling himself tsar. After the Byzantine defenders of Varna fell to him in 1201 he had them buried alive in the moat, and later called himself the Romanslayer, after Basil II the Bulgar Slayer.

Crusaders took Constantinople on 13 April 1204. Kaloyan supported the Greek towns that rose against the Latins, and on 14 April 1205 he defeated Emperor Baldwin I at Adrianople, drawing the heavy cavalry into an ambush by a feigned retreat of the Cumans. Baldwin was captured and died in Tarnovo. Kaloyan then pillaged Thrace and Macedonia, and at Philippopolis he had prominent burghers killed and sent the commoners in chains to Vlachia.

Boniface, king of Thessalonica, was ambushed and killed on 4 September 1207, and Villehardouin says local Bulgarians did it while other sources say Kaloyan arranged it. Kaloyan laid siege to Thessalonica and died there in October 1207. The circumstances are uncertain: Akropolites reports pleurisy and a rumour of divine wrath, and legends say that Saint Demetrius struck him with a lance, a scene painted in churches such as Dečani Monastery. Some historians think he was murdered by his commander Manastras. The place of his grave is unknown.
kama-river: The Kama, also known as the Chulman in Tatar, is 1,805 kilometres long and drains a basin of 507,000 square kilometres. It is the longest left tributary of the Volga and the largest by discharge. It starts near Kuliga in the Udmurt Republic, flows northwest for 200 kilometres, turns northeast near Loyno for another 200 kilometres, then turns south and west through Perm Krai, again through the Udmurt Republic and through Tatarstan, where it meets the Volga south of Kazan. Its largest tributaries include the Vishera, the Chusovaya, the Belaya and the Vyatka.

Before the advent of railroads, important portages connected the Kama with the basins of the Northern Dvina and the Pechora. In the early nineteenth century the Northern Ekaterininsky Canal linked the upper Kama with the Vychegda River, a tributary of the Northern Dvina, but it was mostly abandoned after just a few years because of low use.

The Kama is dammed at Perm by the Kama Hydroelectric Station, at Chaykovsky by the Votkinsk Hydroelectric Station and at Naberezhnye Chelny by the Nizhnekamsk Hydroelectric Station, each forming a reservoir. The reservoirs have significantly altered the native fish communities and allowed alien species to spread: invasive fish make up 8 per cent of the species in the upper reservoirs and 27 per cent in the Votkinsk Reservoir.

Which river is the tributary has long been disputed. At the confluence the Kama carries 4,100 cubic metres a second against the Volga's 3,500, its source lies at 331 metres against the Volga's 228, and its valley is held to be more ancient. The Volga, however, has the larger basin, 604,000 square kilometres against the Kama's 507,000.
kamakura: Kamakura is surrounded to the north, east and west by hills and to the south by the open water of Sagami Bay, which made it a natural fortress. Before tunnels and modern roads linked it to Fujisawa, Ōfuna and Zushi, it could be entered by land only through narrow artificial passes. The seven most important were called Kamakura's Seven Entrances. The name of the city is explained by the most likely theory as a comparison of this enclosed shape with a cooking hearth (kamado) and a warehouse (kura), both of which are open on one side only.

Traces of settlement in the area go back at least 10,000 years. In the Jōmon period the sea stood higher than now, and the flat land up to Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū lay under water, so the oldest pottery comes from hillside settlements dated between 7500 and 5000 BCE. The name appears in the Kojiki of 712, but the city enters the historical record clearly only with the founding of the Kamakura shogunate by Minamoto no Yoritomo. After his family had been almost wiped out by the Taira clan, he became the most powerful man in the land and set up the first military government in Japan, an institution that lasted 141 years.

The fall of the shogunate began the Muromachi period, an age of disorder. Kamakura declined slowly and, as capital of the Kantō region, dominated the east of the country for almost as long as the shogunate had lasted. In 1335 Hōjō Tokiyuki, son of the last regent Takatoki, tried to restore the shogunate by force and defeated Ashikaga Tadayoshi, Kamakura's de facto ruler. Ashikaga Takauji came from Kyoto to help his brother and defeated Tokiyuki at Koshigoe. Kamakura came out of this period almost completely destroyed. In the Edo period it became a popular destination for the townspeople of Edo, and after the Meiji Restoration its temples, beach and reputation made it popular again.

Kamakura is a city in Kanagawa Prefecture, designated as a city on 3 November 1939, with an estimated 172,929 inhabitants in 2020. Its monumental bronze statue of Amida Buddha at Kōtoku-in has stood outdoors since a 15th-century tsunami destroyed the temple that housed it. The city also has the Five Great Zen Temples and thousands of yagura, caves dug into the hillsides in the Middle Ages as tombs for high-ranking people and priests. The Great Kantō earthquake of 1923 devastated much of the city, and damaged temples and shrines have since been restored.
kamal-ud-din-behzad: Behzād was born and lived most of his life in Herat, in present-day western Afghanistan, the cultural and economic capital of the Timurid Empire. The year of his birth is unknown. According to the author Qadi Ahmad he was orphaned young and raised by the painter and calligrapher Mirak Naqqash, a director of the Timurid royal library. He was also a protégé of the vizier, poet and humanist Mir Ali-Shir Nava'i at the court of Sultan Husayn Bayqara, who ruled from 1469 to 1506.

Manuscripts made in the sultan's library in the 1480s show Behzād's participation. In 1486, by decree of Husayn Bayqara, he was appointed head of the royal ateliers in Herat in succession to Mirak Naqqash, and under his leadership the Herat academy reached its highest point. After the sultan's death in 1506, Herat was taken by troops of the Bukhara Khanate under Mohammed Shaybani Khan. A fable says that Shah Ismail I hid him in a cave during the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514.

In 1522 Shah Ismail I employed him at Tabriz, capital of the new Safavid Empire, as director of the royal atelier, calling him a miracle of the century in the decree. Ismail died in 1524, and Behzād's later work is usually associated with Shah Tahmasp I, in whose workshop he served until his death. His tomb lies at Herat beneath Kôh-i Mukhtâr.

Behzād is better understood as the director of a workshop producing manuscript illuminations in a style he conceived than as a lone painter. His compositions use geometric architecture and landscape, with unpatterned areas around which the figures are placed, and he used dark and light contrast more emphatically than other medieval miniaturists. His figures carry realistic gestures and expressions. His best-known works are The Seduction of Yusuf, from Sa'di's Bustan of 1488, and the paintings of the British Library's Nizami manuscript of 1494–95. Most works commonly attributed to him date from 1488 to 1495, and the attribution of individual paintings is often problematic. His fame led many to copy him, and rulers such as the Mughal emperors paid large sums for his paintings.
kamehameha-i: Kamehameha, known as Paiʻea at birth, was born to Kekuʻiapoiwa II, a niece of Alapainui, the ruler of Hawaii Island. By most accounts he was born at Ainakea in Kohala, and his father was Keōua. Sources place his birth anywhere between 1736 and 1761, and his father died while he was very young.

He was raised in the court of his uncle Kalaniʻōpuʻu. After Kalaniʻōpuʻu's death in 1782 the kingship passed to his son Kīwalaʻō, while Kamehameha became guardian of the war god Kūkaʻilimoku and received the Waipiʻo Valley. Chiefs of the Kona district backed Kamehameha, and Kīwalaʻō was defeated at the Battle of Mokuʻōhai.

Kamehameha bought guns and ammunition from British and American traders and was helped by two Westerners, Isaac Davis and John Young, who settled on Hawaii and married Hawaiian women. In 1790 his army invaded Maui while Kahekili II was on Oʻahu and, using cannon from the Fair American, defeated Kahekili's son Kalanikūpule at the Battle of Kepaniwai. When the Puʻukoholā Heiau was completed in 1791 he invited his rival Keōua Kūʻahuʻula to meet him. Keōua was struck down as he landed, and Kamehameha became king of Hawaii Island.

In 1795 he sailed with 960 war canoes and 10,000 soldiers, secured Maui and Molokaʻi at the Battle of Kawela and landed on Oʻahu. At Nuʻuanu his warriors captured the cannon on the Pali ridge, and over 700 of Kalanikūpule's men were driven over the cliff. A first attempt on Kauaʻi in 1796 lost many canoes in rough seas. In April 1810 he negotiated the peaceful unification of the islands with Kaumualiʻi of Kauaʻi, who remained a tributary king.

As ruler he unified the legal system and used tax products to promote trade with Europe and the United States. He proclaimed the Law of the Splintered Paddle: Let every elderly person, woman, and child lie by the roadside in safety.

After about 1812 he lived at Kamakahonu, a compound he built at Kailua-Kona. He died on 8 or 14 May 1819, and his friends Hoapili and Hoʻolulu hid his body according to the custom of hūnākele, because a person's mana was sacred. His burial place remains unknown. He had many wives, and only the children of his highest-ranking wife, Keōpūolani, succeeded him.
The holiday King Kamehameha I Day was first proclaimed in 1871 by his grandson, Kamehameha V. The state of Hawaii gave a statue of him to the National Statuary Hall Collection.
kamehameha-ii: Liholiho was born in November 1797 at Hilo on the island of Hawaiʻi, the first-born son of Kamehameha I and his high-ranking wife Keōpūolani. His mother's sickness had prevented the planned birth at the Kūkaniloko site on Oʻahu. After a few months with a servant of his father, he was taken back by his maternal grandmother and then placed in the care of Queen Kaʻahumanu, who became his official guardian. A Frenchman of about his age, Jean Baptiste Rives, taught the royal princes French and became a close friend. The name ʻIolani means royal hawk, after the Hawaiian hawk whose high flight signified royalty.

Liholiho inherited the throne on the death of Kamehameha I in May 1819, but Kaʻahumanu had no intention of giving him real leadership. Meeting him on the shore at Kailua-Kona wearing Kamehameha's red cape, she announced, We two shall rule the land. He took the title Kamehameha II, though he preferred to be called ʻIolani, and was left with a ceremonial role. Six months into his reign he ate a meal with Kaʻahumanu and his mother, breaking the kapu system in the ʻAi Noa. The priesthood was disbanded and temples and images were destroyed.

His cousin Kekuaokalani, to whom Kamehameha I had left his war god, demanded that the edicts be withdrawn, and at the Battle of Kuamoʻo the king's better-armed forces under Kalanimōkū defeated the last defenders of the old religion.

The first Christian missionaries arrived a few months later. Kamehameha II never converted, since he would not give up four of his five wives or his love of alcohol. He was known as impulsive: on 16 November 1820 he bought the royal yacht Cleopatra's Barge for 8,000 piculs of sandalwood, and in 1821 he ordered a small boat across the channel to Kauaʻi without compass, charts or provisions.

After his mother Keōpūolani died in September 1823, he resolved to visit London, against the advice of Kaʻahumanu and others. In November 1823 he and Queen Kamāmalu sailed on the whaling ship L'Aigle with Boki and other chiefs, and Rives as translator. They reached Portsmouth on 17 May 1824 and were received by a reception of 200 guests on 28 May. The Hawaiian party caught measles, to which they had no immunity, probably on a visit on 5 June. Kamāmalu died on 8 July 1824 and Kamehameha II on 14 July. The bodies were carried home on HMS Blonde, reaching Honolulu on 6 May 1825, and were later moved to the Royal Mausoleum at Mauna ʻAla. His younger brother Kauikeaouli succeeded him as Kamehameha III.
kamehameha-iii: Kauikeaouli was born at Keauhou Bay on Hawaiʻi island, the second son of Kamehameha I and his highest-ranking wife, Queen Keōpūolani, and he was of the highest kapu lineage. At birth he appeared stillborn, and Chief Kaikioʻewa had his prophet Kapihe declare that the baby would live; the child was laid on a rock, fanned, prayed over and sprinkled with water until he breathed and cried. The rock is preserved as a monument at Keauhou Bay. He was raised by Kaikioʻewa. His elder brother Liholiho ruled as Kamehameha II from 1819. Kauikeaouli was torn between the Puritan Christian rules imposed by his stepmother, the regent Kaʻahumanu, and a wish to honour the old traditions.

He came to the throne in 1825, under a regency at first, when the native population was about 150,000, already less than a third of what it had been when Captain Cook arrived in 1778. A series of epidemics halved it again during his reign. In 1838 the missionary William Richards became a political adviser and taught the king and his councillors the Western ideas of the rule of law. A declaration of rights followed in 1839, then the Edict of Toleration, under a French threat of war, which legalised Roman Catholicism, and the Constitution of 1840, Hawaii's first. A legislature and cabinet replaced the informal council of chiefs, and the Constitution of 1852 liberalised politics further.

In February 1843 the British captain Lord George Paulet pressured him into surrendering the kingdom, but the king alerted London, and Admiral Richard Thomas restored it on 31 July. He then said Ua Mau ke Ea o ka ʻĀina i ka Pono, the sovereignty of the land is perpetuated in righteousness. On 28 November Britain and France recognised Hawaiian independence. The Great Mahele of 1848 redistributed land among the government, the king, the nobles and the commoners, and allowed foreigners to own land outright for the first time; many commoners did not know of the programme and lost out. In 1849 a French force under Admiral Louis Tromelin sacked Honolulu.

In 1853 a smallpox epidemic caused thousands of deaths, mostly on Oʻahu. Calls for annexation to the United States grew, and a treaty was negotiated in August 1854 but never signed. He proclaimed neutrality in the Crimean War on 16 May 1854 and died suddenly on 15 December 1854, after a brief illness that may have been related to a stroke. His reign, of 29 years and 192 days, was the longest of the kingdom. His nephew and adopted son Alexander Liholiho succeeded him as Kamehameha IV, who said that Kamehameha III had given his people a constitution and fixed laws and secured their title to their lands.
kamenz: Kamenz, in Sorbian Kamjenc, lies in the west of the historic region of Upper Lusatia, about 40 kilometres north-east of Dresden and 30 kilometres north-west of Bautzen, on the Black Elster river between the West Lusatian Hills and the Lusatian Highlands. The town was built on greywacke and granite rocks that were mined there for centuries. On the Hutberg hill west of the centre a landscape park was laid out in 1893, known for its rhododendron and azalea collections, and the Lessing Tower was put up on the hilltop in 1864.

The settlement arose in the late 12th century around a fortress built to secure the junction of the medieval Via Regia trade route with the Black Elster. The route linked the Low Countries with Silesia. Records first mention the town in 1225, and it became an independent city in 1319, when Emperor Louis IV enfeoffed the West Lusatian lands to King John of Bohemia. In 1346 its citizens joined the Lusatian League for protection against robber barons and to keep the peace.

Hussite forces besieged and occupied it in 1429. In 1469 it passed with the League to King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary and in 1490 it returned to the Bohemian crown, under Vladislaus II, who had a Franciscan monastery founded north of the walls in 1493.

The citizens turned Protestant in 1536. In the Schmalkaldic War of 1546–47 the Upper Lusatian towns refused to support Ferdinand I against the Protestant princes and lost many privileges. By the Peace of Prague of 1635 the Lusatias passed to the Electorate of Saxony. Fires destroyed large parts of the old town in 1707 and again on 4 and 5 August 1842. From 1944 to 1945 a subcamp of the Gross-Rosen concentration camp stood in the town, where forced labourers worked for an aircraft-engine factory. After the war Kamenz was part of East Germany.

Kamenz is a town in the district of Bautzen in Saxony, Germany, and is known as the birthplace of the philosopher and poet Gotthold Ephraim Lessing (1729–1781); a Lessing Museum opened in 1931. Its sights include the Late Gothic St Mary's church, built from 1275 to 1479 and said to be the only church built from granite north of the Alps, and the St Anne abbey church, finished in 1510, which holds five carved wooden altarpieces of the 16th century. The Andreas Fountain on the marketplace dates from 1570.
kamianets-podilskyi: Kamianets-Podilskyi stands on the Smotrych River, 18 km from its confluence with the Dniester, in the Podolian Upland, whose elevated ridges known as Tovtry give the area a canyon-like relief. It is a historical centre of the Podillia region and served as capital of the Duchy of Podolia, the Podolian Voivodeship, the Podolia Eyalet, the Podolia Governorate and the Podolian District. The name means the Stone of Podilia, from the Old Slavic kamen, stone, and the region's name. Some historians hold that the ancient Dacians founded a settlement on the spot called Petridava or Klepidava.

The city is first mentioned in 1062, when it belonged to the principality of Terebovlia, and later to Halych and the Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia. About 1230 Prince Lev Danilovich invited Armenians to defend the eastern border and rewarded them with estates near the town. Mongol invaders destroyed it in 1241. Casimir III of Poland inherited it in 1352, and in 1374 Prince George Koriatovich granted it Magdeburg Law. It became the seat of a Latin Catholic diocese in 1378 and in 1434 the capital of the Podolian Voivodeship. Polish kings expanded the castle to defend Poland against Ottoman and Tatar invasions, so that it was called the gateway to Poland. Separate Ruthenian and Armenian courts worked in the city from the late 15th century.

The Ottomans and their ally the hetman Petro Doroshenko captured the city in 1672, and it became the capital of the Podolia Eyalet. The Ottomans expelled the Armenians in 1674. The population fell almost tenfold under Ottoman rule, which ended in 1699 when the Treaty of Karlowitz returned the city to Poland under Augustus II the Strong. In November 1757 Bishop Dembowski, at the instigation of the Frankists, ordered copies of the Talmud found in his bishopric confiscated and burned; accounts differ over whether up to a thousand copies or only one were destroyed.

After the Second Partition of Poland in 1793 the city belonged to the Russian Empire and was the capital of the Podolia Governorate. The fortifications were disbanded in 1808 and the fortress became a prison. The city was occupied by Austria-Hungary in 1915 and was the temporary capital of the Ukrainian People's Republic in 1919 to 1920. After the Ukrainian-Soviet War it formed part of Soviet Ukraine, and Kamianets-Podilskyi has been part of independent Ukraine since 24 August 1991.

The city had 96,896 inhabitants by a 2022 estimate. Poles, Jews and Ukrainians have dominated its population, with a substantial Armenian minority, and the city still has Polish, Ruthenian and Armenian market squares. Its landmarks include the castle, the Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul, the 14th-century Ruthenian Gate and the 15th-century Saint Nicholas Armenian Church.
kamien-pomorski: Kamień Pomorski lies on the Dziwna strait, where it forms the Kamieński Bay, on the Baltic coast of the West Pomeranian Voivodeship, about 63 km north of the regional capital Szczecin. The centre of the town is about 7 km from the Baltic Sea, to which it has direct access. Its name means Pomeranian Stone and is Slavic in origin. It is associated with a glacial boulder about 20 m across in the bed of the Dziwna, known as the Royal Boulder, which was used as a marker for ships and has been a protected natural monument since 1959. Local legends tell that Duke Bolesław III Wrymouth stood on it in 1121 to greet sailors, and give it other, supernatural origins.

The town was founded at the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries by the Lechitic Wolinians tribe and became part of Poland soon after Mieszko I created the state, around 967. A stronghold was probably built there in the 10th century, and the town is first mentioned in documents in 1124. After the fragmentation of Poland in the 12th century it belonged to the Duchy of Pomerania and was the duchy's first known capital. A bishopric was seated there in 1176, a mint was established in 1180, and the Dominicans were active in the town's religious life by 1228. It received Lübeck city rights in 1274.

Sweden acquired control of the town at the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, although it remained part of the Holy Roman Empire. It became part of the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701 and was administered within the Prussian Province of Pomerania. During the Second World War the Germans ran a forced labour subcamp of the Stalag II-D prisoner-of-war camp there. In 1945 the town returned to Poland under the border changes agreed at the Potsdam Conference. A hoard of early medieval jewellery was found in excavations in the town between 1959 and 1961.

Kamień Pomorski is a spa town and the seat of an urban-rural gmina in Kamień County. It is the second seat of the Archdiocese of Szczecin-Kamień. The Cathedral of St. John the Baptist is a local landmark and has been one of Poland's official national Historic Monuments since 1 September 2005. The town was the birthplace of Ewald Georg von Kleist, the jurist, cleric and physicist who invented the Leyden jar, and of the writer Uwe Johnson.
kamikaze: The Japanese word kamikaze is usually translated as divine wind, from kami, meaning god, spirit or divinity, and kaze, wind. It originated as a makurakotoba, a fixed epithet of waka poetry, modifying the place name Ise. Since August 1281 it has been used for the major typhoons that dispersed the Mongol-Koryo fleets that invaded Japan under Kublai Khan in 1274 and 1281.

The same characters can also be read shinpū, the Chinese-derived pronunciation. In 1937 a Japanese monoplane named Kamikaze made a record-breaking flight from Tokyo to London for the Asahi newspaper group; it was a prototype of the Mitsubishi Ki-15.

In 1944 and 1945 the word was attached to the Japanese special attack units, tokubetsu kōgekitai, whose aviators flew suicide attacks against Allied warships. The navy's air units were officially called shinpū tokubetsu kōgeki tai, divine wind special attack units. During the war itself the pronunciation kamikaze was used only informally in the Japanese press for these attacks; after the war it gained acceptance worldwide and was brought back into Japan.

The attacks began in October 1944, when Japan had lost several decisive battles and many of its best pilots, and no longer commanded the air or sea. The four subunits of the first Special Attack Force, Shikishima, Yamato, Asahi and Yamazakura, took their names from a poem by the classical scholar Motoori Norinaga on the Yamato spirit and mountain cherry blossom in the morning sun. Attacks reached a peak between April and June 1945 at the Battle of Okinawa.

About 3,800 kamikaze pilots died in the war, in attacks that killed more than 7,000 Allied naval personnel and sank several dozen warships; about 19 percent of attacks succeeded. Yet the attacks did not turn the tide: none sank a fleet carrier, cruiser or battleship at Okinawa, and the larger Allied fleet could send damaged ships home for repair. The pilots' training was harsh, with daily beatings recalled by survivors such as Daikichi Irokawa.

The pilots acted within a military culture that prized death over defeat or capture, and a schooling that since the Imperial Rescript on Education of 1890 had taught young Japanese that giving their lives for the state was the highest offering. Many hoped to be enshrined at Yasukuni as guardian spirits. Japanese cinema has returned to the subject repeatedly, from Saigo no Tokkōtai in 1970 to The Eternal Zero in 2013, and the word is now used generically for any attacking vehicle destroyed in its own attack.
kamose: Kamose was the last king of the Theban Seventeenth Dynasty, at the end of the Second Intermediate Period. His prenomen was Wadjkheperre. He was the son of Seqenenre Tao and the brother of Ahmose I, founder of the Eighteenth Dynasty. His mother is unknown but is thought to be Ahhotep I. His father had begun the war against the Hyksos and died fighting them. Originally the Theban rulers had been at peace with the Hyksos kingdom to the north, controlling Upper Egypt up to Elephantine and Middle Egypt as far north as Cusae.

Kamose's records on the Carnarvon Tablet, paralleled in his Theban stelae, report that his council doubted the wisdom of war. They argued that Egypt up to Cusae was loyal and tranquil, with cattle grazing in the Delta marshes. The king answered that he could not bear to sit between a chieftain in Avaris and another in Kush, each holding a slice of Egypt, and he vowed to save Egypt. The tablet says he went north by the command of Amun, but this is common to royal inscriptions and does not show a religious motive.

In his third year he sailed north from Thebes and reached Nefrusy, where Medjay troops overran a garrison loyal to the Hyksos. His second stela tells how his soldiers captured a courier carrying a message from the Hyksos king Apophis to the ruler of Kush, asking for support. Kamose ordered troops to occupy and destroy the Bahariya Oasis to guard his rear. His third year is the only attested date, but he campaigned against Nubia before and after it. Rock inscriptions at Arminna and Toshka name Kamose and Ahmose side by side, which suggests a coregency.

Kamose was buried modestly, in an ungilded coffin lacking a royal uraeus, which may imply that he died before his burial equipment was finished. His mummy was found in 1857 at Dra Abu el-Naga, hidden in a pile of debris, in a painted and stuccoed coffin. Buried with it were a gold and silver dagger, amulets, a scarab, a bronze mirror and a pectoral in the shape of a cartouche with the name of his successor and brother, Ahmose. The coffin remains in Egypt, the dagger is in Brussels and the pectoral and mirror are in the Louvre.
kampala: Kampala is a hilly place whose valleys are filled with sluggish rivers, lakes and swamps. The city proper covers 189 square kilometres, of which 13 are water. Its highest point is the summit of Kololo hill at 1,311 metres, in the centre of the city, and its lowest is the shore of Lake Victoria to the south at 1,135 metres. It lies on the East African Plateau between the two arms of the East African Rift and has a tropical rainforest climate with two wetter seasons.

The area of hills and swamps that became Kampala was part of the core of the highly centralised Kingdom of Buganda. Each Kabaka, on coronation or later in his reign, could set up his capital, the Kibuga, on a new hill, so the royal capital shifted. The first written description of the Kibuga was by the explorer Richard Burton in The Lake Region of East Africa, published in 1860, drawing on the information of an Arab trader. He described a settlement a day's journey long, with a palace at least a mile long and circular huts in a line, surrounded by a strong fence with four gates.

The name Kampala at first referred only to Old Kampala hill, where Fort Lugard stood. The hill had been a hunting reserve of the Kabaka, with several kinds of antelope, especially the impala, and the British officials who were allotted it called it the Hill of the Impala. In 1900 the regents of the infant Kabaka Daudi Cwa II signed the Buganda Agreement with Sir Harry Johnston for the British government. It created new forms of land tenure, among them freehold, Crown land and mailo, and divided the land in a way that came to shape the development of Kampala.

Kampala is the capital and largest city of Uganda, with a city proper of nearly two million people and a metropolitan area that includes the neighbouring districts of Wakiso, Mukono, Mpigi, Buikwe and Luweero. The city is the seat of the Buganda kingdom at Mengo. The Kasubi Tombs, burial ground of the Buganda kings, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Uganda Museum and the National Theatre are among its cultural institutions. A Bahá'í House of Worship, the Mother Temple of Africa, stands on Kikaya Hill on its outskirts.
kana: Old Japanese was written entirely in Chinese characters, and a set of them called man'yōgana was first used to represent the sounds of grammatical particles and morphemes. There was no consistent method, so one sound could be written with many characters; the Man'yōshū, an anthology assembled sometime after 759, uses as many as almost twenty for the mora ka. Hiragana developed from cursive man'yōgana, and katakana from abbreviated parts of regular-script man'yōgana, first as a system of glosses adding readings or explanations to Buddhist sutras. The shapes of many hiragana resemble Chinese cursive script, and those of many katakana the Korean gugyeol.

Kana is traditionally said to have been invented by the Buddhist priest Kūkai in the ninth century. He certainly brought the Siddhaṃ script of India home from China in 806, and his interest in the sacred aspects of speech led him to conclude that Japanese would be better written phonetically.

Each kana corresponds to one syllable or phoneme. Apart from the five vowels it is always a consonant followed by a vowel, with the single exception of the sign for the nasal n, which is usually romanised n. The limited number of Japanese phonemes and the rigid syllable structure make kana an accurate representation of the spoken language. Voiced consonants are written with the voicing mark dakuten, and p sounds with the half-voicing mark handakuten.

The name is a compound of kari, meaning borrowed, and na, name, and was used in contrast to mana, true name, the kanji used for their meaning. Hiragana was historically called women's script because it was used by women, while men, who were more educated, wrote phonetic kanji, called otokogana. Until the 18th century the script was seen from a Sinocentric view; the kokugaku movement then began to treat it as a national writing system distinct from Chinese characters.

Hiragana and katakana did not quickly supplant man'yōgana. The present set was codified only in 1900, and the older variants are called hentaigana. The spelling reforms of 1946 abolished the kana for wi, we and wo, keeping wo only as the accusative particle. Hiragana is the default script for native words, particles and inflections, while katakana is used for words of foreign origin, foreign names, onomatopoeia, emphasis and technical terms. Small kana written beside rarer kanji to show their pronunciation are called furigana, and are used widely in children's books.
kanagawa-prefecture: Kanagawa is a small prefecture at the south-eastern corner of the Kantō Plain, between Tokyo to the north, the foothills of Mount Fuji to the north-west, and Sagami Bay and Tokyo Bay to the south and east. It covers 2,415 square kilometres, and the Miura Peninsula separates the two bays. Topographically it has three areas: a mountainous west with the Tanzawa Mountain Range and the volcano Mount Hakone, a hilly east formed by the Tama Hills and the Miura Peninsula, and a central region of river terraces and low land along the Sagami, Sakai, Tsurumi and Tama rivers.

Archaeological sites go back to the Jōmon period. The imperial dynasty is believed to have ruled the area from the 5th century onward, though in ancient times its plains were sparsely inhabited. In medieval Japan it belonged to the provinces of Sagami and Musashi, and Kamakura in central Sagami was the seat of the Kamakura shogunate and the capital of Japan from 1185 to 1333. In the Edo period the daimyō of Odawara Castle governed western Sagami, while the Tokugawa shogunate in Edo governed the eastern part directly.

Commodore Matthew Perry landed in Kanagawa in 1853 and 1854 and signed the Convention of Kanagawa, which opened Japanese ports to the United States. Yokohama, the largest deep-water port in Tokyo Bay, was opened to foreign traders in 1859 and grew into the largest trading port in Japan. Yokosuka, nearer the mouth of the bay, developed as a naval port. The Meiji government built Japan's first railway, from Shinbashi in Tokyo to Yokohama, in 1872.

The Great Kantō earthquake of 1923 had its epicentre deep beneath Izu Ōshima in Sagami Bay. It devastated Yokohama and Tokyo; at Kamakura the dead from earthquake, tsunami and fire exceeded 2,000, and at Odawara ninety percent of the buildings collapsed at once. American bombing in 1945 heavily damaged Yokohama, Kawasaki and other cities. After the war General Douglas MacArthur, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, landed in Kanagawa. The prefecture's population was about 1.9 million in 1945 and grew rapidly as part of the Greater Tokyo Area.

Yokohama is the capital and largest city, with Kawasaki, Sagamihara and Fujisawa among the other major cities. Kanagawa has 9,221,129 inhabitants (1 April 2022), making it the second most populous prefecture in Japan, and became so in 2006. Kamakura and Hakone are popular destinations for visitors from Tokyo, and Fuji-Hakone-Izu National Park lies partly within the prefecture. Shin-Yokohama and Odawara stations are on the Tōkaidō Shinkansen.
kanak-people: The Kanak are the indigenous Melanesian inhabitants of New Caledonia in the south-western Pacific. They traditionally speak diverse Austronesian languages of the New Caledonian branch of Oceanic. Melanesian settlement on Grande Terre dates back at least to the Lapita culture, about 3000 BP, and obsidian from New Guinea was found with the earliest Lapita pottery there. Their origin is unclear.

The word Kanak derives from the Hawaiian kanaka maoli, 'ordinary person', which Europeans applied to Pacific islanders. Before European contact there were no unified states in New Caledonia and no single name for its people. In 1984 Melanesian leaders adopted the spelling Kanak in place of the colonial Canaque.

James Cook landed in 1774, when there were reportedly 70,000 Kanaks, and named the islands New Caledonia. French Catholics arrived in 1843, and France annexed the islands in 1853. Kanaks were used as forced labour on French plantations, ranches and public works, and moved to reserves covering only 10 per cent of their ancestral lands, their numbers having fallen sharply through disease. France sent 20,000 convicts between 1864 and 1897 and mined nickel from 1864 and copper from 1875. The Kanak revolt of 1878 was suppressed by the better-armed French; the Kanak leader was decapitated and his head displayed in the Museum of Natural History.

The United Nations listed New Caledonia as a non-self-governing territory in 1946, and Kanaks gained voting rights in 1951. The FLNKS was formed in 1984. The Ouvéa cave hostage taking ended with 21 deaths, 19 of them Kanaks. The Matignon Accord of 6 November 1988 proposed a referendum on independence; Jean-Marie Tjibaou, who signed it, was assassinated on 4 May 1989 by a Kanak activist. The Nouméa Accord of 5 May 1998 gave a degree of autonomy. Referendums in 2018, 2020 and 2021 rejected independence, the last boycotted by pro-independence Kanaks.

According to the 2019 census Kanaks make up 41.2 per cent of New Caledonia's population, about 112,000 people. The Jean-Marie Tjibaou Cultural Centre at Nouméa, formally established in May 1998, followed Tjibaou's proposal for an agency to develop Kanak culture. Wooden carvings of hawks, ancient gods, serpents and turtles are popular. Music, dance and song form part of ceremonies that cement relations within the clan and with ancestors.
kanazawa: Kanazawa lies in north-western Ishikawa Prefecture in the Hokuriku region, bordered by the Sea of Japan to the west and Toyama Prefecture to the east, between the Sai and Asano rivers. Its name means marsh of gold and is said to come from the legend of the peasant Imohori Togoro, who was digging potatoes when flakes of gold washed up. The area was originally known as Ishiura and was part of ancient Kaga Province.

During the Muromachi period Kaga Province came under the Ikkō-ikki, followers of the Jōdo Shinshū priest Rennyo, who displaced the Togashi clan and set up a theocratic republic later called the Peasants' Kingdom. Their stronghold, the Kanazawa Gobo, stood on the tip of the Kodatsuno Ridge, a natural fortress around which a castle town developed. In 1580 Oda Nobunaga sent Shibata Katsuie and his general Sakuma Morimasa to conquer the Ikkō-ikki. After Nobunaga's assassination in 1582 Maeda Toshiie displaced Morimasa and founded Kaga Domain. At Sekigahara in 1600 Maeda sided with Tokugawa Ieyasu and enlarged his holdings to 1.2 million koku, by far the largest domain under the shogunate. The Maeda ruled from Kanazawa Castle to the end of the Edo period.

The Maeda enlarged the castle and planned the surrounding castle town for defence. Before the Maeda the town had a population of only 5,000; by 1700 it exceeded 100,000, rivalling Rome, Amsterdam and Madrid, and reached about 120,000 in 1710. All samurai of Kaga, whatever their income, lived in Kanazawa, and by the late 17th century over three-quarters of the town was samurai housing.

The Maeda directed their wealth into arts and crafts rather than military pursuits, which helped ease the shogunate's suspicion of this Tozama daimyō. Toshitsune formed the Kaga Workmanship Office and promoted lacquer and gold-and-lacquer-work, and Maeda Tsunanori collected art and artisans from across the country. After the Meiji Restoration the modern city was created on 1 April 1889, with an area of 10.40 square kilometres that grew by annexation to 468.64.

Kanazawa is the capital of Ishikawa Prefecture, with an estimated 466,029 people in 2018. The Higashi Chaya District keeps geisha houses of the Edo period with plain two-storey wooden façades, and merchant houses were long and thin because houses were taxed on frontage width. Gold leaf is central to its crafts: Kanazawa produces 99% of Japan's high-quality gold leaf, which covered the Golden Pavilion in Kyoto, and its lacquerware is traditionally decorated with gold dust. The cultural landscape of its castle town has been designated an Important Cultural Landscape.
kanchanaburi: Kanchanaburi is a town municipality in Kanchanaburi Province, about 120 km west of Bangkok and south-east of Erawan National Park. It lies where the Khwae Noi and Khwae Yai rivers converge into the Mae Klong River, on the northern bank of the river. Its position at the edge of a mountain range keeps it much cooler than other provinces of central Thailand. It has a tropical savanna climate, with dry winters, a very hot April and a monsoon season that runs from May to October.

In the late 18th century King Rama I established Kanchanaburi as a defensive outpost against possible Burmese attacks, in what is now Lat Ya Sub-district. From the Ayutthaya period through the Thonburi and Rattanakosin periods it remained an important outpost against Burmese invasions. During the reign of King Rama III the town was moved about 16 km to the south-east, to its present site at the confluence of the two rivers. A royal decree of 25 March 1935 set out the area of the town's two subdistricts, Ban Nuea and Ban Tai.

In 1942 Kanchanaburi was under Japanese control. Asian forced labourers and Allied prisoners of war building the Burma Railway constructed a bridge here, an event later fictionalised in films including The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957). Almost half of the prisoners working on the project died from disease, maltreatment or accidents. There were four prisoner-of-war camps in or near the town, among them Tamarkan, a work camp used to build the bridge. When the railway was finished, most prisoners were concentrated in the Kanchanaburi area, and many were sent on to Japan or French Indo-China.

The town keeps a memorial and two museums to commemorate the dead of the railway: the Thailand–Burma Railway Centre, opened in March 2003, and the JEATH War Museum, which are devoted to the bridge and the Death Railway. The Kanchanaburi War Cemetery lies in the town, and the Chungkai War Cemetery is about 5 km away. Kanchanaburi is also the birthplace of the Buddhist monk Phrabhavanaviriyakhun and lies close to Wat Tham Phu Wa, a temple with grotto shrines in a limestone cave system.
kanchipuram: Kanchipuram lies about 72 km south-west of Chennai on the banks of the Vegavathi River, a tributary of the Palar River, on flat land that slopes to the south and east. The name is Tamil, from kanchi and puram, said to mean the city of kanchi flowers. The city has two divisions: Big Kanchi, or Shiva Kanchi, in the west, where most Shiva temples stand, and Little Kanchi, or Vishnu Kanchi, on the eastern fringe, where most Vishnu temples stand.

The earliest references are in the works of the grammarian Patanjali, who lived between the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE. Sangam literature of about 300 BCE mentions it. Whether it was an early Chola capital is contested: the historian P. T. Srinivasa Iyengar argued that Sangam Tamil culture did not spread through the district and pointed to the Sanskrit origin of the name. The Kalbhras ruled before the Pallavas, who made it their capital between the 4th and 9th centuries.

The Cholas did not make it their capital but kept a palace there, and the city grew eastwards. The Varadharaja Perumal Temple was renovated by the Cholas in 1053 and expanded under Kulottunga Chola I and Vikrama Chola. Raja Raja Chola I (985–1014) is said to have invited weavers from Saurashtra to settle, and more weavers came from Andhra Pradesh in the 15th century under Vijayanagara rule, when the population reached 25,000. The city was razed in the French siege of 1757.

Kanchipuram was a centre of learning, called the ghatikasthanam, or place of learning. Buddhism is believed to have flourished there between the 1st and 5th centuries; Buddhists such as Dignaga and Buddhaghosa are associated with it, and its institutions helped spread Theravada Buddhism to the Mon. It was also a major centre of Jainism, and the Pallava king Mahendra Varman I is said to have turned from Jainism to Hinduism under the influence of the Nayanmar Appar, after which Sanskrit gained prominence.

Hindus count it among the seven holiest cities, the Sapta Puri, which the Garuda Purana says give moksha. Fifteen of the 108 Vishnu temples praised in the Naalayira Divya Prabandham are there, and the city is important to Sri Vaishnavism, Shaktism and Shaivism. In 2021 India placed eleven of its temples, among them the Kailasanathar and Vaikunta Perumal temples, on its tentative list for World Heritage status.
kandahar: Kandahar lies between the Arghandab River and the Tarnak River at an elevation of about 1,010 metres. Its position on the main trade route linking South Asia with West Asia and Central Asia made it a frequent target of conquest. The climate is hot and semi-arid, with very dry summers and cool winters. Scholars derive the name probably from Gandhara: early Arab writers often gave Gandhara itself as Kandahar, and the geographer al-Ma'sudi held that Gandharians settled on the banks of the Arghastan and carried the name with them.

The region is one of the oldest known areas of settlement. Farming villages appeared in Afghanistan around 5000 BCE, and the site of Deh Morasi Ghundai lies 27 kilometres south-west of the city. Mundigak, established around 3000 BCE, served as the provincial capital of Arachosia. Alexander the Great founded what is now Old Kandahar in 330 BCE, near Mundigak, as Alexandria Arachosia. After a brief conflict in 305 BCE, Seleucus I ceded Arachosia to the Mauryas.

Arab armies began the conquest of the region in the 7th century; Abbad ibn Ziyad governed Sijistan from 673 to 681. In 870 Yaqub ibn Layth Saffari, a Saffarid ruler, made Islam the official religion of the area. The Ghaznavids later held the city, which appears to have been renamed Teginabad for a time. The chronicler Minhaj-i-Siraj attributed the fall of the Ghaznavids to their loss of Kandahar.

Mirwais Hotak, a chief of the Ghilji, killed the Safavid governor Gurgin Khan, an ethnic Georgian, and founded the Hotak dynasty in Kandahar. He is said to have resisted Persian attempts to convert the people from Sunni to Shia Islam. He died in November 1715 and was succeeded by his brother Abdul Aziz, who was killed by Mirwais's son Mahmud Hotak. In 1747 Ahmad Shah Durrani made Kandahar the capital of the Durrani Empire. The British occupied it briefly in the 19th century.

Kandahar is the capital of Kandahar Province and has an estimated 732,629 settled residents, most of them Pashtuns who speak Pashto. The municipality is divided into 15 city districts. Its economy rests on agriculture, trade and transport, and the surrounding region is known for grapes and pomegranates.

The Mausoleum of Ahmad Shah Durrani stands near the last surviving historical city gate. Opposite it is the Khirka Sharif, which holds a cloak attributed to Muhammad and is brought out only in times of great crisis. Mullah Omar displayed it in November 1996 to have himself declared Amir al-Mu'minin.
kanem-bornu-empire: The Kanem–Bornu Empire was based around Lake Chad and at various times ruled areas that are now parts of Nigeria, Niger, Cameroon, Libya, Algeria, Sudan and Chad. Its early history is poorly known. It is believed to have been founded around the year 700, though later and earlier dates have been proposed, in the lands between Lake Chad and the Bahr el Ghazal. The Duguwa dynasty ruled from the capital Njimi in Kanem and used the title mai. The empire was sustained by the trans-Saharan trade. The name Kanem–Bornu is a modern historians' name, an amalgamation of the empire's two central regions, and not a name the state used itself.

In the 11th century the empire converted to Islam and the Sayfawa dynasty replaced the Duguwa. The mai Dunama II Dibalemi brought it to its height in the 13th century. It controlled Saharan trade routes and exported salt, ivory, slaves and animal products. In the 14th century economic factors and conflict with the Bilala led to the loss of Kanem, and Umar I Idrismi re-centred the empire in Bornu. After a century of instability the mai Ali I Gaji founded Ngazargamu, around 1472, as a permanent capital. The empire reached its peak under Idris IV Alooma in the late 16th century and began a slow decline in the 17th.

The Fula jihads of the early 19th century nearly ended it and moved the centre of regional power west to the Sokoto Caliphate. The al-Kanemi dynasty, ruling as shehus, replaced the Sayfawa. In 1893 the Sudanese slave raider Rabih az-Zubayr defeated Bornu armies and took Kukawa, which was plundered and burned, its 120,000 to 200,000 inhabitants killed, enslaved or dispersed. The al-Kanemi dynasty was restored in 1900 under colonial suzerainty, and in 1902 the territories were absorbed into the French, British and German colonial empires.

The mai was variously equated to an emperor or a king, and after the conversion rulers were also called sultan and emir. Any son of a mai could succeed, which led to succession conflicts and civil wars, and hardly any mai was fully secure. Perhaps in the 13th century the empire moved to a feudal system with a class of princes and a large system of titles. The mai held audience from a wooden cage called the zanadir. All land belonged formally to the sovereign, who granted fiefs under the chima system to courtiers, princes, princesses and clerics. Most fiefs returned to the ruler at the holder's death. The Borno and Dikwa emirates in Nigeria survive as remnants of the regime.
kanesh: Kültepe, Turkish for ash-hill, lies about 20 km northeast of the modern city of Kayseri on the Central Anatolian plateau. The site has two parts: a circular mound, about 500 m across and some 20 m high, and a lower town to its northeast. The mound was inhabited, with breaks, from the Early Bronze Age through the Roman Empire, while the lower town was occupied only from the last decades of the third millennium BCE to the early sixteenth century BCE. Its ancient name appears as Kaneš in Assyrian inscriptions of the 20th and 19th centuries BCE and as Neša in later Hittite ones.

In the early second millennium BCE a kārum, the Assyrian word for a trading district, was established in the lower town. Local officials set it aside for Assyrian merchants, who could trade there without paying taxes as long as the goods stayed inside. Soldiers and merchants from Assyria lived there for hundreds of years, exchanging local tin and wool for luxury goods, foodstuffs, spices and woven fabrics from the Assyrian homeland and Elam.

It appears to have been the administrative and distribution centre of the whole network of Assyrian colonies in Anatolia, and the trade was run by families rather than the state. The kārum was destroyed by fire at the end of its two main levels, II and Ib, and its inhabitants left most of their possessions behind.

Local kings reigned at Kaneš in this period, among them Ḫurmili, Paḫanu, Inar and Waršama. Uḫna, king of Zalpuwa, raided the city and carried off its Šiuš idol. Pitḫana, king of Kuššara, then conquered Neša in the night, and his son Anitta made it his capital and recovered the idol. In the 17th century BCE Anitta's descendants moved their capital to Hattusa, founding the line of Hittite kings, and the Hittite language was called Nešili, the Neša tongue.

Over 22,000 cuneiform tablets have been recovered, mainly from the kārum, and only about forty from the mound. Written in Old Assyrian, they record trade between the colony and Assur and between merchants and local people, and they are the oldest documents from Anatolia. Their Hittite loanwords and names are the oldest record of any Indo-European language. The letters of women such as the businesswomen Zizizi and Taram-Kubi show their part in the trade. Ernest Chantre began excavating in 1893, Bedřich Hrozný found over 1,000 tablets in 1925, and Tahsin Özgüç led the Turkish excavations begun in 1948 until 2005. The site was placed on Turkey's tentative World Heritage list in 2014.
kangxi-emperor: The Kangxi Emperor was born on 4 May 1654 in the Forbidden City, Beijing, the third son of the Shunzhi Emperor, and was given the personal name Xuanye. He was enthroned on 7 February 1661 at the age of seven, though his era name Kangxi was first used on 18 February 1662. Four regents appointed by his father held actual power: Sonin, Suksaha, Ebilun and Oboi. After Sonin died, Oboi put Suksaha to death and became sole regent, an arrangement the young emperor and the court accepted for some years.

In 1673 three Ming generals who had aided the Qing, Wu Sangui, Geng Jingzhong and Shang Zhixin, controlled large fiefs in the south and west. Against the advice of most of his advisers, Kangxi tried to make them give up their lands, and the result was a rebellion lasting eight years. He relied mainly on Han Chinese Green Standard Army soldiers, granted clemency to common people caught up in the war, and won in 1681. In later years he blamed himself in part for the loss of life.

In 1683 Qing ships under Admiral Shi Lang defeated the Ming loyalist forces of the Kingdom of Tungning off Penghu, and Zheng Keshuang surrendered Taiwan. Border conflicts with the Tsardom of Russia on the Amur ended with the Treaty of Nerchinsk in 1689, which set a border between Russia and China. Against the Dzungar Khanate the emperor campaigned in person. In 1720 a larger expedition took Lhasa from the Dzungars, who had held it for three years.

At court Kangxi ordered the compilation of the Kangxi Dictionary, the Complete Tang Poems and the Complete Classics Collection of Ancient China, and persuaded scholars still loyal to the Ming to work on the dictionary without formally serving the Qing. He welcomed Jesuits such as Ferdinand Verbiest, who ran the imperial observatory, and in 1692 issued an Edict of Toleration for Catholicism. That tolerance ended with the Chinese Rites controversy.

The succession was disputed for years. His son Yinreng was named crown prince at the age of two, but was later deposed, and the princes quarrelled over the throne in what is known as the Nine Lords' War. Kangxi died on 20 December 1722 at the age of 68. According to official records he had summoned seven sons to his bedside, and the fourth prince, Yinzhen, became the Yongzheng Emperor. His reign of 61 years is the longest of any Chinese emperor, and began the High Qing era.
kanishka: Kanishka belonged to the Kushan dynasty and was a descendant of Kujula Kadphises, who founded the Kushan Empire. The Rabatak inscription lists his line: Kujula Kadphises was his great-grandfather, Vima Taktu his grandfather and Vima Kadphises his father. He was of Yuezhi ethnicity, and his native language was probably Tocharian.

Earlier scholars believed he took the throne in 78 CE and that this year began the Saka calendar era. Historians no longer regard it as the date of his accession, and Falk estimates that he came to the throne in 127 CE.

Kanishka's empire extended from southern Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, north of the Amu Darya, to northern India as far as Mathura, and it included Kashmir, where the town of Kanishkapur still contains the base of a large stupa. The Rabatak inscription claims that he held Pataliputra, and a Buddhist text known through a Chinese translation of 472 refers to his conquest of that city. His hold over Central Asia is less well established, although several of his coins have been found in the Tarim Basin.

Around 127 he replaced Greek with Bactrian as the official language of administration. His early coins carry Greek legends and Greek deities such as Helios and Selene, while later coins carry Bactrian legends and Iranian deities such as Mithra and Nana. Both are written in a modified Greek script with an extra letter for the sound sh.

Kanishka never converted to Buddhism but gave it royal sponsorship. Buddhist tradition says he presided over the 4th Buddhist Council in Kashmir, with Vasumitra and Ashwaghosha, and holds that he was close to the scholar Ashvaghosha. He encouraged both the Gandhara school of Greco-Buddhist art and the art of Mathura. His coins with Buddhist figures are rare, well under one percent of the total.

His chief Buddhist monument was the Kanishka Stupa at Puruṣapura, now Peshawar. Archaeologists who found its base in 1908 and 1909 estimated a diameter of 286 feet, or 87 metres, and Chinese pilgrims such as Xuanzang reported a height of 600 to 700 Chinese feet. The reliquary found beneath it is dated to the first year of his reign in 127 CE, though recent scholars attribute it to his successor Huvishka. Buddhist monks of Gandhara carried Mahayana teachings to China from the middle of the 2nd century, and the Kushan monk Lokaksema, about 178, became the first translator of Mahayana scriptures into Chinese.
kannada: Kannada, like Malayalam and Tamil, is a South Dravidian language and a descendant of Tamil-Kannada, from which it derives its grammar and core vocabulary. Its history is divided into Old Kannada, from 450 to 1200, Middle Kannada from 1200 to 1700, and Modern Kannada from 1700.
