From the start Charles favoured a third, Croatian, political entity beside Austria and Hungary, but the Hungarian Parliament vetoed the proposals. On 14 October 1918 he issued a People's Manifesto, and on 29 October the Croatian Sabor ended all ties with Hungary and Austria. On 11 November 1918 he issued a proclamation recognising the Austrian people's right to determine the form of the state and relinquishing every participation in the administration, although the word abdication was never used. He wrote privately that he had not abdicated and never would. In April 1919 the National Assembly dethroned the Habsburgs and banished him from German-Austria for life.

Charles went into exile in Switzerland and in 1921 made two attempts to reclaim the Hungarian throne, which failed largely because the regent, Admiral Miklós Horthy, refused his support. He was arrested and, on 19 November 1921, arrived at his last place of exile, the Portuguese island of Madeira, where he died of respiratory failure on 1 April 1922. Historians have been mixed in their judgements. Helmut Rumpler called him far too weak for the challenges facing him, while others see a brave and honourable man who tried to stop the war. The Catholic Church beatified him in 2004.
karl-kautsky: Karl Kautsky was born in Prague on 16 October 1854. His father Johann was a Czech theatrical scene designer and his mother Minna Jaich an actress and writer, and the family moved to Vienna in 1863. After a year at the Melk seminary, which he found oppressive, he attended the Academic Gymnasium in Vienna from 1866 to 1874, a mediocre student whose interests ran to the Paris Commune and to history and philosophy. For two years from 1868 he considered himself a Czech nationalist. At about twenty he joined the Austrian Social Democratic Workers' Party in January 1875, and he became a Marxist in the early 1880s while in exile in Zurich.

In 1883 Kautsky founded Die Neue Zeit, which he edited until 1917 and which became the most prestigious international Marxist journal. From 1885 to 1890 he lived mainly in London and became a close friend of Friedrich Engels. After the Anti-Socialist Laws lapsed he wrote the theoretical section of the SPD's Erfurt Program of 1891, with Eduard Bernstein writing the short-term demands. From 1896 he defended orthodoxy against Bernstein's revisionism.

In August 1914 he urged the SPD's parliamentary group to abstain on war credits, and when it voted for them he broke with the party and in 1917 co-founded the Independent Social Democratic Party of Germany. After the revolution of 1918 to 1919 he chaired the Socialization Commission, and he criticised the Bolsheviks in The Dictatorship of the Proletariat (1918). He rejoined the SPD in 1922, drafted its Heidelberg Program in 1925 and moved to Vienna in 1924. He fled to Amsterdam after the Anschluss of 1938 and died there on 17 October 1938.

Kautsky held that a socialist revolution was inevitable but could not be forced, and that a socialist party should organise workers and win reforms within parliamentary democracy until conditions were ripe. After the Russian Revolution of 1905 he took a centrist position between reformism and radicalism, and he opposed the council system in 1918 as undemocratic. He also tried to join Marxism with Darwin, arguing that humanity inherited communist instincts of solidarity from its animal ancestors. Leszek Kołakowski called him the chief architect and embodiment of Marxist orthodoxy, and he was known in his time as the Pope of Marxism.
karl-marx: Karl Marx was born on 5 May 1818 to Heinrich Marx and Henriette Pressburg at Brückengasse 664 in Trier, then part of the Kingdom of Prussia. His family was originally Jewish but had converted to Christianity before his birth. His father, a lawyer, had converted to the state Evangelical Church of Prussia to keep his career after Prussia annexed the Rhineland and Jewish emancipation was abrogated. Heinrich was a man of the Enlightenment and a classical liberal who took part in agitation for a constitution and reforms.

Marx was the third of nine children and became the eldest son when his brother Moritz died in 1819. He was baptised into the Lutheran Church on 28 August 1824. His father educated him privately until 1830, when he entered the Gymnasium zu Trier. Its headmaster, Hugo Wyttenbach, employed many liberal humanists, and in 1832 police raided the school and found literature promoting political liberalism among the students. Marx earned a doctoral degree in philosophy from the University of Jena in 1841, then turned to radical journalism.

In Paris Marx wrote his Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and began a close collaboration with Friedrich Engels. After moving to Brussels they were active in the Communist League. In London Marx wrote the Grundrisse notebooks and the three volumes of Das Kapital, the second and third of which Engels published after his death, in 1885 and 1894. He became a leading figure in the International Workingmen's Association, and in 1875 wrote the Critique of the Gotha Programme.

His thought drew on Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel's dialectic, on the classical political economy of Adam Smith and David Ricardo, and on French socialist thought. Unlike Hegel, who saw spirit driving history, Marx argued for the primacy of matter over idea. He held that societies develop through class conflict, in capitalism between the bourgeoisie who control the means of production and the proletariat who sell their labour power for wages, and he criticised utopian socialists for relying on small-scale communities.

Marx died on 14 March 1883 and was buried in Highgate Cemetery. His ideas had a profound impact on world politics after the Russian Revolution of 1917. His followers have often disagreed over how to interpret him, and tendencies including Leninism, Marxism–Leninism, Trotskyism, Maoism and Luxemburgism each claim to be his most accurate interpreter. In scholarship his work contributed to the birth of modern sociology, and Isaiah Berlin considered him the true founder of the discipline in so far as anyone can claim the title.
karl-philipp-prince-of-schwarzenberg: Karl Philipp was born on 18 or 19 April 1771 in Vienna, one of thirteen children of Johann Nepomuk Anton of Schwarzenberg and Marie Eleonore, Countess of Öttingen-Wallerstein; seven of the children did not reach adulthood. The family held land in Franconia and Bohemia and was close to the House of Habsburg, and in 1788 he entered the Austrian army as a lieutenant. In 1789 he fought against the Ottoman Empire in the Austro-Turkish War, and he became a major in 1792.

In the French Revolutionary War Schwarzenberg served in the advance guard of Prince Josias of Coburg in 1793. At Le Cateau-Cambrésis in 1794 his charge at the head of his regiment, supported by twelve British squadrons, broke a French corps of around 25,000 men and captured 32 guns, and he was decorated with the Knight's Cross of the Military Order of Maria Theresa. He became a general-major in 1796 and a Generalleutnant in 1799. In 1809 he led a cavalry division at the Battle of Wagram, which the Austrians lost.

In 1812, after the Treaty of Paris made Austria an ally of France, he took an Austrian corps of around 30,000 men to the Grande Armée for the invasion of Russia, trying to satisfy Napoleon without angering Russia. His troops won at Gorodetschna and Wolkowisk, and in late November withdrew into winter quarters at Bialystok under a verbal agreement with the Russians. Of the 30,000, 7,000 were killed in battle and another 4,000 died of disease and exposure. When Austria joined the Sixth Coalition in 1813 he became commander-in-chief of the allied Army of Bohemia, about 230,000 men. His army was mauled at Dresden on 26 and 27 August, but beat pursuing French forces at the Second Battle of Kulm on 17 September.

At the Battle of Leipzig on 16 to 18 October 1813 Schwarzenberg directed the allied army with Emperor Alexander I of Russia and Emperor Francis of Austria. In 1814 he invaded France through Switzerland, won at Bar-sur-Aube on 27 February, repelled Napoleon at Arcis-sur-Aube on 20 and 21 March and won at Fère-Champenoise on 30 March. Paris was captured on 31 March, and Napoleon abdicated at Fontainebleau on 11 April. Schwarzenberg's health declined afterwards: a stroke disabled him in 1817, and a second struck him at Leipzig, where he died on 15 October 1820. Austria held three days of mourning. Alexander I said that Europe had lost a hero and he a friend.
karl-polanyi: Karl Polanyi was born in Vienna on 25 October 1886 and raised in Budapest by a Jewish family that spoke German and was assimilating into the secular middle class. His father, Mihály Pollacsek, was a railway entrepreneur; his younger brother was the philosopher Michael Polanyi. He studied law at the University of Budapest, came under the influence of the legal philosopher Gyula Pikler, and in 1908 became the first president of the freethinking Galileo Circle. He took a doctorate in law at Kolozsvár in 1909 and was called to the bar in 1912. In June 1914 he helped Oszkár Jászi found the National Citizens' Radical Party and became its secretary.

Polanyi served as a second lieutenant in the Austro-Hungarian cavalry on the Russian Front until he was hospitalised in 1917. He supported the republican government of Mihály Károlyi, left Hungary for Vienna in 1919 and did not return after Admiral Horthy's regime took power. From 1924 to 1933 he was a senior editor of the magazine Der Österreichische Volkswirt, where he began to criticise the Austrian school of economics. He married the communist revolutionary Ilona Duczyńska, and their daughter Kari Polanyi Levitt also became an economist.

After Hitler's accession in January 1933 the magazine's liberal publisher could not keep a prominent socialist, and Polanyi moved to London. He worked as a journalist and tutor and from 1936 as a lecturer for the Workers' Educational Association, but never found a post at a British university. In 1940 he joined Bennington College in Vermont, and from 1947 to 1953 he taught at Columbia University. His wife could not obtain a United States visa because she had been a communist, so they lived in Canada and he commuted to New York. He died at Pickering, Ontario, in 1964.

His best-known book, The Great Transformation (1944), questions whether a self-regulating market is a sound idea. It describes the enclosure process in England and the making of the modern economic system early in the 19th century, and holds that market societies in modern Europe were not inevitable but historically contingent. He called the interplay of marketisation and the push for social protection against it the Double Movement.

Polanyi is remembered as the originator of substantivism, which stresses that economies are embedded in society and culture. With a grant from the Ford Foundation he studied the economies of ancient empires, and his Columbia seminar led to Trade and Market in the Early Empires (1957). His Dahomey and the Slave Trade: An Analysis of an Archaic Economy appeared in 1966. His approach has been applied to Pre-Columbian America and ancient Mesopotamia, though its usefulness for ancient societies in general has been questioned.
karl-renner: Karl Renner was born on 14 December 1870, the 18th child of a poor ethnic German family of wine-growers in Unter-Tannowitz, now Dolní Dunajovice in the Czech Republic, then part of the Margraviate of Moravia. Because of his intelligence he attended a selective gymnasium at nearby Nikolsburg, and from 1890 to 1896 he studied law at the University of Vienna. In 1895 he was one of the founders of the Friends of Nature organisation and designed its logo.

Renner joined the Social Democratic Workers' Party of Austria in 1896 and sat in the Reichsrat from 1907 until its dissolution in November 1918. With Otto Bauer and Adolf Braun he founded and edited the party's journal Der Kampf, and he published his ideas under pseudonyms to protect his post as the Reichsrat's librarian. He was counted a leader of Austro-Marxism, and his book of 1904 on the social function of private law made him one of the founders of the sociology of law.

In 1918 he became the first State Chancellor of the Republic of German-Austria, a post he held until 1920. Like other Austrian socialists he favoured union with Germany, but the Entente forbade it, and at St Germain he had to accept the loss of South Tyrol and of the German-speaking parts of Bohemia and Moravia. He was President of the National Council from 1931 to 1933. After the party was banned in 1934 he welcomed the Anschluss of 1938, and on 2 April 1938 he appealed to Austrians to vote yes in the plebiscite. His offer to serve the Nazi government was declined.

On 3 April 1945, as Soviet troops advanced on Vienna, Renner made contact with them. On 20 April the Soviets told him to form a provisional government, which took office seven days later, declared Austria independent of Nazi Germany and called for a democratic state on the lines of the First Republic. Communists held a third of the posts, and the Western Allies did not at first recognise it. The Federal Assembly elected Renner president on 20 November 1945. He died in Vienna on 31 December 1950. He is often called the Father of the Republics. The survivor Marko Feingold, head of the Salzburg Jewish community, said in 2013 that Renner had long been known in his party as an antisemite.
karlis-ulmanis: Kārlis Ulmanis was born on 4 September 1877 into a prosperous farming family. He studied agriculture at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich and at Leipzig University, then worked in Latvia as a writer, lecturer and manager in agricultural posts. He was politically active in the 1905 Revolution and was briefly imprisoned in Pskov before fleeing to avoid arrest by the Russian authorities. In exile he studied at the University of Nebraska under the name Karl August Ulmann, took a degree in agriculture and lectured there before buying a dairy business in Houston, Texas, which ran into financial difficulties. He returned to Latvia in 1913 after a general amnesty declared by Nicholas II.

Late in the First World War Ulmanis founded the Latvian Farmers' Union, one of the two most prominent parties of the country. He was a principal founder of the People's Council, which proclaimed Latvian independence on 18 November 1918, and he became prime minister of the first provisional government. After the War of Independence of 1919 to 1920 a constitutional convention made Latvia a parliamentary democracy. Ulmanis served as prime minister on three occasions between 1918 and 1931.

He formed a fourth government in March 1934. On the night of 15 to 16 May 1934, with the support of the Minister of War Jānis Balodis, he proclaimed a state of war and dissolved all political parties and the Saeima. The coup was bloodless and was carried out by the Aizsargi national guard and army units loyal to him. About 2,000 Social Democrats were at first detained, along with members of right-wing groups such as Pērkonkrusts. In 1936 he combined the offices of president and prime minister, though the constitution said otherwise. His was a non-party, personal dictatorship, with censorship, a corporate organisation of the economy and a policy of Latvianisation in education and business that reduced the influence of minorities.

After the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact of August 1939 placed Latvia in the Soviet sphere, Ulmanis signed a mutual assistance treaty in October and allowed Soviet bases. When the Soviet Union occupied Latvia on 17 June 1940 he ordered no resistance. He was forced to resign as president on 21 July 1940, was arrested and was sent to Stavropol, where he worked as an agronomist for a year. Imprisoned in July 1941, he was evacuated in 1942 to Krasnovodsk and died of dysentery on 20 September 1942. His burial place is unknown.

Opinions on his rule diverge. The Soviet régime called him a fascist, many exiles saw his years as a golden age, and historians generally agree on his positive early role as prime minister. His grand-nephew Guntis Ulmanis was elected President of Latvia in 1993.
karlovac: Karlovac lies in central Croatia, 56 kilometres south-west of Zagreb and 130 km north-east of Rijeka. Four rivers give it the name grad na četiri rijeke, the town on four rivers: the Kupa, Korana and Mrežnica flow through the built-up area, and the Dobra a few kilometres outside the centre. Croatians also call it grad parkova, the city of parks. Most of the parks are planted in the former trenches dug around the old fort, and one part of the centre keeps the name Šanac, trench.

The Austrians built Karlovac from scratch in 1579 to strengthen their southern defences against the Ottomans. It was part of a bargain between the Protestant nobility of Inner Austria and Archduke Charles II: in return for religious freedom the nobles agreed to pay for a new fortress. It was a six-pointed star on the Zrinski estate near the old town of Dubovac, begun on 13 July 1579 under the architect Matija Gambon. It was built on terrain exposed to flooding and unhealthy water, deliberately, to hamper the Turkish advance. A fire in 1594 burned all its buildings, and they were rebuilt by 1610.

As an outpost of the Habsburg monarchy, Karlovac was one of the first headquarters of the general command of the Military Frontier. The Uskok leader Ivan Vlatković, whose raids and piracy troubled the Habsburgs, was executed there on 3 July 1612. Ottoman forces besieged the city seven times, the last in 1672, and never took it. After the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 it lost its military importance and became a market for wheat, corn, salt, timber and tobacco.

Maria Theresa founded the Gymnasium in 1766. A plague in 1773 killed almost half the population. In 1776 she restored the city to the Croatian crownland, and in 1781 Joseph II confirmed it as a free royal town. It flourished on its roads to the sea and its river traffic until the railway of 1861 ended its era as a major trade centre.

Karlovac is the administrative centre of Karlovac County; its population was 49,377 at the 2021 census. The star shape of the old fortress can still be seen around the centre. The city suffered damage in the Croatian War of Independence of 1991 to 1995, and a former Austrian barracks at Turanj now holds a museum of its military history. Its music school, founded on 1 December 1804, is one of the oldest in this part of Europe.
karlskirche: In 1713, a year after the last major plague epidemic in Vienna, Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, pledged to build a church dedicated to his namesake patron saint, Charles Borromeo, who was revered as a healer of plague sufferers and was a leading figure of the Counter-Reformation. An architectural competition was announced, which Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach won over competitors including Ferdinando Galli-Bibiena and Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt. Construction began in 1716 under the supervision of Anton Erhard Martinelli. After the elder Fischer's death in 1723, his son Joseph Emanuel Fischer von Erlach completed the building in 1737 with modifications to the original plans.

The church stands on the Karlsplatz, on the border of Wieden and the Innere Stadt. The elder Fischer united very different elements. The façade leading to the porch corresponds to a Greek temple portico, and the two flanking columns, made by Lorenzo Mattielli, were inspired by Trajan's Column in Rome. Beside them, two tower pavilions show the influence of Roman Baroque architects such as Bernini and Borromini. A dome rises above a high drum, which the younger Fischer shortened and partly altered. The church originally had a direct line of sight to the Hofburg and was the imperial patron parish church until 1918.

The programme of images came from the imperial official Carl Gustav Heraeus and ties Saint Charles Borromeo to his imperial benefactor. The pediment relief shows the cardinal virtues, with the patron saint at its apex. The columns carry spiral reliefs of scenes from the saint's life, and are meant to recall Boaz and Jachim, the two columns before the Temple at Jerusalem, as well as the Pillars of Hercules and symbols of imperial power. Inside, the dome fresco by Johann Michael Rottmayr and Gaetano Fanti shows the intercession of Charles Borromeo, supported by the Virgin Mary.

The high altarpiece of the saint's ascension was conceived by the elder Fischer and executed by Ferdinand Maxmilian Brokoff, and side chapels hold altar paintings by Daniel Gran, Sebastiano Ricci, Martino Altomonte and Jakob van Schuppen. The church is considered the elder Fischer's major work and an expression of the Austrian joie de vivre that followed the victorious end of the Turkish Wars.

The neighbouring Spitaler Gottesacker cemetery was the burial place of Antonio Vivaldi on 28 July 1741, although his grave has been lost, and the church holds regular Vivaldi concerts in his honour. Hedy Lamarr married Friedrich Mandl in its chapel on 10 August 1933. Since the restoration of the Karlsplatz as an architectural ensemble in the late 1980s the church has drawn attention for its dome and columns. It is cared for by the Knights of the Cross with the Red Star.
karlsruhe: Karlsruhe lies on the right bank of the Upper Rhine, near the French border, between the Mannheim-Ludwigshafen conurbation to the north and Strasbourg to the south. It stands almost wholly on the Upper Rhine Plain, with the Turmberg to the east and the borders of the Kraichgau, which leads to the northern Black Forest. Its climate is oceanic and its winters are milder than those of most German cities.

According to legend, the name Karlsruhe, meaning Charles's repose or Charles's peace, was given when Margrave Charles III William of Baden-Durlach woke from a dream in which he saw himself founding a new city, after a hunting trip. A variation says that he built the new palace to find peace from his wife. The palace was built in 1715, and a settlement grew around it, for which a mayor was appointed from 1718. From 1812 the mayors bore the title of Lord Mayor.

Karlsruhe was the capital of the Margraviate of Baden-Durlach from 1718 to 1771, of the Margraviate of Baden from 1771 to 1803, of the Electorate of Baden from 1803 to 1806, of the Grand Duchy of Baden from 1806 to 1918 and of the Republic of Baden from 1918 to 1945. It became a major city in the 19th century.

Jews settled there soon after its founding, attracted by the privileges the founder offered to settlers without distinction of creed, and several Jewish families are recorded in 1717. On 9 to 10 November 1938 one synagogue was burned and another damaged, and deportations began on 22 October 1940, when 893 Jews were sent to the Gurs camp in France. Of the 1,280 Jews deported directly from Karlsruhe, 1,175 perished. A new community formed after the war and built a synagogue in 1971.

After the Second World War the provinces of Baden and Württemberg were merged, and Stuttgart became the capital of the new state. In compensation Karlsruhe applied to become the seat of the highest courts.

Karlsruhe is the third-largest city of Baden-Württemberg, with about 310,000 inhabitants, and the seat of the Federal Constitutional Court and the Federal Court of Justice. The palace houses the Baden State Museum. The Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, which grew from the University of Karlsruhe, is the oldest technical university in Germany, and the Centre for Art and Media (ZKM) opened in a former weapons factory in 1999.
karlstad: Karlstad is built on the delta where Klarälven, Sweden's longest river, runs into Vänern, Sweden's largest lake. It has the second largest lake port in the country after Västerås. The city is reputed to be one of the sunniest in Sweden, and a statue commemorates a local waitress known as Sola i Karlstad, the Sun in Karlstad, for her sunny disposition. On the largest islet there was a place of counsel called Tingvalla in the medieval age, with roots in the Viking Age before 1000, which was also used as a market place.

The Swedish Duke Charles, later King Charles IX, granted Karlstad its city charter on 5 March 1584, and the city's name means Charles' city. He also gave it the right to be the governmental seat of the region and a substantial amount of land. The duke built his own house in the city, the Kungsgården, on the site where Christian Haller built the cathedral in 1724 to 1730.

The most significant coup d'état in modern Swedish history began in Karlstad. During the night of 7 March 1809 Major General Georg Adlersparre used part of the western army stationed in Värmland to occupy the city, from which his force proclaimed a revolution. On 9 March he and his soldiers began their march towards the capital to end the reign of King Gustav IV Adolf. Karlstad suffered four major fires, and after the last, on 2 July 1865, only the cathedral and a few houses remained.

It was rebuilt on a grid pattern with wide streets lined with trees. A small Jewish community formed in the 1800s and built a synagogue in 1899, which was demolished in 1961. In 1905 the agreement to dissolve the union between Norway and Sweden was negotiated and signed in Karlstad.

Karlstad is the capital of Värmland County and the largest city in the province of Värmland, with 67,122 inhabitants in the city proper in 2020. It has a cathedral and Karlstad University, which was granted university status in 1999. The cathedral and the grid of the rebuilt centre recall the fire of 1865.
karlstejn-castle: Work on Karlštejn began in 1348 under King Charles IV, who as Holy Roman Emperor personally supervised the construction and the interior decoration. The works were directed by Vitus of Bítov, later the castle's burgrave, but no records name the builder. Some historians have speculated that Matthias of Arras was the architect, though he died in 1352. The project was finished nearly twenty years later, in 1365, when the Chapel of the Holy Cross in the great tower, regarded as the heart of the treasury, was consecrated. The village that grew up during the building took the castle's name and later changed it more than once.

The castle stands on a promontory of the hill Kněží Hora above the Berounka river, about 30 kilometres south-west of Prague. Its core is built in three parts on terraces: the imperial palace on the lowest, the Marian tower above it and the great tower highest of all. The palace is about 12.5 metres wide and 46 metres long. The emperor lived on its second floor and the empress with her retinue on the third. The great tower is 60 metres high, with walls between 4 and 7.5 metres thick, and it is fortified separately. The well tower was the first part to be built, and an underground channel brought in water from a nearby stream.

The Chapel of the Holy Cross held valuable state documents with the symbols of state power, the Imperial Regalia and later the Bohemian Crown Jewels. When the Hussite Wars broke out the Imperial Regalia were taken away in 1421 and brought via Hungary to Nuremberg. In 1422 Hussite attackers besieged the castle, and Prince Sigismund Korybut had catapults hurl dead bodies and 2,000 carriage-loads of dung over the walls, apparently spreading infection among the defenders. The Bohemian crown jewels were later returned and kept there for almost two centuries.

The castle was rebuilt in late Gothic style after 1480 and in Renaissance style in the last quarter of the 16th century, and a fire damaged the great tower in 1487. In 1619, during the Thirty Years' War, the coronation jewels and the archive were taken to Prague, and in 1620 the castle was handed to Ferdinand II. Swedish forces captured it in 1648, after which it fell into disrepair. Josef Mocker carried out a Gothic Revival reconstruction between 1887 and 1899, which gave the castle its present look.
karluks: The Karluks were a nomadic Turkic tribal confederacy living around the Black Irtysh and the Tarbagatai Mountains, west of the Altay, between about the 5th and 8th centuries. The first Chinese reference to them, in 644, calls them the Lion Karluks. Three member tribes of the Göktürk Khaganate formed the Uch-Karluk, or Three Karluks, union, whose leader first held the title Elteber and later Yabgu. After the khaganate split around 600, the union became subordinate to the Western Turkic Khaganate. In 650, at the time of their submission to the Chinese, they had three tribes, and by 665 a Yabgu with a powerful army led the union.

In the 8th century the Karluks rose against the Göktürks and formed a new confederation with the Uyghurs and the Basmyls. They remained within the Chinese sphere of influence until the Battle of Talas in 751, when the Arab general Ziyad ibn Salih defeated the Chinese. In 766, after overrunning the Türgesh in Jetisu, they formed a khanate under a Yabghu and moved their capital to Suyab. The Karluk Yabgu state sat on the trade route to China, and its ruler profited from the slave markets of the Syr Darya, selling guards to the Abbasid caliphs.

Karluk independence ended around 840, when the Kyrgyz, who had allied with them against the Uyghurs, took part of Jetisu. Several Muslim historians say that supreme authority among the Turkic tribes then passed to the Karluk leaders, who took the title Khagan. The Kara-Khanid Khanate grew out of a confederation of Karluks, Chigils, Yagmas and other tribes, and the Kara-Khitans later ruled the region from about 1130. In 1211 Arslan Khan Karluk killed the Kara-Khitan governor of Kayalik and declared loyalty to Genghis Khan.

The Karluks were hunters, nomadic herdsmen and farmers, living in the countryside and in towns built around trading posts on the caravan roads. The Karluk Yabghu state was an association of semi-independent districts and cities, each with its own militia; the capital, Suyab, could field 20,000 warriors. Most Karluks first followed Tengrianism. They converted to Nestorian Christianity at the end of the 8th century, and a Karluk yabghu is reported to have become Muslim under Caliph Mahdi. They were the most open of the Turkic peoples to Muslim culture. The Karluk language became the basis of the later Chagatai language, and most Uzbeks and Uyghurs descend from Karluk tribes.
karnak: The Karnak Temple Complex is a mixture of temples, pylons, chapels and other buildings near Luxor. The ancient Egyptians called the area Ipet-isut, the Most Select of Places, and it was the main place of worship of the Theban Triad of the 18th Dynasty, headed by the god Amun. The complex has four main parts: the Precinct of Amun-Re, the largest, the Precinct of Mut, the Precinct of Montu and the dismantled Temple of Amenhotep IV. Its distinctive feature is the length of time over which it was built and used. About thirty pharaohs contributed to it, from Senusret I in the Middle Kingdom into the Ptolemaic Kingdom, although most surviving buildings date from the New Kingdom.

Major building in the Precinct of Amun-Re took place in the Eighteenth Dynasty, when Thebes became the capital of the unified country. Thutmose I raised an enclosure wall between the Fourth and Fifth pylons, the earliest part still standing in place. Hatshepsut restored the Precinct of Mut and erected twin obelisks at the temple entrance; one still stands, the second-tallest ancient obelisk standing anywhere. She also built the Red Chapel, intended as a barque shrine.

The Great Hypostyle Hall, begun perhaps in the Eighteenth Dynasty, was mostly built under Seti I and Ramesses II. It covers 5,000 square metres and has 134 columns in 16 rows. Merneptah recorded his victories over the Sea Peoples on the walls of the Cachette Court. Amenhotep IV, Akhenaten, built a temple east of the main complex that was destroyed immediately after his death, so thoroughly that its layout is unknown. Nectanebo I of the Thirtieth Dynasty added the First Pylon and the massive enclosure walls. By the 4th century CE Karnak was mostly abandoned, and Christian churches were founded among the ruins.

In medieval Europe the exact place of Thebes was unknown. The first European description of the complex was by an unknown Venetian in 1589, and the name Karnak is first attested in 1668, when the Capuchin brothers Protais and Charles François d'Orléans travelled through the area. The first drawing is in Paul Lucas's account of 1704. Scientists of the Napoleon expedition, among them Vivant Denon, described it in 1798 and 1799. Karnak was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979 with the rest of Thebes.
karnataka: Karnataka lies on the south-western coast of India, bordered by the Lakshadweep Sea to the west and by Goa, Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kerala. It has three principal zones: the coastal region of Karavali and Tulu Nadu, the hilly Malenadu region of the Western Ghats, and the Bayaluseeme plains of the Deccan Plateau, where most of the state lies. Its two main river systems are the Krishna and its tributaries in the north and the Kaveri and its tributaries in the south. Most rivers flow east to the Bay of Bengal, while the Sharavati and Netravati flow west.

The name is generally derived from the Kannada words karu and nādu, meaning elevated land. It may also be read as black region, after the black cotton soil of the Bayaluseeme. The British used Carnatic, sometimes Karnatak, for both sides of peninsular India south of the Krishna.

Karnataka's prehistory goes back to a Paleolithic hand-axe culture, and Neolithic and megalithic cultures are also found there. Gold found at Harappa has been traced to mines in Karnataka, which has led scholars to propose contacts with the Indus Valley Civilisation around 3300 BCE. Before the third century BCE most of the region belonged to the Mauryan Empire of Ashoka, and four centuries of Satavahana rule followed.

The decline of Satavahana power led to the earliest native kingdoms, the Kadambas and the Western Gangas, which marked the region's emergence as an independent political entity. The Kadamba dynasty, founded by Mayurasharma, had its capital at Banavasi, and the Western Ganga dynasty ruled from Talakad. Religious thinkers also shaped the region. Adi Shankara (788–820 CE) chose Sringeri for the first of his four monasteries, and Madhvacharya (1238–1317) taught the Dvaita school of Vedanta. The Haridasa devotional movement shaped the culture of South India over some six centuries.

The state was formed as Mysore State on 1 November 1956 under the States Reorganisation Act and renamed in 1973. Its capital and largest city is Bengaluru, and the 2011 census recorded about 61 million inhabitants in 31 districts. Kannada, one of the classical languages of India, is the principal official language, with Tulu an additional official language. The government has a Legislative Assembly of 224 members and a Legislative Council.

Bandipur and Nagarhole National Parks were included in the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve in 1986. Yakshagana, a classical dance drama of the coastal and Malnad regions, is among the major theatrical forms, and the Mysore style of Bharatanatya is also associated with the state.
karpathos: Karpathos is the second largest of the Greek Dodecanese islands, about 47 kilometres south-west of Rhodes, and its highest point is Kali Limni at 1,215 metres. Pigadia, officially Karpathos, in the south-east is its capital and main port, and the villages of Olympos and Diafani lie in the north. Because of its remote location the island has kept many peculiarities of dress, customs and dialect. Homer calls it Krapathos, and in myth it is the homeland of the Titan Iapetus and the birthplace of the sea god Proteus. The British explorers Theodore and Mabel Bent spent the spring of 1885 mostly excavating the site of Vroukounta in the far north.

In ancient and medieval times the island was closely connected with Rhodes. Its cities appear on the tribute lists of the Delian League, and the Karpathians sided with Sparta in the Peloponnesian War in 431 BCE. They lost their independence to Rhodes in 400 BCE, and the island fell to Rome in 42 BCE. After the division of the Roman Empire in 395 CE it became part of the Byzantine Empire, and in the 14th century it was a see of the Latin Church.

In 1304 it was given as a fief to the Genoese corsairs Andrea and Lodovico Moresco, but in 1306 it passed to Andrea Cornaro. The Cornaro family held it until 1538, when it passed to the Ottoman Turks. The island rebelled during the Greek War of Independence in 1821 to 1822 but returned to Ottoman rule, and in 1835 Sultan Mahmud II granted it the privilege of the maktu tax system, under which tax was a fixed annual sum.

Italy occupied Karpathos on 12 May 1912 during the Italo-Turkish War, and the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 confirmed the Dodecanese as Italian possessions. The Italians stayed until September 1943, and German forces then held the island until 4 October 1944. Italy ceded it to Greece in the Paris Peace Treaties of 1947, and it formally joined the Kingdom of Greece on 7 March 1948. Economic problems after the war drove many Karpathians to emigrate to cities on the U.S. eastern seaboard.

The municipality of Karpathos, with the small island of Saria, had 6,567 inhabitants in 2021, a number that more than doubles in summer when expatriates return. The most important festival is that of the Dormition of Mary on 15 August.
kars: Kars is the seat of Kars Province and Kars District in north-eastern Turkey. Strabo's geography places it in the ancient region of Chorzene, part of the province of Ayrarat in the Kingdom of Armenia. Its name may derive from the Armenian word hars, meaning bride, or from the Georgian kari, meaning gate. Its winters are freezing, with four months of snow cover on average.

Little is known of Kars's early history, but in medieval times it had its own dynasty of Armenian rulers and was the capital of the region of Vanand. By 888 it belonged to the Armenian Bagratunis, and it was their capital from 929 to 961, when its cathedral, later the Church of the Holy Apostles, was built. In 963 it became the capital of a separate kingdom, still called Vanand. In 1064 its king, Gagik-Abas, paid homage to the Seljuk Turks, and in 1065 he ceded the kingdom to the Byzantine Empire, after which the Seljuks took the city. Zakare of the Zakarids captured it in 1206, the Mongols in 1242, and Timur levelled it in 1387.

Kars then passed between Turkic dynasties and the Safavid dynasty, and the Ottomans took it in 1585. Murad III rebuilt the fortifications, which withstood a siege by Nader Shah in 1731, though Nader Shah routed an Ottoman army there in 1745. Russia took the city in 1828 but returned it. In 1855 the Russians took it after an Ottoman garrison led by British officers, including General William Fenwick Williams, held out through a siege until cholera and hunger forced surrender. The Russians stormed it again in the war of 1877–78 and made it the capital of Kars Oblast.

In the First World War the Ottomans captured Kars in April 1918, and in May 1919 it came under the Armenian Republic as the capital of its Vanand province. Turkish forces under General Kâzım Karabekir took it with little resistance on 30 October 1920. The Treaty of Kars of 23 October 1921, signed by Turkey and the Soviet republics, established Turkey's present north-eastern boundaries. After the Second World War the Soviet Union demanded the region back in 1945 and dropped its claims by 1948.

Kars has a mixed population of Azerbaijanis, Kurds and Turks, and Kafkas University was founded there in 1992. The citadel on its rocky hill has Bagratuni walls on the north side and probably took its present form in the thirteenth century under the Zakarids. Below it stands the former Armenian church of the Holy Apostles, converted to a mosque in 1579 and again in 1993. Russian-era buildings give the city a distinct look, and it is the setting of Orhan Pamuk's novel Snow.
kartikeya: References to Skanda in Sanskrit literature go back to the 5th century BCE, in the works of Pāṇini, and the mythology of Kartikeya became widespread in North India around the 2nd century BCE. Archaeological evidence from the 1st century CE and earlier links his images with Agni, the god of fire. In the Tamil south, the Tolkappiyam mentions Murukan as the god of the hilly regions, and scholars of religion hold that the Tamil Muruga merged with the Vedic Skanda Kartikeya over time.

The accounts of his birth differ. The Ramayana calls him a child of Rudra and Parvati, born with the help of Agni and Ganga. According to the Skanda Purana, six sparks from Shiva became six boys, raised by the Krittikas and later fused by Parvati into the six-headed Kartikeya, whose name means of the Krittikas.

Kartikeya is the Hindu god of war, the son of Shiva and Parvati and the brother of Ganesha. He is shown as an ever-youthful man, riding or standing near a peacock and holding a spear called the vel. Coins of the Yaudheyas and the Kushan period from the 1st and 2nd centuries CE show him with one head or six, one-headed images being more common, and the six-headed form in sculpture dates from after the Gupta Empire.

In the Kanda Puranam and the Kumarasambhavam he is appointed commander of the devas to save them from the asuras. Shiva gives him celestial weapons, the vel and an army of 30,000 warriors, and he destroys the asuras Tarakasura and Surapadma. He is also regarded as a philosopher and a teacher of Shaiva Siddhanta.

Kartikeya was the patron deity of the Yaudheyas, whose coins found at Rohtak show him with a spear and a peacock, and the Kushan Empire took up his imagery after meeting them. In Tamil Nadu he is the patron god of the Tamil language, and the Tirumurukarruppatai is devoted to him. Many of his temples stand on hills, among them the Six Abodes of Murugan. Devotees keep Thaipusam, which commemorates his victory over the asuras, and carry the kavadi as an offering. In Chinese Buddhism he appears as Weituo, a guardian of monasteries.
karun-river: The Karun is the Iranian river with the highest water flow and the country's only navigable river, about 950 kilometres long. It rises in the Zard Kuh mountains of the Bakhtiari district in the Zagros Range, on slopes of 4,221 metres, and receives many tributaries such as the Dez and the Kuhrang. It flows past Shushtar and Ahvaz, the capital of Khuzestan Province, and reaches the Arvand Rud, or Shatt al-Arab, at Khorramshahr. Near its mouth the delta forks into two branches, the Bahmanshir and the Haffar, which enclose the island of Abadan.

In early classical times the river was called the Pasitigris, and Greek writers also knew it as the Eulaeus, the Hebrew Ulai. The name Karun is a corruption of Kuhrang, the name of its source peak and of one of its main tributaries. Medieval Arab and Persian geographers also called it Dujail, which could be translated as Little Tigris.

The Karun lies between the Susa plain, site of cultures going back to the fifth millennium BCE, and the plain of the Zohreh River to the south, where a culture of the same period is now being excavated, notably at Tal-e Choga Sofla. The Elamite civilization later held the valley. Mesopotamian powers such as Ur and Babylon overthrew the Elamites at several points, but the Elamite state lasted until about 640 BCE, when the Assyrians overran it and destroyed Susa, one of its largest cities.

In the 3rd century CE, in the Sassanid era, the first known major bridge across the river was built by Roman captives, among them the emperor Valerian. It gave its name to the bridge and dam called Band-e Kaisar, Caesar's dam, at Shushtar. In one of several competing theories on the location of the Garden of Eden, the Karun is taken to be the Gihon River of Genesis. In 1888 the Lynch Brothers opened the first regular steamship service on the river, linking Khorramshahr and Ahvaz.

The river's watershed covers 65,230 square kilometres, and it provides irrigation to over 280,000 hectares of plain. Much of the transport and resources of Khuzestan are tied to it, and since the discovery of oil at Masjed Soleyman it has been an important route for petroleum to the Persian Gulf. Several dams on the main stem, among them Gotvand, Masjed Soleyman, Karun-1, Karun-3 and Karun-4, generate hydroelectric power and provide flood control. The largest city on the river is Ahvaz.
karur: Karur lies on the plains of Tamil Nadu, on the banks of the Amaravathi, Kaveri and Noyyal rivers, at an average elevation of about 101 metres. Its climate is hot and semi-arid, and it receives about 590 to 600 mm of rain a year, most of it from the northeast monsoon in October and November. The soils are black and red and suit the crops of the Kaveri delta. The name comes from Karuvur, the Chera capital of the same name; in Tamil it means embryo town. The town was also called Brahmapuri, in vernacular speech Tiruvanilai and Pasupati.

The Cheras, one of the three kingdoms of the Sangam period (3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE), ruled the region from their capital at Vanchi-Karuvoor. The Tamil epic Silappadikaram has the Chera king Senguttuvan ruling from Karuvur. Karur lay in the Kongu Nadu region of ancient Tamilakam, on a trade route from the west coast to Tamil Nadu. Excavations have yielded pottery, bricks, Roman amphorae, rings and coins, and early Tamil Brahmi writing has been found on coins, seals and rings from the Amaravati river bed. About 150 CE Ptolemy named an inland trading centre of South India, Korevora.

The Pandyas gained influence here in the seventh century under Arikesari Maravarman, and the Cholas led by Aditya I conquered the region in the ninth century. It was directly under the Imperial Cholas until 1064, after which the Kongu Cholas ruled it autonomously. Later it passed to the Vijayanagara Empire, the Madurai Nayaks and the Kingdom of Mysore. The British East India Company captured Karur for the third time in 1790, and its fort held a British garrison until 1801. The region joined the Madras Presidency, and the municipality was constituted in 1874.

Karur is the headquarters of Karur district, with 70,980 people in its older limits at the 2011 census, and Tamil is the main language. Agriculture and textiles are the base of its economy, and it is also a centre of bus-coach building. Its temples include the Pasupatheeswarar Siva temple. The medieval poet Karuvurar, one of the nine who sang the Thiruvichaippa, was born there.
kashgar: Kashgar, also called Kashi in Chinese, lies in the Tarim Basin region of southern Xinjiang, near China's border with Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. For over 2,000 years it has been a strategically important oasis on the Silk Road linking China with Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. It stands at the convergence of widely different cultures and empires and has been under Chinese, Turkic, Mongol and Tibetan rule. Its earliest recorded names are Shufu and Shule, and Ptolemy calls it Kasi. The name Kashgar did not appear in Chinese records until the Song dynasty.

The earliest mention of Kashgar comes from a Han dynasty envoy who travelled the Northern Silk Road. In 76 BCE the Chinese conquered the Xiongnu, Khotan, Kashgar and other Tarim Basin states. Its people practised Zoroastrianism and Buddhism before Islam. In the Tang period a long struggle began between China and the Western Turks for the basin, and the king of Kashgar sent emissaries to the Tang capital in 635 and 639. The Arabs invaded in 711, but Islam was established at Kashgar only in the 10th century, under the Kara-Khanid Khanate.

Genghis Khan swept away the Kara-Khitai in 1219, and Kashgar then came under the Chagatai Khans. Marco Polo visited the city and recorded numerous Nestorian Christians with their own churches. In the 14th century the Chagataid khan Tughluq Timur converted to Islam. The Qing defeated the Dzungar Khanate and took control of Kashgar in 1759, settling emigrants of other ethnic groups near a Manchu garrison. The Dungan Revolt of 1862 to 1877 reached the Tarim Basin, and in 1864 the people of Kashgar rose against their rulers and called on the Kyrgyz chief Sadik Beg, who was reinforced by Buzurg Khan and his general Yakub Beg.

From 1912 to 1928 Yang Zengxin governed Xinjiang, and the Republic created Shule County at Kashgar in 1913. The British consulate at Chini Bagh watched local developments. In September 1949 the provincial authorities declared their allegiance to the Chinese Communist Party, and units of the People's Liberation Army entered southern Xinjiang, including Kashgar, from October.

Kashgar is a county-level city and the administrative centre of Kashgar Prefecture, which had about 4 million people in 2010. The city had 711,300 inhabitants in 2019. In 1986 the Chinese government designated it a city of historical and cultural significance. It is a terminus of the Karakoram Highway. It has a cool arid climate and is one of the driest cities in the world, with about 85 millimetres of precipitation a year.
kashmir: Kashmir is the northernmost geographical region of the Indian subcontinent. Until the mid-19th century the name meant only the Kashmir Valley between the Great Himalayas and the Pir Panjal Range, and it has since come to include the larger area of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. The earliest text to mention the name is Pāṇini's Ashtadhyayi in the 5th century BCE, which calls the people Kashmirikas. The Ancient Greeks called it Kasperia. In the 11th century the poet Bilhana called it Sharada Desha, land of Sharada, and Kashmir was the seat of Sharada Peeth, a historical centre of learning.

In the first millennium Kashmir became an important centre of Buddhism. The Karakotas, most notably Lalitaditya Muktapida, ruled in the second half of that millennium, followed by the Loharas, and Kashmir Shaivism arose in the ninth century. Hindu rule ended in 1339 when Shah Mir became the first Muslim ruler and founded a dynasty that ruled until 1568, most notably under Zain Ul Abedin. The native Chak dynasty followed, until Akbar conquered the region in 1586. Mughal rule lasted until 1751, followed by the Afghan Durrani Empire, until the Sikhs under Ranjit Singh annexed Kashmir. Sikh rule was generally considered oppressive.

Gulab Singh, anointed Raja of Jammu in 1822, rose in the Sikh court and with his general Zorawar Singh conquered Rajouri, Kishtwar, Kargil, Ladakh and Baltistan, surrounding the valley. After the Sikh defeat in the First Anglo-Sikh War, the British, under the Treaty of Amritsar in 1846, made over to Gulab Singh for 75 lakhs the mountainous country east of the Indus and west of the Ravi, including the Vale of Kashmir. The resulting princely state combined Buddhist Ladakh, mixed Jammu, the overwhelmingly Muslim valley with a small Hindu minority of Kashmiri Pandits, Shia Baltistan and the Gilgit Agency.

When British rule ended in 1947 the ruler, Hari Singh, hesitated over accession, and after a Pakistani-sponsored guerrilla onslaught he appealed for help and acceded to India on the condition of Indian military aid. A ceasefire under United Nations auspices was agreed at the end of 1948. The region is divided among three countries: India administers Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, Pakistan administers Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, and China administers Aksai Chin and the Trans-Karakoram Tract. Neither India nor Pakistan has formally recognised the accession of the areas the other claims. The two countries fought further wars over the territory in 1965 and 1999.
kasimov: The first inhabitants of the area were a Finnic tribe called the Meshchyora, later assimilated by Russians and Tatars. The Vladimir-Suzdal ruler Yuri Dolgorukiy founded the town in 1152 as Grodets, then Gorodets Meshchyorsky. The Mongols destroyed it in 1376, and it was soon rebuilt as Novy Nizovoy. After the Battle of Suzdal in 1445, in which Grand Duke Vasily II was taken prisoner, the Meshchyora lands were given to Oluğ Möxämmäd, Khan of the Kazan Khanate, as a ransom for the sovereign's life.

In 1452 Vasily II, Grand Prince of Moscow, gave the town to the Kazan prince Qasim, who served as tribute inspector of the Great Horde and then entered Russian service. By other accounts Qasim and his brother Yosif fled from Kazan after losing a contest for the throne to their brother Mäxmüd. After 1471 the town was known as Qasim city, and it remained the capital of the Qasim Khanate until the khanate was absorbed into Russia in 1681.

A group of Tatars settled in Kasimov in the 15th century and are now known as Qasim Tatars. They speak the Mishar dialect, mixed with the Middle Tatar dialect of the Tatar language. In the 19th century the town became known for its waiters, who staffed many of the hotels of St Petersburg. In the 17th century it was divided in three: the Old Town and the Tatar Town, ruled by the khan and Tatar noblemen, the Yamskoy Town of Russian commoners, ruled from Moscow, and the Marfin Town, ruled by the Kasimov voivodes.

Historical buildings include the Khan's Mosque, with a limestone minaret dated either to 1467 or to the 1550s, the mausoleum of Shahghali Khan of 1555 and that of Afghan Moxammad Khan of 1658. Four Russian Orthodox churches also stand there: the Church of the Epiphany, St Nicholas Church and Trinity Church of the 17th century, and the Cathedral of the Ascension of the 19th century.
kassaman: Under French rule the native population of Algeria was given very few political rights for a century. A nationalist movement began in the 1920s and gained strength after World War II, when a government commitment to grant French Algeria autonomy failed to materialise. A prominent member of the movement was Moufdi Zakaria, a Mozabite Berber poet affiliated with the Algerian People's Party. He was jailed and tortured on several occasions between the 1920s and 1962.

He wrote the words in April 1955, during one of these imprisonments, in Barberousse Prison. Since he had no paper or writing instruments, he reportedly wrote the lyrics with his own blood on the walls of his cell. The music was composed by the Egyptian composer Mohamed Fawzi, who was asked to take on the task after two earlier submissions by other composers, one of them by Mohamed Triki, had been rejected.

The lyrics read as a war song. They promote nationalist ideals on the front line, glorify the actions of the National Liberation Front and present armed uprising as the only route to independence. The song alludes to France, the former colonial ruler, in connection with the violent struggle for independence, and foretells that a day of reckoning will come for it. Usually only the first verse is performed, for brevity, as at sporting events.

The words and music were officially adopted in 1962, the year in which the Évian Accords were signed. They paved the way for a referendum in which Algerians voted overwhelmingly for independence, which was then granted. Although Kassaman was intended only as a provisional national anthem, it has endured. In November 2008 an amendment to Article 5 of the Constitution of Algeria declared it immutable, given its association with the country's revolution, and confirmed that the anthem comprises all of its verses, ending the discussion of whether the unfavourable reference to France was still appropriate.
kassel: Kassel lies on both sides of the Fulda River in northern Hesse. It was first mentioned in 913, when King Conrad I signed two deeds there, in a place called Chasella or Chassalla, a fortification at a bridge over the Fulda. The origin of the name is unproven: it may come from the ancient Castellum Cattorum, a castle of the Chatti, or from words meaning a valley and a hall. A deed of 1189 shows that Cassel had city rights, though the date they were granted is not known. The first castle was built in 1277 and later replaced by a Renaissance palace that burned down in 1811.

In 1567 the Landgraviate of Hesse, until then centred in Marburg, was divided among four sons, and Kassel became the capital of Hesse-Kassel and a centre of Calvinist Protestantism in Germany. Strong fortifications protected the Protestant stronghold, and the Rosicrucian Fama Fraternitatis was first published there in 1617. In 1685 Landgrave Charles gave refuge to 1,700 Huguenots, in the new borough of Oberneustadt. In the late 18th century Hesse-Kassel sold auxiliary troops to the British crown to help suppress the American Revolution, and the money financed palaces. The Brothers Grimm lived in Kassel in the early 19th century, where they collected and wrote most of their fairy tales.

Napoleon annexed the Electorate, and Kassel was the capital of the Kingdom of Westphalia under his brother Jérôme from 1807. The Electorate was restored in 1813 and annexed by Prussia in 1866, after it sided with Austria in the Austro-Prussian War. Kassel then ceased to be a princely residence but became an industrial centre and railway junction, home of Henschel & Son, the largest locomotive maker in Germany at the end of the 19th century. After the Battle of Sedan in 1870 Napoleon III was held prisoner at Wilhelmshöhe Palace.

In the Second World War a subcamp of Dachau provided forced labour for the Henschel works, which included tank plants. The heaviest bombing destroyed 90 per cent of the downtown area, killed some 10,000 people and left 150,000 homeless. The US 80th Infantry Division took the city in house-to-house fighting from 1 to 4 April 1945. Most old buildings in the centre were not restored, and large parts of the inner city were rebuilt in the style of the 1950s, though the Museum Fridericianum was restored. Kassel had 201,048 inhabitants in December 2020 and has a university. The Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the documenta exhibitions of contemporary art are held there.
kassites: The origin of the Kassites is uncertain. Several names thought to be Kassite appear in economic documents of the Ur III period, but their origin there is ambiguous, and many historians place their original homeland in the Zagros Mountains. One theory makes them a Caucasian people akin to the Hurrians with an Indo-European ruling element; another, disputed, derives them from the region of the Caspian Sea. Their language is most likely an isolate, related to neither Indo-European nor Semitic languages, though some linguists propose a link to Hurro-Urartian. The earliest person with a Kassite name in Babylonia is recorded in 1770 BCE, and a year name of Samsu-iluna of Babylon refers to a campaign against the Kassite army.

After the Hittite sack of Babylon in 1531 BCE the Kassites took control of Babylonia, which they held until about 1155 BCE on the short chronology. Their rulers regained the idol of Marduk, returned it to Babylon and made him the equal of the Kassite god Shuqamuna; they renamed the city Karanduniash. The fall of the First Sealand dynasty in 1460 BCE left a power vacuum that they filled. After the Hittites destroyed Mitanni in the early 14th century BCE, Assyria rose, and the Kassites, Hittites and Assyrians formed a three-way balance with Elam and Egypt exerting influence, joined by trade, treaties and intermarriage. Fourteen of the Amarna Letters are exchanges between the pharaoh and the Kassite king.

Under Kurigalzu I, in the mid-14th century BCE, the Kassites conquered Elam and sacked Susa. He also founded the new city of Dur-Kurigalzu, with palaces and temples to Enlil, Ninlil and Ninurta. Conflict with Assyria continued for centuries, and for a time early in the reign of Tukulti-Ninurta I Assyria had the upper hand. The Elamites of the Shutrukid dynasty finally conquered Babylonia in the 12th century BCE and carried off the statue of Marduk. According to the Assyrian Synchronistic Chronicle, which is not considered reliable, the last king, Enlil-nadin-ahi, was taken to Susa in 1155 BCE and died there.

Kassite Babylonia was ruled by kings through a bureaucracy supported by an aristocracy of chariot warriors, and their arrival coincided with the introduction of the horse-drawn chariot. Over the centuries the Kassites were absorbed into the Babylonian population, and eight of the last kings bore Akkadian names. After the dynasty was overthrown the provincial administration continued, and the country remained united under the Second Dynasty of Isin. About 12,000 documents of the period have been recovered, only about a tenth of them published; kudurrus, stone stelae recording land grants, are another major source. Groups called Kassites, known to the Greeks as Cossaei, lived in the mountains for centuries and were a target of Alexander the Great's last winter campaign, in 324/323 BCE.
kastamonu: Kastamonu lies at an elevation of 904 metres in the southern part of Kastamonu Province in northern Turkey, and it is the seat of the province and of its central district. Several explanations of its name are given. One derives it from Paphlagonia, the Greek name for the Black Sea region, whose Paphlagonians dominated it about 1000 BCE. Another derives it from Kastama, a name for the same region in the Hittite period. A third combines Gas, the Kashkas who were among the first settlers, with Tumanna, the name of a city or region there, and a fourth combines the Latin kastra, castle, with the Komnenos dynasty of Byzantine emperors.

Ibn Battuta visited the city, called it one of the largest and finest cities, with abundant commodities and low prices, and stayed forty days. The city's best-known Sufi saint is Sheikh Shaban Veli, who died in 976 AH, or 1569 CE. In the early 20th century nickel was mined in the area around Kastamonu.

On 23 August 1925 Mustafa Kemal, later known as Atatürk, began the Dress Code Revolution at Kastamonu with a speech on the hat and dress reform during a visit to the city, given in the building of the Republican People's Party. The building is now the Archeological Museum of Kastamonu, which also exhibits the possessions Atatürk used on that visit.

Kastamonu has a population of 125,622 at the 2021 count. Its Kastamonu Lisesi, also known as Abdurrahman Paşa Lisesi, was the first modern high school established in Anatolia in the late Ottoman Empire. Kastamonu University was founded in 2006 by uniting colleges, schools and institutes that had belonged to Ankara University and Gazi University. The city is the main railway terminus of the West Black Sea region. Taşköprü, in the province, is known for kuyu kebabı, a lamb dish slow-cooked in a sealed pit.
kasubi-tombs: The site covers around 26 hectares on Kasubi hill, about 5 kilometres north-west of the centre of Kampala. A royal palace there was built in 1882 by Muteesa I, the 35th kabaka of Buganda, to replace one built by his father Ssuuna II in 1820, and it became a royal burial ground on his death in 1884. It is one of 31 royal tombs across the kingdom since its founding in the 13th century. Traditionally a king's body was buried in one place and his jawbone, believed to hold his soul, had a separate shrine; Kasubi is unusual in holding the tombs of four kabakas: Muteesa I, Mwanga II, Daudi Chwa II and Sir Edward Muteesa II.

A gatehouse leads to a small courtyard, the drum house holding the royal drums, and then to the circular main courtyard on the hilltop, enclosed by a reed fence. Opposite the entrance stands the main building, Muzibu Azaala Mpanga, 31 metres in circumference and 7.5 metres high. It is circular, with a dome of thick thatch resting on 52 rings of palm fronds, which stand for the 52 clans of the Baganda, over a frame of wooden poles, reed wattle and daub. Steel, concrete and brick were added in a renovation of 1938, largely hidden behind traditional materials.

The tombs lie in a sacred forest inside the building, hidden by a barkcloth curtain, on floors covered with lemon grass and palm-leaf mats. Around the courtyard stand houses for the kabaka's widows, who tend the graves, and for royal officials, among them the Nalinya, the spiritual guardian. The Ngo clan makes and decorates bark cloth there and the Ngeye clan keeps up traditional thatching. Bark cloth fig trees mark the boundary.

The kingdom of Buganda managed the site until Milton Obote abolished it in 1966, and again after it was reinstated in 1993. The site became protected under Ugandan law in 1972. It remains an important spiritual and political place for the Baganda. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in December 2001, describing it as an outstanding example of building with purely vegetal materials in the region.

On 16 March 2010 fire almost completely destroyed the main buildings, though the inner sanctum, with the remains of the kabakas, was reported intact. The site was placed on the list of World Heritage Sites in Danger in July 2010. Reconstruction began in 2014, with funds raised by a campaign called Etofaali and by Japan.
kasur: Kasur is a city south of Lahore in the Pakistani province of Punjab, near the border with India, and the headquarters of Kasur District. Its name comes from the Arabic and Persian qasur, meaning palaces or forts. The city is an aggregation of fortified hamlets overlooking the alluvial valleys of the Beas and Sutlej rivers. According to a legend, it was founded by Prince Kusha of the Ramayana, son of Rama and Sita, but historical records reject an ancient founding and date it to 1525, when it began as a fortified settlement.

The region was agricultural, with forests, in the time of the Indus Valley civilisation, and was ruled in turn by the Maurya Empire, the Indo-Greek kingdom, the Kushan Empire, the Gupta Empire and others. In 1005 Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni took over the region, and Sufi missionaries sent there made Punjab predominantly Muslim. The Kheshgi tribe of Pashtuns, migrating from Kabul in 1525 in the reign of Babur, built small forts and established the Kheshgi chieftaincy. Kasur grew into a town of fortified hamlets called kots, and under Mughal rule it flourished in commerce and trade. It became the home of the Sufi saint and poet Bulleh Shah, who is buried in a large shrine there.

After the decline of the Mughal Empire the region fell into a power vacuum, and Ahmad Shah Durrani captured Kasur. The Sikhs sacked the city in 1747 under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and again in 1763. Ranjit Singh of the Sikh Empire captured it in 1807 in the Battle of Kasur. In the First Anglo-Sikh War the city was occupied by Company forces on 10 February 1846. Under British rule canals irrigated large areas of the district, and riots in April 1919 after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre destroyed civic infrastructure, including the railway station.

After the formation of Pakistan in 1947 the Hindus and Sikhs of Kasur migrated to India, while Muslim refugees from India settled there. The population is overwhelmingly Punjabi-speaking, with Urdu the second language. Kasur emerged after independence as a major centre of leather tanning, and it remains known as the burial place of Bulleh Shah.
kate-sheppard: Kate Sheppard was born Catherine Wilson Malcolm on 10 March 1848 at Liverpool, to Scottish parents. After her father died in 1862 she lived with an uncle, a Free Church of Scotland minister at Nairn, who instilled in her the values of Christian socialism. In 1868 the family sailed for New Zealand, arriving at Lyttelton in February 1869. In Christchurch she joined the Trinity Congregational Church and became part of the city's intellectual life. She married the shop owner Walter Allen Sheppard on 21 July 1871, and their only child, Douglas, was born in 1880. She taught Sunday school and served on the YWCA's committee.

Her activism began after the American temperance speaker Mary Leavitt toured New Zealand in 1885. Sheppard helped found a Christchurch branch of the Women's Christian Temperance Union, and when petitions on women's issues were rejected she concluded that politicians would ignore women while they could not vote. In 1887 she became the union's national superintendent for franchise and legislation. A suffrage bill failed by one vote that year. In 1888 she published the pamphlet Ten Reasons Why the Women of New Zealand Should Vote, sending a copy to every member of the House of Representatives, and later Should Women Vote?

Her first petition, with 10,085 signatures, was presented in 1891, and a second, with 20,274, followed. The third, presented in 1893, carried 31,872 women's signatures, the largest petition presented to Parliament up to then. The Electoral Bill of 1893 passed the Legislative Council by 20 votes to 18 on 8 September, and Governor David Boyle signed it on 19 September. By the election on 28 November, 88 percent of women had enrolled and nearly 70 percent voted. Women could not stand for Parliament until 1919.

In 1896 Sheppard became the first president of the National Council of Women of New Zealand, and she edited the union's journal The White Ribbon. She spent time in England, promoting suffrage there, and later withdrew from politics because of ill health while continuing to write. She revived the National Council in 1918. She died at Christchurch on 13 July 1934, aged 86, leaving no living descendants. Her portrait has appeared on the New Zealand ten-dollar note since 1991, and a memorial to her stands in Christchurch.
kateb-yacine: Kateb Yacine was born in Constantine, into a scholarly maraboutic Chaoui Berber family from Sedrata. His birth name was Yacine Kateb, but he said he had grown so used to teachers calling out surnames first that he took Kateb Yacine as a pen name. His father was a lawyer and the family followed his postings. He attended the Quran school at Sedrata in 1937, the French school in Lafayette in Little Kabylie in 1938, and in 1941 became a boarder at the colonial collège of Setif.

In his third year there he took part in the demonstrations of 8 May 1945, which ended in a massacre of Algerians by the French army and police, between six and eight thousand according to the figures given, forty-five thousand according to nationalists. Three days later he was arrested and imprisoned for two months. From then on he was a partisan of the nationalist cause. He was expelled from the collège and sent by his father to the high school in Bône. His first collection of poetry appeared in 1946.

Kateb went to Paris in 1947 and joined the Algerian Communist Party that May. He published Nedjma ou le Poème du Couteau in the Mercure de France and worked as a journalist at Alger Républicain from 1949 to 1951. After his father died in 1950 he worked as a longshoreman in Algiers, and he lived in Paris until 1959. His play Le cadavre encerclé was published in Esprit in 1954 and banned in France. The novel Nedjma appeared in 1956. During the war of independence he was forced abroad by harassment from the DST. He returned to Algeria in 1962 and, in 1967, left for Vietnam and wrote L'Homme aux sandales de caoutchouc, a play celebrating Ho Chi Minh.

In 1970 he settled in Algeria and gave up writing in French, turning to popular theatre, epics and satires in dialectal Arabic. With the Théâtre de la Mer of Bab El Oued, from 1971, he toured Algeria for five years, playing to workers, farmers and students. He was criticised for stressing Berber tradition and the Tamazight language, and for liberal positions on gender equality. He regarded French as the Algerians' spoil of the war for independence. He received the Grand prix national des Lettres in France in 1987. He died on 28 October 1989, leaving unfinished a work on the Algerian riots of October 1988.
kateri-tekakwitha: Kateri Tekakwitha was born around 1656 in the Mohawk village of Ossernenon, in what is now northeastern New York. Her name, Tekakwitha, means she who bumps into things in Mohawk. Her father, Kenneronkwa, was a Mohawk chief, and her mother, Kahenta, was an Algonquin woman who had been captured in a raid, adopted into the tribe and earlier baptised by French missionaries. When Tekakwitha was around four, her parents and brother died of smallpox. She survived with facial scars and impaired eyesight and went to live with her father's sister and her husband, a chief of the Turtle Clan.

In 1666 the French burned the three Mohawk villages, and the peace that followed required the Mohawks to tolerate Jesuit missionaries. At eleven she met the Jesuits Jacques Frémin, Jacques Bruyas and Jean Pierron. Pressed to think of marriage around thirteen, she refused.

In the spring of 1674 she told the Jesuit Jacques de Lamberville of her wish to become a Christian. He baptised her on Easter Sunday, 18 April 1676, giving her the name Catherine, of which Kateri is the Mohawk form. Some Mohawks opposed her conversion and accused her of sorcery, and others stoned and harassed her. She fled about 200 miles to the Christian mission of Sault Saint-Louis, Kahnawake, near Montreal, and joined it in 1677.

At Kahnawake she practised severe penances, which some priests opposed because of her poor health. With her friend Marie Thérèse Tegaianguenta she tried to found a Native religious order, which the Jesuits rejected. In 1679, on the Feast of the Annunciation, she consecrated herself to Jesus as her husband.

Tekakwitha died on Holy Wednesday, 17 April 1680, in the arms of Marie-Thérèse. The Jesuits Claude Chauchetière and Pierre Cholenec wrote her biographies in 1695 and 1696. She is often called the Lily of the Mohawks.

The cause for her canonisation was begun by American Catholics at the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1885, and some 906 Native Americans signed letters supporting it. Pope John Paul II beatified her on 22 June 1980 and Benedict XVI canonised her on 21 October 2012, the first Native American woman of North America to be canonised.
kathiawar: The peninsula covers about 61,000 square kilometres and faces the Arabian Sea on the south and south-west. From the heads of its two gulfs the Little Rann of Kutch and the waste tracts of Khambhat, half salt morass and half sandy desert, reach inland towards each other, so that only one narrow neck on the north-east joins Kathiawar to the mainland of Gujarat. Two belts of hill country cross it, and nine rivers drain it radially; they carry little water outside the monsoon months, and dams have been built on some of them. Most of the natural vegetation is dry scrub. The region has also been called Sorath.

The name Kathiawad seems to derive from the early settlements of the Kathis, who entered Gujarat from Sindh in the early centuries of the Common Era; Saurashtra comes from Sanskrit words meaning good nation. In the reign of Chandragupta Maurya the region was governed by Pushyagupta, and under Ashoka by the Yavana Tushaspa. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, of the first century CE, calls the coast Syrastrene and describes a fertile country yielding wheat, rice, sesame oil, clarified butter and cotton cloth, with many cattle. The Junagadh rock inscription attributed to Rudradaman I, dated to 150 CE, also mentions the region.

After Indian independence in 1947, 217 princely states of Kathiawar, among them the former Junagadh State, were merged on 15 February 1948 into the United State of Kathiawar, renamed Saurashtra State in November 1948. Vallabhbhai Patel spent much time persuading the princes; Maharaja Krishnakumar Sinhji of Bhavnagar State was the first to offer his state. Rajkot was the capital and Uchharangray Navalshankar Dhebar the first chief minister. On 1 November 1956 Saurashtra was merged into Bombay state, and when that state was divided along linguistic lines in 1960 it became part of Gujarat.

The region now comprises eleven districts of Gujarat, with part of Ahmedabad district; historically it also took in Diu. Gir National Park and its surroundings hold the last remaining population of Asiatic lions, and the peninsula has two further national parks, the Blackbuck National Park at Velavadar and the Marine National Park in the Gulf of Kutch. Severe droughts have repeatedly left farmers without crops or drinking water. A campaign to build check dams from the late 1990s raised water tables, but in 2019 a severe drought struck again and water had to be brought by tanker from the Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada River.
kathmandu: Kathmandu lies in the northwestern part of the Kathmandu Valley, north of the Bagmati River, at an elevation of about 1,324 metres. The city covers 50.7 square kilometres and is bounded by Lalitpur, also called Patan, with which it forms one urban area surrounded by a ring road. It is dissected by eight rivers, of which the main one is the Bagmati. The valley is an ancient lake basin with fertile soil and flat terrain, which helped form a society based on agriculture.

Its position between India and China made it an important trading centre. Trade flourished along an offshoot of the Silk Road linking India and Tibet, and Lhasa Newar merchants of Kathmandu conducted trade across the Himalaya and helped spread art styles and Buddhism across Central Asia.

Archaeological excavations in Kathmandu have found evidence of ancient civilisations. The oldest finding is a statue from Maligaon dated to 185 CE. The excavation of Dhando Chaitya uncovered a brick with an inscription in Brahmi script, which archaeologists believe is two thousand years old. Historically the valley was known as the Nepal Mandala and was the cultural and political hub of the Newar people. From ancient times until the medieval period Kathmandu was known as Kantipur, which derives from Sanskrit words meaning beauty and place, giving the sense of city of light.

The name Kathmandu comes from Kasthamandap, a public pavilion made of wood, from the Sanskrit words for wood and pavilion. It was rebuilt in 1596 in the period of King Lakshmi Narasimha Malla, and according to legend all its timber came from a single tree. The earliest Western reference to the city is in the account of the Portuguese Jesuit Father Joao Cabral, who passed through the valley in the spring of 1628 and was received by the king, probably Lakshminarasimha Malla. He reported that they reached Cadmendu, the capital of the kingdom of Nepal.

Kathmandu is the capital and largest city of Nepal and its main governmental, financial, industrial and cultural centre. The 2021 census recorded a population of 845,767, with approximately 4 million in the surrounding metropolitan area. Its people are multi-ethnic, with a Hindu majority and a significant Vajrayana Buddhist presence. Since 1985 it has hosted the headquarters of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation.

Hindu and Buddhist practice has influenced the monuments of the city over the centuries. In 2006 UNESCO declared seven groups of monuments in the valley a World Heritage Site, among them Durbar Square, Swayambhu Mahachaitya, Bouddha and Pashupatinath.
kathmandu-valley: The Kathmandu Valley is a bowl-shaped valley in the Himalayan mountains of Nepal, at the crossroads of ancient civilisations of the Indian subcontinent and the wider Asian continent. Historically the valley and adjoining areas formed a confederation known as the Nepal Mandala. Until the 15th century Bhaktapur was its capital, when Kathmandu and Lalitpur were established as two further capitals. The name Kathmandu comes from Kasthamandap, a wooden pavilion in Kathmandu Durbar Square built in 1596 by King Lakshmi Narasimha Malla, said to contain no iron nails or supports.

The Newars are the indigenous inhabitants and the creators of the valley's historic civilisation, and their language is Newar, not to be confused with Nepali.
