The valley's trademark is the multiple-roofed pagoda, which may have originated there. A Newar artisan, Araniko, travelled to the court of Kublai Khan in the 13th century and influenced styles in China and Tibet.

The valley's origin is explained in legend. According to the Swayambhu Purana it was once a lake called Nagahrada, inhabited by Nagas. Vipassi Buddha planted a lotus seed in it, which grew into a radiant manifestation of the primordial Buddha called Svayambhu, and the bodhisattva Manjushri drained the lake by cutting a gorge. In a Hindu account Krishna drained the lake by cutting through the southern hills with his Sudarshana Chakra.

Kathmandu, Lalitpur, Bhaktapur and a ring of smaller cities form the largest urban agglomeration in Nepal, with about 5 million people. The valley has at least 130 important monuments, including pilgrimage sites for Hindus and Buddhists. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 1979, with seven component sites, among them Pashupatinath Temple, Boudhanath Stupa and Swayambhunath.
kathua: Kathua lies at the foothills of the Sivaliks at an average elevation of 393 metres. The Sivalik hills and the snow-capped Kailash Kund range stand to the north, and the city is surrounded by three rivers: the Ravi is 7 km down from the town, and the Ujjh about 11 km along the Jammu highway. The town itself stands on the banks of a khad, the Dogri word for a seasonal stream, which divides it into two boroughs, Parliwand, meaning the other side, and Orliwand, meaning this side. The large Ranjit Sagar Lake lies 25 km away and cools the climate.

The climate is monsoon-influenced and humid subtropical. Rainfall averages around 1,700 millimetres a year, mainly in the monsoon of July and August and in winter, when western disturbances bring rain. Summers are hot, with temperatures that may reach 40 degrees, and winter nights can fall below 0. Kathua has no snowfall, and temperatures stay 3 to 4 degrees lower than at Jammu.

Kathua is the headquarters of Kathua district and a municipal council of 27 wards, in the Jammu division of Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, a region whose status is disputed. It lies along NH-44 and is linked by rail to the major cities of India. Jammu Airport is the nearest major airport. An army cantonment adjoins the city, and its industrial area includes a textile park, a biotechnology and pharmaceutical research park and cement works.

The municipal council and its outgrowth areas had a population of 59,688, with a literacy rate of 86.46%. Dogri is the mother tongue of most people, alongside Hindi, and Urdu predominates in official documents together with English. Hinduism is the largest religion, followed by over 91% of the people, with Sikhism second at 4.75% and Islam and Christianity smaller.
kato-kiyomasa: Katō Kiyomasa was born in what is now Nakamura-ku, Nagoya, to Katō Kiyotada, whose wife Ito was a cousin of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's mother. His father died while he was young, and he soon entered Hideyoshi's service, receiving a stipend of 170 koku in 1576 at the age of 15. He fought at the Battle of Yamazaki in 1582 and at Shizugatake in 1583, where his achievements made him one of Hideyoshi's Seven Spears of Shizugatake and brought 3,000 more koku. In 1584 he fought at Komaki and Nagakute against the Tokugawa. After the Kyūshū campaign of 1587 he was granted 250,000 koku in Higo, roughly half the province, with Kumamoto Castle as his residence.

Kiyomasa was one of three senior commanders in the Imjin War against Joseon Korea (1592–1598). Together with Konishi Yukinaga he captured Seoul, Busan and many other cities, defeated the last Korean regulars at the Battle of the Imjin River and pacified Hamgyong. He held two Korean princes hostage to force lower officials to surrender. A noted castle-builder, he built strategic Japanese-style castles in the lands he took, among them Ulsan, whose siege, begun on 22 December 1597, was his best-known battle: he defended it against a Chinese army under Yang Hao said to number 60,000. Ishida Mitsunari did not report his bravery to Hideyoshi. Like other daimyō he brought captive Korean potters back to Kyūshū.

After Hideyoshi's death in 1598 a group of seven generals including Kiyomasa turned against Mitsunari over his reports of the Korean war, and Tokugawa Ieyasu mediated. Kiyomasa then sided with Ieyasu, and in the Sekigahara campaign of 1600 he fought Mitsunari's allies on Kyūshū and took a number of castles. As a reward he received the other half of Higo, bringing his income to nearly 500,000 koku.

In his later years Kiyomasa tried to mediate between Ieyasu and Toyotomi Hideyori. In 1611, on a sea voyage to Kumamoto after one such meeting, he fell ill and died shortly after he arrived. He was buried at Honmyō-ji in Kumamoto and is enshrined at many Shinto shrines, among them Katō Shrine in Kumamoto. His son Katō Tadahiro succeeded him, but Tokugawa Iemitsu confiscated the fief and exiled him in 1632 on suspicion of conspiracy. A devoted follower of Nichiren Buddhism, Kiyomasa encouraged Nichiren temples in his lands. He is noted for brutally suppressing Christianity and clashed with Konishi Yukinaga, who held the other half of Higo and was a Christian. In 1910 he was posthumously promoted to junior third court rank.
katsushika-hokusai: Hokusai's date of birth is unclear but is often given as 31 October 1760, in the Katsushika district of Edo. It is believed his father was Nakajima Ise, a mirror-maker for the shōgun. He began painting around the age of six. At twelve he was sent to work in a bookshop and lending library, at fourteen he became an apprentice to a woodcarver, and at eighteen he entered the studio of Katsukawa Shunshō, a master of ukiyo-e, which then concentrated on courtesans and kabuki actors. He published his first prints, of kabuki actors, in 1779.

After Shunshō's death in 1793 Hokusai explored other styles, including European ones known to him from French and Dutch copper engravings, and was expelled from the Katsukawa school by Shunkō, the chief disciple. In his own words, the embarrassment he suffered at Shunkō's hands motivated the development of his style. He turned from actors and courtesans to landscapes and the daily life of people of many social levels, a breakthrough for ukiyo-e. He used at least thirty names in his lifetime.

By 1800 he had taken the name Katsushika Hokusai, meaning north studio, in honour of the North Star, a symbol of a deity in his Nichiren Buddhism, and he published two collections of landscapes. He taught about 50 pupils over his life. On 5 October 1817 he painted the Great Daruma, 18 by 10.8 metres, in Nagoya before a large crowd. Between 1804 and 1815 he illustrated books with the novelist Takizawa Bakin.

In 1811 he took the name Taito. The first volume of the Hokusai Manga, a collection of drawings of objects, plants, animals and ordinary people, appeared in 1814 and was an immediate success; by 1820 twelve volumes had been produced. After 1820, as Iitsu, he made Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji in the early 1830s, including The Great Wave off Kanagawa. From 1834, as Gakyō Rōjin Manji, the Old Man Mad About Art, he produced One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji.

A fire in 1839 destroyed Hokusai's studio and much of his work,. At 83 he went to Obuse in Shinano Province at the invitation of a wealthy farmer, and he kept working almost until the end. He died on 10 May 1849 and was buried at the Seikyō-ji in Tokyo. Hokusai's prints were collected by European artists including Degas, Gauguin, Manet and van Gogh. Claude Debussy is believed to have been inspired by The Great Wave in La Mer, which first appeared in 1905.
kattegat: The Kattegat is a sea of roughly 24,000 square kilometres, bounded by the Skagerrak in the north, Jutland in the west, the Danish Straits and Zealand in the south and the Swedish provinces of Bohuslän, Västergötland, Halland and Scania in the east. The Baltic Sea drains into it through the Danish Straits. Its main islands are Samsø, Læsø and Anholt, and the cities and ports on its shores include Gothenburg, Aarhus, Aalborg, Halmstad, Varberg and Frederikshavn.

It is rather shallow, mostly less than 25 metres deep with an average of 22 metres, and dangerous to navigate because of sandy and stony reefs and shifting currents. The Baltic Current carries fresher water north along the Swedish coast, while a deeper current brings salt water in from the Skagerrak. The sea is therefore stratified into two layers, separated by a halocline at an average depth of 15 metres. Tides change the water level by only 15 to 30 centimetres.

According to Danish reference works, the name comes from the Dutch katte, cat's, and gat, passage. Captains of the Hanseatic fleets in the late Middle Ages compared the Danish Straits to a passage so tight that even a cat would have difficulty squeezing through, because of the many reefs and shoals. An archaic name for the Kattegat together with the Skagerrak was the Norwegian Sea or Jutland Sea, and its ancient Latin name was Sinus Codanus.

Control of and access to the Kattegat has been important throughout the history of international seafaring. Until the completion of the Eider Canal in 1784 it was the only sea route into and out of the Baltic region. From 1429 the Danish royal family, and later the state of Denmark, profited greatly from the Sound dues, a toll charged for passage through the Øresund. Copenhagen sheltered and repaired ships and offered trade and protection from piracy. The dues were lifted in 1857.

Boundaries differ by authority. A convention signed by Denmark, Norway and Sweden on 31 December 1932 drew the line with the Skagerrak from Skagen to Vinga Lighthouse, and other definitions place it further north or south, so that Gothenburg lies on the Kattegat under some and on the Skagerrak under others. Artificial channels, dredging and a network of lights now protect the heavy international traffic on the sea.

In the northern Kattegat, cold seeps known as bubbling reefs rise in shallow water, built up by methane and carbonate into pillars up to 4 metres tall. They are protected as a Natura 2000 habitat. Since the 1950s a bridge across the Kattegat joining Jutland and Zealand has been proposed.
kauai: Kauaʻi has an area of 1,456 square kilometres, making it the fourth largest of the Hawaiian Islands, and lies 117 kilometres northwest of Oʻahu across the Kauaʻi Channel. It is about five million years old, the oldest of the main islands, though Niʻihau is older. Its highest peak is Kawaikini at 1,598 metres, and Mount Waiʻaleʻale, 1,569 metres high, has an average annual rainfall of 11.7 metres on its east side, one of the wettest spots on earth. Rain has carved deep valleys and canyons with many waterfalls, and the flow of the Waimea River formed Waimea Canyon, about 910 metres deep.

It is uncertain when people first reached the Hawaiian Islands. Early archaeological studies suggested that Polynesian explorers from the Marquesas or Society Islands arrived as early as 600 CE, with a second wave from Tahiti around 1100, while later analyses suggest the first settlers came between 900 and 1200. Kauaʻi had its own dialect of Hawaiian, which still survives on Niʻihau.

In January 1778 the British navigator James Cook arrived at Kauaʻi by accident during his third voyage, the first recorded contact between a European and the indigenous people of the islands. By 1795 Kamehameha I had united most of the islands in the Kingdom of Hawaii, but Kauaʻi stayed independent. His attempt to conquer it in 1796 was cancelled because of stormy seas, and a second invasion planned from Oʻahu was cancelled after an epidemic broke out among his forces. In 1810 Kaumualiʻi, who had ruled Kauaʻi since 1803, agreed to be Kamehameha's vassal and to cede the island on his death by making Kamehameha's son his heir.

In 1816 Georg Anton Schäffer, a German working for the Russian-American Company, involved Kaumualiʻi in a plan to place Kauaʻi under the protection of the Russian Empire, and a fort was built at Waimea in 1817. On Kamehameha's orders Kaumualiʻi dismissed the Russians. From 1835 sugarcane plantations were the island's most important industry for about a century; the last, the Gay & Robinson Plantation, stopped planting in 2008.

Kauaʻi calls itself the Garden Isle and holds Waimea Canyon State Park and Nā Pali Coast State Park. It forms most of Kauaʻi County, which also includes Niʻihau, Kaʻula and Lehua, and its population was 73,298 in 2020.
kaub: Kaub lies on the right bank of the Rhine in the district of Rhein-Lahn-Kreis in Rhineland-Palatinate, about 50 kilometres west of Wiesbaden, and is part of the municipality of Loreley. It is connected to Wiesbaden and Koblenz by railway. The restored castle of Gutenfels stands on a hill above the town, and the castle of Pfalzgrafenstein, known as the Pfalz, sits on a rock in the middle of the river. According to legend the Palatine countesses awaited their confinement in the Pfalz, but in reality it served as a toll-gate for merchandise on the Rhine. Historically the town's trade consisted mainly of the wines of the district.

Kaub is first mentioned in 983. It originally belonged to the lords of Falkenstein. In 1260 the Counts of Katzenelnbogen divided their county and selected the inhabitants of Kaub, and in 1277 the town passed to the Rhenish Electorate of the Palatinate. It received civic rights in 1324. In 1477 it was passed as a deposit to the Counts of Katzenelnbogen again, but that family died out in 1479.

On New Year's night 1813 to 1814 Blücher crossed the Rhine at Kaub with the Prussian and Russian armies in pursuit of the French, and the town has a statue of the general. From 1919 to 1923 Kaub was part of the temporary Free State of Bottleneck.

Kaub is home to the Kaub gauging station, a decisive measuring point for the water level of the Rhine. The town lies at the shallowest part of the Middle Rhine, which ships carrying freight from the North Sea ports must pass on their way to the south-west of Germany. When the gauge falls to 78 centimetres, a low-water threshold is declared, and at that level four times as many barges are needed to carry the same volume of goods as at the high level of 250 centimetres. The town has a Roman Catholic and an Evangelical church.
kaunas: Kaunas stands at the confluence of Lithuania's two largest rivers, the Nemunas and the Neris, near the Kaunas Reservoir, the largest body of water in the country. Its name is of Lithuanian origin and most likely derives from the personal name of an unknown ruler of the castle, a name taken from an adjective meaning one who likes to fight. A 16th-century legend in the Bychowiec Chronicle instead says that it was founded by Romans led by a patrician named Palemon, who fled from the Emperor Nero, and that his son Kunas built a fortress at the confluence.

A settlement stood on the site of the Old Town by the 10th century at the latest. Kaunas was first mentioned in written sources in 1361. The brick Kaunas Castle defended its residents against the Teutonic Order, and with the castle at Grodno it was one of only two brick castles on the Nemunas, which was the main front line between the Crusaders and the Lithuanians. In 1408 Vytautas the Great granted Kaunas city rights and chose its coat of arms, which shows an aurochs. After the third partition of the Polish–Lithuanian state in 1795 the city passed to the Russian Empire, and Napoleon's Grand Army passed through it twice in 1812, devastating it both times.

After Vilnius was occupied by the Red Army in 1919, the Lithuanian government made Kaunas its main base, and it became the temporary capital when Vilnius was annexed by Poland. It held that position until 28 October 1939. In June 1940 the Soviet Union occupied and annexed Lithuania. On 29 June 1941 over 9,200 Jews were murdered in the Kaunas pogrom, and nearly 50,000 people, over 30,000 of them Jews, were killed at the Ninth Fort during the Nazi occupation. The Red Army took the city on 1 August 1944, and the region became a centre of the partisan war against Soviet rule, which ended by 1953.

Kaunas is the second-largest city in Lithuania after Vilnius and the capital of Kaunas County. It is the seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Kaunas. The interwar city was known for its Art Deco and Lithuanian National Revival architecture, and in 2023 it became a World Heritage Site.
kavad-i: Kavad was born in 473, a son of the Sasanian shah Peroz I. The nobles crowned him in 488, at the age of 15, to replace his deposed and unpopular uncle Balash. He inherited an empire at its lowest ebb. Drought, famine and defeats by the Hephthalites had emptied the treasury, since the Hephthalites had seized large parts of the eastern provinces and exacted heavy tribute, and rebellions were under way in Armenia and Iberia. The nobility and clergy acted as king-makers. For his first five years Kavad was tutored by Sukhra, who was the real ruler, and in 493 Kavad exiled him to Shiraz.

Kavad turned to the priest Mazdak, whose movement called for the sharing of wealth and property and loosened marriage laws, and used it to curb the nobility and clergy. Royal granaries were distributed and land was shared among the lower classes. The nobles deposed him and imprisoned him in the Castle of Oblivion in Khuzestan, replacing him with his brother Jamasp. He escaped with the help of his wife and his friend Siyawush, fled east and regained the throne with a Hephthalite army, in 498/9.

In his second reign he began reforms later completed by his son Khosrow I: a poll tax, a review of taxable land, and a division of the empire into four frontier regions, each under a spāhbed. By the 520s he no longer needed Mazdak and withdrew his support; the Shahnameh tells of the killing of Mazdak's followers under Khosrow, though the story's validity is uncertain. When the Byzantine emperor Anastasius I refused subsidies, Kavad invaded in 502, starting the Anastasian War, took Amida after a three-month siege, and made peace in 506. By 513 he had retaken Khorasan from the Hephthalites.

In 528 the Iberian War began with the Byzantines, partly because they would not recognise Khosrow as Kavad's heir. It was largely indecisive, though the Sasanians lost at Dara and Satala. Kavad died of an illness on 13 September 531 while his army besieged Martyropolis. Khosrow I succeeded him and executed his brothers and their offspring after a plot to put another Kavad on the throne. Historians regard Kavad's reign as a turning point and him as one of the most effective Sasanian kings; the Iranologist Nikolaus Schindel called him a genius in his own right, even if of a somewhat Machiavellian type.
kavad-ii: Kavad II was born Sheroe, a son of Khosrow II and Maria, a Byzantine woman whom some Eastern sources considered a daughter of the emperor Maurice. Byzantine sources do not report that Maurice had such a daughter, and the historian Nikolaus Schindel thinks Maria more likely belonged to the Sasanian aristocracy. Khosrow II's war on the Byzantines, begun in 602, had turned against him by 627, when Emperor Heraclius was seizing territory in Adurbadagan. Sheroe was held in a fortress outside Babylon with some brothers.

After the Byzantines sacked Dastagird on 6 January 628, Khosrow II fled to Ctesiphon and planned to crown his son Mardanshah as heir. Learning of this, Sheroe wrote to the general Gurdanasp, leader of the opposition, promising to make peace with the Byzantines and to raise the conspirators' rank.

The conspirators staged the coup on the night of 23 and 24 February 628, having first assured themselves through envoys that Heraclius would talk peace. Khosrow II was found hiding in the palace gardens and imprisoned, and Sheroe took the throne on 25 February as Kavad. His backers pressed him to kill his father, and Khosrow II was executed on 28 February 628 by Mihr Hormozd. Kavad II also had all his brothers, seventeen or eighteen, executed, at the urging of his minister Piruz Khosrow; his sisters Boran and Azarmidokht reproached him, and he is said to have felt remorse.

He sent envoys to Heraclius, addressing him as brother in a letter that survives in part in the Chronicon Paschale. Most of Khosrow's conquests were to be given up, ending the war of 602 to 628, though the general Shahrbaraz refused to withdraw from Byzantine territory. Kavad II also let the Church of the East again nominate its own catholicos, a privilege lost since 609.

Kavad II died of the Plague of Sheroe, which al-Masudi said killed at least a third of Iran's population; sources differ on whether he ruled six, seven or eight months. His seven-year-old son Ardashir III succeeded him under the regent Mah-Adhur Gushnasp.

Al-Tabari judged him a bad ruler, while the Chronicle of Seert is kinder. Michael Bonner and Touraj Daryaee blamed the killing of his brothers for the disruption of the succession, whereas Schindel suggests it may have averted a civil war and that a longer reign might have prevented the collapse of the Sasanian state and the Arab-Islamic conquest.
kayah-state: Kayah State, also called Karenni State, lies in eastern Myanmar. It is bounded on the north by Shan State, on the east by Thailand's Mae Hong Son Province, and on the south and west by Kayin State. Its area is 11,670 square kilometres, and its capital is Loikaw. The relief is mountainous, and the Salween River crosses the state. The Lawpita Dam, built in 1950 under a reparation agreement with Japan, produces a quarter of the hydroelectric power generated in Myanmar. The Karenni, also known as Red Karen or Kayah, a Sino-Tibetan people, form the majority of the population, with Bamar, Shan and Karen minorities.

The Karenni States were a group of states, among them Kantarawadi, Kyebogyi and Bawlake, south of the Federated Shan States and east of British Burma. In 1875 Britain and the Burmese king Mindon Min recognised the area as belonging neither to Burma nor to Britain, so the states were never fully incorporated into British Burma. In 1892 their rulers accepted a stipend and were recognised as tributary. In the 1930s the Mawchi Mine in Bawlake was the most important source of tungsten in the world.

The 1947 Constitution of the Union of Burma provided that the three states be amalgamated into one constituent state, Karenni State, with the possibility of secession after ten years. Karenni accounts say that the central government then invaded, and on 9 August 1948 the leader U Bee Htu Re began a resistance, remembered as Karenni Resistance Day. He was assassinated on 8 September 1948 by central government militia, a date remembered as Karenni Martyr's Day. In 1952 the former Shan state of Mong Pai was added and the whole renamed Kayah State, possibly, according to one view, to drive a wedge between the Karenni and the Karen people in Karen State, both of whom were fighting for independence.

In 1957 pro-independence groups formed the Karenni National Progressive Party, backed by its own army, the Karenni Army, which has fought ever since apart from a brief ceasefire in 1995. In 1996 the State Law and Order Restoration Council stepped up its campaign with a population transfer, forcibly moving villagers to relocation sites to deprive the pro-independence forces of support, and the Myanmar government has been accused of massive human rights violations in the region.

Kayah State is the smallest of Myanmar's seven states, with a population of 286,738 in the 2014 census, though it is larger than Yangon Region. The Karenni, Shan, Intha, Bamar and Pa-O live in different parts of the state, and ethnolinguists distinguish many groups. In the 2014 census Buddhists made up 49.9 per cent of the population and Christians 45.8 per cent.
kayak: The original kayaks (Inuktitut qajaq, Yup'ik qayaq, Aleut iqyax) were developed by the Inuit, Yup'ik and Aleut, who used them on inland lakes, rivers and the coastal waters of the Arctic Ocean, North Atlantic, Bering Sea and North Pacific. Western Alaskan Natives built the frame of wood, while the eastern Inuit used whalebone because their landscape had no trees. The oldest surviving kayaks are in the North America department of the State Museum of Ethnology in Munich, the oldest dating from 1577.

Subarctic peoples made several kinds of boat for different purposes. The Aleut baidarka was built with two or three cockpits to carry hunters, passengers or goods. The umiak was a large open-sea canoe of seal skins and wood, between 5.2 and 9.1 m long, originally paddled with single-bladed paddles by more than one paddler.

The traditional kayak has an enclosed deck and one or more cockpits, each seating one paddler, which sets it apart from an open-deck canoe. The cockpit is sometimes covered by a spray deck that keeps out waves and splashes. The paddler's body is part of the structure, and design is largely a matter of trade-offs, such as directional stability against manoeuvrability and stability against speed. In general a longer kayak is faster and tracks better, and a shorter one turns more easily.

Modern kayaks are usually made of fibreglass or of rotationally moulded polyethylene and are mostly commercial products, rather than boats built by their users. They serve touring, racing, whitewater, surf, fishing and recreational purposes, and the term is now applied even to sit-on-top craft and inflatables that look little like the traditional boat.

Contemporary traditional-style kayaks trace their origins mainly to the native boats of Alaska, northern Canada and south-west Greenland. John MacGregor introduced a kayak to England and Europe in 1860. Folding kayaks with collapsible wooden frames covered in rubberised canvas, called foldboats, became widely popular in Europe from 1907, when Johannes Klepper and others began to mass-produce them. By 1929 Klepper and Company were making 90 foldboats a day, and by the mid-1930s an estimated half a million were in use in Europe. First Nation masters of the roll taught that technique to Europeans in these years.

Kayaks were adapted for military use in the Second World War, mainly by British Commandos and special forces; the Royal Marines Boom Patrol Detachment made what is perhaps the best-known use of them in the Operation Frankton raid on Bordeaux harbour.
kayes: Kayes lies in western Mali on the Sénégal River, about 420 kilometres north-west of Bamako, and is the capital of the administrative region of the same name. It had 127,368 inhabitants at the 2009 census. The name derives from the Soninke language, and several etymologies are possible: kharré, a low humid place that floods in the rainy season, kayé, a type of grass, or khayé, the Soninke name for the rhun palm.

The climate is hot and semi-arid, with all the rainfall between June and October, around 650 millimetres a year. The town is nicknamed the pressure cooker of Africa for its extreme heat, which the iron-rich mountains around it are said to increase.

The area around Kayes was historically part of the Soninke states of Diarra and Gajaaga. The important trading centre of Goundiourou, known in Arabic sources as Ghiyaru, stood just across the river and was later rebuilt just south of the modern city. Kayes itself was founded in the second half of the 19th century, when Guéssé Sidy, a prince of Khasso, established a base to protect the western approaches to the kingdom's capital, Medina.

Before French expansion Kayes was still a small village. In 1881 the French chose it for a fort and barracks, the headquarters of their presence in the central Sudan, since Medina was difficult to reach by boat. By 1886 the post was fortified, and by 1889 a market town of 6,000 people had grown up around it. Kayes was the furthest point reachable by boat on the Sénégal, and the French built a railway from there to Bafoulabe, completed in 1890, which reached Bamako in 1904. A line to Thiès, begun in 1907 and interrupted by the First World War, was completed in 1923.

In 1892 Kayes became the capital of the French Sudan. Bamako replaced it as capital of the state of Haut Sénégal-Niger on 17 October 1899 and of all French Sudan in 1908. During the Second World War part of Poland's gold reserve, evacuated in 1939, was stored in Kayes for several years before being sent to the United States in 1944.

Kayes lies on the Route Nationale 1, 612 km by road from Bamako and 96 km from the border with Senegal, and has an international airport and a station on the Dakar-Niger Railway. The area is rich in gold and iron. Sites nearby include the Fort du Médine, the Félou Falls, the Gouina Falls, the tata of Koniakari built by El Hadj Umar Tall, and the Manantali Dam.
kayqubad-i: Alā ad-Dīn Kayqubād was born about 1192, the second son of the Seljuk sultan Kaykhusraw, who gave him the title malik and the governorship of Tokat while he was young. When the sultan died after the battle of Alaşehir in 1211, Kayqubad and his elder brother Kaykaus struggled for the throne.

Kayqubad had allies in Leo I, king of Cilician Armenia, and in his uncle Tughrilshah, ruler of Erzurum, but most of the emirs supported Kaykaus. He fled to the fortress at Ankara and sought help from the Turkman tribes of Kastamonu, but was soon caught and imprisoned by his brother in a fortress in western Anatolia. Kaykaus died unexpectedly in 1219 or 1220, and Kayqubad was released and became sultan.

Kayqubad expanded the sultanate at the expense of the Mengujek Beylik and the Ayyubids, and established a Seljuk presence on the Mediterranean by taking the port of Kalon Oros, later renamed Ala'iyya after him. He reduced Cilician Armenia to a vassal state and, in 1221 or 1222, launched a naval attack on Sudak that defeated the combined forces of the Rus and the Cumans. Jalal al-Din Mangburni, fleeing the Mongol destruction of the Khwarezmian Empire, unsettled Anatolia, and Kayqubad first sought an alliance against the Mongols.

When it failed he defeated Jalal al-Din at the Battle of Yassıçimen, between Sivas and Erzincan, in 1230, and established Seljuk rule over Erzurum, Ahlat and the Lake Van region. The Artuqids and the Ayyubids of Syria recognised his sovereignty. In 1234 he defeated the allied Ayyubid forces under al-Kamil, took Siverek, Urfa, Harran and Raqqa, and forced the Komnenos dynasty of the Empire of Trebizond to renew its pledges of vassalage. He also captured several fortresses in Georgia, and the queen of Georgia gave her daughter Tamar in marriage to his son Kaykhusraw II.

Kayqubad died at Kayseri on 31 May 1237, given poison at a feast; poison was later found in DNA analysis of his bones. He was the last of his line to die independent. Kaykhusraw II took the throne and had his half-brothers Rukn al-Din and Kilij Arslan and their mother strangled.

Kayqubad built a large number of mosques, medreses, caravanserais, bridges and hospitals, completed the Seljuk Palace in Konya, and built the Kubadabad Palace on Lake Beyşehir, the castle and Red Tower at Alanya and the citadel walls of Konya. After the Mongol invasion the people of Anatolia looked back on his reign as a golden age, and later beylik rulers traced their pedigrees to him.
kayseri: The city lies on a low spur at the foot of Mount Erciyes, a dormant volcano that rises to 3,917 metres, more than 1,500 metres above the city's mean altitude. In antiquity the mountain was Mount Argaeus. The site stood at a crossing of trade routes: that from Sinope to the Euphrates, and the Persian Royal Road from Sardis to Susa during more than two centuries of Achaemenid rule. In Roman times a route from Ephesus to the east crossed it as well.

Kayseri has been equated with the early Hittite kingdom of Kussara, mentioned in early Assyrian trading records, and a first period of prosperity is dated to about 2000 BCE, when it served as a trading post between Assyrians and Hittites. As Mazaca it was the residence of the kings of Cappadocia. According to Armenian tradition it was founded by Mishak. In 14 CE the last king, Archelaus, renamed it Caesarea in Cappadocia in honour of Augustus. In the fourth century Basil of Caesarea founded there a large complex of charitable institutions, a monastery and churches, known as the Basiliad.

From the mid-seventh century Arab attacks on Cappadocia became common and the city was besieged several times; Muawiyah took it temporarily in 647. The Seljuk ruler Alp Arslan demolished the city and massacred its population in 1067, and it stood uninhabited for about half a century. The Danishmendids rebuilt it in 1134. Under the Sultanate of Rum, from 1178 to 1243, it was one of the sultanate's most important centres, until it fell to the Mongols in 1243. In 1277 Sultan Baybars, after his victory at Elbistan, entered the city and massacred its Christians while sparing the Muslim inhabitants. The Eretnids held it in the fourteenth century and the Ottomans took it in 1515.

The Seljuk period left the Hunat Hatun Complex, the Kiliç Arslan Mosque, the Grand Mosque and the Gevher Nesibe hospital. The Grand Mosque was begun by the Danishmend emir Melik Mehmed Gazi and finished by the Seljuks. During the Turkish War of Independence the building of the Kayseri Lyceum housed the Turkish Grand National Assembly while the Greek army advanced on Ankara.

Kayseri is the capital of Kayseri province in Central Anatolia. Its huge basalt walls, dating to the reign of Justinian in the sixth century, were repeatedly repaired by Seljuks, Ottomans and later authorities. The suburb of Talas was the ancestral home of Calouste Gulbenkian, Aristotle Onassis and Elia Kazan, and the architect Mimar Sinan was born in 1490 at Ağırnas nearby. The archaeological site of Kanesh-Kültepe lies 20 km to the north-east. Public investment in the 1920s and 1930s brought a textile factory and an aircraft factory to the city, and its merchants later built an industrial base.
kaysone-phomvihane: Kaysone Phomvihane was born on 13 December 1920 in Naxeng village, Savannakhet Province, in what was then French Indochina. His father, Nguyễn Trí Loan, a Vietnamese, was a civil servant in the French colonial administration, and his mother, Nang Dok, was a Lao farmer. He studied in Hanoi, first medicine and then law, without completing a degree. He later said he became a revolutionary at sixteen out of patriotism. In Hanoi he joined student activities linked to the Indochinese Communist Party and protested against the Japanese occupation, and he received his first military and political training from the Viet Minh.

On 23 August 1945 Kaysone took part in seizing power from the Japanese in Savannakhet. On 20 January 1949 he founded the Lao Issara army, forerunner of the Lao People's Army, and in August 1950 became Minister of Defence in the resistance government formed under Souphanouvong. The Lao People's Party was founded on 22 March 1955 at Nameo village and elected him general secretary. Although Souphanouvong was the movement's public leader, real power lay with Kaysone. After fighting resumed in 1964 he moved the leadership into caves at Viengxay, where they withstood American bombing. The party was renamed the Lao People's Revolutionary Party in 1972.

After the fall of Saigon in April 1975 the party took power with little bloodshed. On 2 December 1975 Kaysone presided over the session that proclaimed the Lao People's Democratic Republic and became its first prime minister. He kept Laos closely allied with Vietnam, and sided with it in the split with China in 1978. At the Fourth Party Congress in November 1986 he launched chintanakan mai, the New Economic Mechanism, which gradually opened the economy to market forces within a socialist framework.

In October 1990 three officials who had called for a multiparty system and free elections were arrested; Kaysone held to Marxism-Leninism and the party's monopoly of power. At the Fifth Party Congress in March 1991 he became party chairman, and in August 1991 the Supreme People's Assembly adopted the first constitution and elected him president. He died in Vientiane on 21 November 1992, aged 71, and was given a state funeral with Buddhist rites.

In Laos he is revered as a Father of the Nation. Statues of him were placed in every provincial capital, and a museum in his honour was built in Vientiane. In January 2016 the party's Tenth Congress placed Kaysone Phomvihane Thought alongside Marxism-Leninism as its ideological foundation.
kazan: Kazan lies at the confluence of the Volga and the Kazanka rivers. In Tatar a kazan is a cauldron, and the name perhaps describes the topographic basin around the city. Its central part is divided by the Bolaq canal and Kaban Lakes into two districts: the Kazan Posad, historically Russian, on the hill, and the Old Tatar Quarter, historically Tatar, between the canal and the Volga, where the mosques stand. Its symbol is Zilant, a mythical dragon-like creature, and the first official coat of arms was approved on 18 October 1781.

According to the official version adopted today, the city is more than 1,000 years old, with an estimated date of the urban settlement of 1004 to 1005. The dating rests on finds in the Kazan Kremlin, among them a Czech coin, remains of masonry and a wooden city fence, and handicrafts.

In 1552 Tsar Ivan the Terrible conquered the city after a siege. During the governorship of Alexander Gorbaty-Shuysky most of the Tatar residents were forcibly Christianised or deported, and mosques and palaces were ruined. The survivors were moved 50 kilometres away, and Tatars in Russian service were settled in the Tatar Bistäse near the city wall. Several great fires destroyed much of the city, and after one of them, in 1579, the icon Our Lady of Kazan was discovered there.

In 1708 the Tsardom of Kazan was abolished and Kazan became the seat of Kazan Governorate. After a visit by Peter the Great it became a centre of shipbuilding for the Caspian fleet. Pugachev's Rebellion, which began in 1773, seized and largely destroyed the city, which was rebuilt under Catherine the Great.

In 1918 Kazan was the capital of the Idel-Ural State, which the Bolshevik government suppressed, and in August of that year the Czechoslovak Legions briefly occupied it. In 1920 it became the centre of the Tatar Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic. From the Treaty of Rapallo of 1922 until 1933 the German and Russian armies jointly ran the Kama tank school there.

Kazan is the capital and largest city of Tatarstan, with over 1.3 million inhabitants, and the most populous city on the Volga. It is known for the mix of Tatar and Russian cultures. The Kazan Kremlin, a citadel declared a World Heritage Site in 2000, holds the five-domed Annunciation Cathedral of 1561 to 1562 and the Söyembikä Tower, named after the last queen of Kazan.
kazanlak: Kazanlak lies in Stara Zagora Province, in the middle of the Kazanlak Valley at the foot of the Balkan Mountains. The valley formed in the Quaternary Period, when the Balkan and Sredna Gora ranges rose, and hot mineral springs near Ovoshtnik, Yagoda and Pavel Banya mark its fault line. It is drained by the Tundzha river, which rises in the highest part of the Balkan east of Mount Botev and flows on to join the Maritsa. The average altitude is 350 m, and the soils suit oil-producing crops and herbs.

The oldest settlement in the area of the modern town dates from the Neolithic, in the sixth to fifth millennium BCE. In the fourth and third centuries BCE the lands on the upper Tundzha lay within the dominion of the Thracian ruler Seuthes III and held an important place in Hellenistic Thrace. The Thracian city of Seuthopolis was uncovered near Kazanlak when the Koprinka Reservoir was built. Close to it stands a Thracian tomb with a vaulted brick tholos, a narrow corridor and a round burial chamber, painted with murals of a Thracian couple at a ritual funeral feast. It belongs to a large necropolis, in a region where more than a thousand tombs of kings and aristocrats are found.

After the liberation of Bulgaria the town numbered about 9,000 people in the 1880s, and it grew steadily by migration from the countryside, passing 60,000 at its peak in 1985. The Iskra chitalishte, a reading centre founded in 1860, holds a library, theatre, cinema and museum, and it hosted the first Bulgarian opera, Siromahkinya. The Iskra Town History Museum was founded on 29 June 1901 by Peter Topuzov.

Kazanlak is the centre of rose oil extraction in Bulgaria, and the oil-producing rose of Kazanlak is one of the country's widely recognised national symbols. The town's Rose Museum began as a small exhibition in 1967 and became an independent museum in 1969. The Thracian tomb has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1979. Nearby, the Shipka National Park preserves the battlefield of the Russian-Turkish Liberation War of the 1870s, with the Freedom Monument opened in 1934.
kazanlak-tomb: The Thracian Tomb of Kazanlak is a vaulted-brickwork beehive, or tholos, tomb near the town of Kazanlak in central Bulgaria. It is part of a large royal Thracian necropolis in the Valley of the Thracian Rulers, near the ancient Thracian capital of Seuthopolis, in a region where more than a thousand tombs of royalty and members of the Thracian aristocracy can be found. The tomb lies in the Kazanlak Valley, enclosed between the Balkan Mountains to the north and the Sredna Gora range to the south.

The site consists of a narrow corridor leading to a round, domed chamber of the size required for the burial. Both are painted with murals in fresco, showing a Thracian couple at a ritual funeral feast. The walls were painted a sanguine or dark reddish colour.

The dome mural shows a seated couple, on separate ornate chairs, grasping each other's wrists as others approach in a procession with trays and various items. Horn musicians play as they walk. Saddled horses are led or held without riders, an attendant holds the team of horses drawing an awaiting chariot, and a chariot race in progress is depicted at the top of the dome. The border at the base of the dome has cattle skulls draped with scarves across their horns, alternating with an equilateral-cross design interpreted as a flower. Other bands include an egg-and-dart pattern of Hellenistic style.

The art historian Lyudmila Zhivkova interprets the shared gesture of the central figures as a moment of tenderness and equality, but not all specialists share that reading. The paintings are the best-preserved artistic works of the Hellenistic period in Bulgaria, and the monument has been on UNESCO's World Heritage list since 1979. To protect the delicate paintings the tomb is closed to the public, and a full-size exact replica was built nearby for visitors. The seated woman of the mural appears on the reverse of the Bulgarian 50 stotinki coin issued in 2005.
kazi-nazrul-islam: Nazrul Islam was born on 24 May 1899 in Churulia, in the Burdwan district of the Bengal Presidency, into a Bengali Muslim family. His father, Kazi Faqeer Ahmed, was the imam and caretaker of the local Pirpukur mosque. After his father's death in 1908, at the age of ten, Nazrul took his place as caretaker and later worked as muezzin. Attracted to folk theatre, he joined a travelling group run by his uncle Fazle Karim, for which he acted and wrote songs, poems and plays, among them plays on characters of the Mahabharata. Through this work he began to study Bengali and Sanskrit literature and the Puranas.

He joined the British Indian Army in late 1917 and left in 1920, settling in Calcutta, where he published his novel Bandhan-hara in 1920. His poem Bidrohi, The Rebel, and his publication Dhumketu, The Comet, made him known as the Rebel Poet and drew him into the independence movement. In 1930 his book Pralayshikha was banned and he was charged with sedition; he was jailed and released in 1931, after the Gandhi–Irwin Pact.

Lacking formal education, Nazrul did not follow the conventions of Rabindranath Tagore and faced criticism from Tagore's followers, though he looked to Tagore as a mentor. He introduced the ghazal into Bengali and used many Arabic and Persian words. Between 1928 and 1935 he published ten volumes with 800 songs, over 600 of them based on classical ragas. His songs, nearly 4,000 in all, are known as Nazrul Gīti. He also directed a film and from 1939 supervised music programmes for Calcutta Radio.

Nazrul wrote that quarrels between religions were those of priests and imams, not of ordinary Hindus and Muslims, and opposed religious, caste and gender bigotry; fundamentalists condemned his views. In the early 1940s he began to lose his voice and memory, and in Vienna the neurosurgeon Hans Hoff diagnosed Pick's disease, judged incurable.

On 24 May 1972, with the consent of India, Bangladesh brought him to Dhaka. He was given Bangladeshi citizenship in February 1976 and died on 29 August 1976. He received the Padma Bhushan in 1960. His writings inspired Bengalis in the Bangladesh Liberation War.
kazys-grinius: Kazys Grinius was born on 17 December 1866 at Selema, near Marijampolė, in Congress Poland, then part of the Russian Empire, the third of eleven children of a farmer with 15 hectares. At school he helped publish a newspaper inspired by the first Lithuanian newspaper Aušra and smuggled banned Lithuanian publications from Prussia. He studied medicine at Imperial Moscow University and led a secret society of Lithuanian students. After practising as a doctor in Marijampolė and elsewhere, he helped found the Lithuanian Democratic Party in 1902, and was jailed several times by the Tsarist authorities for cultural activism.

During the First World War he worked in the northern Caucasus, where he cared for Lithuanian refugees. At Kislovodsk, on 8 October 1918, Bolshevik forces shot his wife and fatally injured his daughter. He returned to Lithuania in November.

Grinius led a bloc of the Popular Socialist Democrats and the Peasant Union at the elections to the Constituent Assembly in April 1920, and on 19 June 1920 became prime minister. His government signed a peace treaty with the Soviet Union, settled the border with Poland and saw Lithuania accepted into the League of Nations; it also reformed taxes and founded Vytautas Magnus University. The coalition broke up and he resigned in 1922. He helped prepare the permanent constitution and sat in the Seimas as a defender of press freedom and minority rights.

The Third Seimas elected him President on 7 June 1926. He signed a non-aggression pact with the Soviet Union that recognised Lithuanian rights to the Vilnius region, and ended martial law. On 17 December 1926, his birthday, nationalists took control of the military and civilian institutions, arrested him and Mykolas Sleževičius and installed a new government under Antanas Smetona. Grinius resigned to 'save Lithuania from possible misfortunes'. Smetona's party said a Communist takeover was imminent; Grinius's memoirs say this was false.

Grinius returned to medicine in Kaunas. In 1942, under German occupation, he signed a memorandum protesting repression of the local population, Jews included, and was deported to Selema. From October 1941 to spring 1942 he and his wife Kristina hid a Jewish acquaintance, Dmitry Gelpernas, and he was recognised as Righteous Among the Nations in 2016. In 1944 he emigrated to the West, in 1947 to the United States, and he died in Chicago on 4 June 1950. His remains were buried near Selema in 1994.
kde-domov-muj: The song was written by Josef Kajetán Tyl for his comedy Fidlovačka and set to music by František Škroup. Tyl is said to have considered leaving it out of the play because he doubted its quality. It nevertheless soon became the most popular song of Fidlovačka, which gained popularity among Czechs who were seeking to revive their identity within the Habsburg monarchy, and it quickly became their unofficial patriotic anthem.

Soon after Czechoslovakia was formed in 1918, the first verse of the song became the Czech part of the national anthem, followed by the first stanza of the Slovak song Nad Tatrou sa blýska, with official translations into German and Hungarian. During the German-occupied Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia from 1939 to 1945 the state kept the song as its anthem. It was usually played alongside the German anthems, the Deutschlandlied and the Nazi Horst-Wessel-Lied.

When Czechoslovakia split in December 1992, the Czech Republic kept Kde domov můj and Slovakia kept Nad Tatrou sa blýska. Slovakia extended its anthem with a second verse, but the Czech anthem was adopted unextended, in its single-verse version, and its lyrics are fixed in Czech Act No. 3/1993.

The melody has been taken up by other composers. Johann Strauss the Younger included its motif in his Slaven-Potpourri of 1847, and in 1882 Antonín Dvořák used it in his overture to Šamberk's play Josef Kajetán Tyl, which is often performed alone as Domov můj, a concert work of some ten minutes. Rainer Maria Rilke paid tribute to it in two poems in German, published in 1895.

Otakar Jeremiáš orchestrated the anthem in three versions, for large orchestra in 1930, for small orchestra in 1932 and for organ and orchestra in 1932, and they are still performed. In 2008 the Czech government released an official recording of the anthem by the National Theatre Opera Chorus and Orchestra, in four versions.
kebra-nagast: The Kebra Nagast is divided into 117 chapters and is clearly a composite work, which Edward Ullendorff called a gigantic conflation of cycles of tales. According to the colophon on most copies, it was written in Coptic, translated into Arabic in 1225, and then put into Ge'ez by a team of Ethiopian clerics, which has led scholars to date its composition to between 1314 and 1322.

Other sources attribute it to a fourteenth-century writer, Nebura'ed Yeshaq of Aksum. Many scholars doubt that a Coptic version ever existed. Its sources include the Hebrew Bible, the Book of Enoch, the Book of Jubilees, Syriac works, rabbinical material and patristic writings. Historian Stuart Munro-Hay noted that no record shows Ethiopian monarchs claiming descent from Solomon before the 13th century.

The text is framed as a debate among the 318 fathers of the First Council of Nicaea on the question of what the glory of kings consists in. It centres on Queen Makeda, known as the Queen of Sheba, who travels to Jerusalem after hearing of Solomon's wisdom and there turns from worship of the sun to the God of Israel. Solomon tricks her into sleeping with him and gives her a ring, and she bears Menelik on the way home.

At 22 Menelik visits Solomon and is recognised by the ring. The young men sent home with him take the Ark of the Covenant from the Temple, and Menelik learns on the journey that it is with him. The Ark flies him home, and Makeda abdicates in his favour. A later part of the work is a collection of prophecies, with a marked anti-Jewish tone, which ends by foretelling that Ethiopia's power will eclipse that of Rome.

Modern scholarship holds that the stories were largely created to legitimise the Solomonic dynasty's rise to power in the 13th century, which ended the Zagwe dynasty. Harold G. Marcus calls the work a pastiche of legends, and David Northrup calls the descent from Solomon and Sheba a myth. Many Ethiopian Christians nevertheless hold it to be historically reliable, and Ullendorff described it as the repository of Ethiopian national and religious feelings.

The Jesuit Pedro Páez translated much of it in the early 1620s. James Bruce brought a copy home from Gondar, which is now in the Bodleian Library, and the full text was first published by Carl Bezold in 1905. E. A. Wallis Budge's English translation appeared in 1922 and 1932.
kedarnath: Kedarnath lies in the Himalayas about 3,583 metres above sea level, on a barren stretch of land beside the Mandakini River, near the Chorabari Glacier. It is 223 kilometres from Rishikesh and about 86.5 kilometres from Rudraprayag, and the nearest roadhead is at Gaurikund, about 16 kilometres away. Behind the town and its temple stand Kedarnath peak at 6,940 metres and the Kedar Dome at 6,831 metres. Heavy snow closes the temple in winter. From November to April the palanquin carrying the idol of Kedarnath is taken to the Omkareshwar Temple in Ukhimath, and priests and summer residents move to nearby villages.

The name means Lord of the Field, from the Sanskrit kedara, field, and natha, lord. The Kashi Kedara Mahatmya says that the crop of liberation grows here. The construction of the temple is credited to the Pandava brothers of the Mahabharata, though that epic names no place called Kedarnath. One of the earliest references is in the Skanda Purana, from about the 7th or 8th century, which names Kedara as the place where Shiva released the waters of the Ganga from his matted hair, so forming the Ganges.

The temple is said to have been rebuilt by Adi Shankaracharya. Hagiographies based on Madhava's Sankshepa-Shankara-Vijaya say the 8th-century philosopher died near the Kedarnath mountains, while others, based on Anandagiri's Prachina-Shankara-Vijaya, say he died at Kanchipuram. The ruins of a monument to his purported resting place stand at Kedarnath. By the 12th century the site was a prominent pilgrimage centre, mentioned in the Kritya-kalpataru of the Gahadavala minister Bhatta Lakshmidhara.

Kedarnath is a town in Rudraprayag district and the most remote of the four Chota Char Dham pilgrimage sites. The 2011 census recorded a population of 830, though the numbers of pilgrims between May and October run into thousands a day. Nearby are the Bhairavnath Temple, whose deity is believed to protect the town in winter, the glacier-lake Chorabari Tal, the Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary and the Adi Shankaracharya Samadhi. On 16 and 17 June 2013 flash floods destroyed much of the town and killed thousands of people, but the temple itself survived.
keelung: Keelung lies in the northern part of Taiwan Island and covers 132.76 square kilometres. Mountains to the east, west and south separate it from its neighbouring county, while the northern part faces the ocean and has been a deep-water harbour since early times. The city is nicknamed the Rainy Port, with yearly rainfall averaging upwards of 3,700 millimetres, an effect related to the Kuroshio Current.

The Ketagalan were its first inhabitants. The Taiwanese name Ke-lâng, written with characters meaning rooster cage, is more likely derived from Ketagalan than from the shape of a mountain. In 1875 the late Qing authorities gave it the new official name Jilong, meaning base prosperous.

The Spanish expedition to Formosa in the early 17th century made the first contact with the West, and the Spanish built San Salvador de Quelung, a fort serving as an outpost of the Manila-based Spanish East Indies. From 1642 to 1661 Keelung was under Dutch control. The Dutch East India Company took over the Spanish fort, reduced its size and renamed it Fort Noort-Hollant. After Koxinga attacked Fort Zeelandia, the Dutch returned in 1663, but they left in 1668 after harassment by aboriginals, when trade with Qing China through Keelung fell short of their hopes.

In 1863 the Qing Empire opened Keelung as a trading port, and the city developed quickly on placer gold and high-quality coal from the Keelung River basin. An earthquake and tsunami in 1867 caused serious damage and cost hundreds of lives. During the Sino-French War the French attempted an invasion in the Keelung Campaign (1884–85). Liu Mingchuan, who led the defence of Taiwan, recruited Aboriginals to serve with the Chinese soldiers, and the Qing forces pinned the French down at Keelung for eight months before the French withdrew.

After the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895 handed Taiwan to Japan, a five-phase construction of Keelung Harbor began. By 1916 its trade exceeded that of Tamsui and Kaohsiung. The city was upgraded in 1924, and in the Pacific War it was nearly destroyed by Allied bombers. After the handover to the Republic of China in October 1945 the city and harbor were rebuilt, and by 1984 the harbor was the seventh largest container harbor in the world.

The Keelung Ghost Festival dates to 1855, when rival clans that had fought bitterly agreed to bury their dead together and keep the peace through competition in folk performances. It was the first folklore custom included in Taiwan's national cultural heritage list. The National Taiwan Ocean University stands in the city.
kefalonia: Kefalonia, also written Cephalonia, is the largest of the Ionian Islands and the sixth-largest island in Greece, after Crete, Euboea, Lesbos, Rhodes and Chios. The main island covers 773 square kilometres. Its highest mountain is Mount Ainos, at 1,628 metres, whose summit is covered with Greek fir and black pine and is a national park. Argostoli and Lixouri are its largest towns. The island lies just south-east of a major active fault zone where the Eurasian and Aegean plates meet, and a series of thrust faults is responsible for its continuing uplift.

Archaeological finds on the island go back to about 40,000 years before the present, and a survey in the Leivatho area has found dozens of sites from the Palaeolithic to the Venetian period. The Mycenaean era is represented in the small archaeological museum of Argostoli. In antiquity the people lived in four cities, Cranii, Sami, Pale and Pronnoi, which formed a federation called the tetrapolis. Legend explained the island's name through Cephalus, who helped Amphitryon of Mycenae in a war and was rewarded with the island of Same.

In the late Roman Empire Cephalonia belonged to the province of Achaea, and the four ancient cities survived into late antiquity, with Sami probably the capital. In 1222 the Frankish Crusaders established the Diocese of Kefalonia-Zakynthos. Turkish rule lasted until 1500, when a Spanish-Venetian army captured the island, a rare Venetian success in the Second Ottoman-Venetian War. Refugees from the lost Venetian fortresses of Modon and Coron and colonists from Crete arrived, and Venetian pressure for olive plantations led to the first exports of olive oil to Venice.

When France conquered Venice in 1797, Cephalonia became part of the French département of Ithaque. In 1798 a combined Russian and Turkish fleet forced the French out, and from 1799 to 1807 the island belonged to the Septinsular Republic, nominally under Ottoman sovereignty but protected by Russia. In 1864 it joined the Greek state with the other Ionian Islands.

In the Second World War Axis forces occupied the island, mostly Italian troops until late 1943. After Italy's armistice in September 1943 the Italian division Acqui, having voted in a referendum among its soldiers, fought the German forces that came to take control, which prevailed after the siege of Argostoli. The earthquake of 1953 was so destructive that of 200 olive presses working before it, thirteen remain. Argostoli is the seat of administration, and Cephalonia is a regional unit of the Ionian Islands region. Tourism, begun in the early 19th century, grew widely from the 1980s.
kehl: Kehl lies in the region of Baden on the Rhine, at the confluence with the smaller Kinzig, directly opposite Strasbourg. It has around 38,000 inhabitants and is the third-largest city of the Ortenaukreis after Offenburg and Lahr. Four bridges join it to Strasbourg: the Passerelle des Deux Rives for pedestrians and cyclists, the Bridge of Europe, the Beatus-Rhenanus Bridge for the tramway, and the Rhine Bridge for the railway. The Jardin des Deux Rives extends on both banks, and the two cities share some municipal services.

The village of Kehl was first mentioned in 1038, and the first permanent bridge to Strasbourg was completed in 1338. France took the place in 1678 as part of Strasbourg's defences, and in 1683 the architect Vauban turned it into a fortress. Louis XIV had annexed the Imperial City of Strasbourg in 1681, and the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697 confirmed this but restored the territories on the right bank to the Empire, so that Kehl passed the following year to the Margraviate of Baden. On 7 May 1770 Marie Antoinette was handed over by Austria to France on an island in the Rhine near Kehl, later called the Kommissionsinsel.

Kehl received town rights in 1774 from Charles Frederick, Margrave of Baden. It was badly damaged in the French Revolutionary Wars, above all in the Rhine Campaign of 1796, with two battles of Kehl and an Austrian siege that ended in its surrender on 9 January 1797. It was returned to Baden in 1803 and again in 1815, when the fortress was dismantled. The first port facility was built between 1842 and 1847, and the first railway bridge in 1861 gave a direct link from Paris to Vienna.

Under the Treaty of Versailles the harbour was placed under French administration for seven years. In September 1939 the population was evacuated to the Black Forest, since Kehl lay in the so-called Red Zone. On 10 November 1938 the synagogue was broken into and its ritual objects destroyed, Jewish men were deported to Dachau, and the building was demolished in 1939. France administered Kehl after the war and released it in stages between 1949 and 1953.

Kehl is a border city in Baden-Württemberg with a large Rhine port, the Häfen Kehl, and the seat of the Kehl University of Applied Sciences. Tramway line D from Strasbourg was extended to Kehl station in 2017 and to the town centre in 2018.
kemalism: Kemalism, also called Atatürkism, grew out of the efforts to save the Ottoman Empire that began chiefly with the Tanzimat reforms of the 19th century. The Young Ottomans tried to build an Ottomanism that would check the rising ethnic nationalisms, and after their suppression under Sultan Abdul Hamid II the Young Turks took up their legacy. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk spent his formative years in Salonica. In the army he joined the Committee of Union and Progress, abandoned Ottoman nationalism for Turkish nationalism and adopted a secular outlook.

His defence of Gallipoli in the First World War made his career, and after the Ottoman defeat he led the Turkish War of Independence against the Allies' planned partition of Anatolia and Eastern Thrace. By 1923 his government in Ankara had abolished the Ottoman monarchy and proclaimed a Republic.

Atatürk described his ideology as based on science and reason and avoided dogma. It rests on six principles, symbolised by the Six Arrows: republicanism, populism, nationalism, laicism, statism and reformism. Republicanism replaced dynastic rule with popular sovereignty and constitutional limits on government. Populism rejected class conflict in favour of national unity, and it also meant state supervision of religious schools and organisations. Laicism, closer to French laïcité than to the Anglo-American idea of secularism, aims to keep religion out of government and the reverse.

Its first steps were the abolition of the caliphate in March 1924 and the replacement of the Shaykh al-Islām by the Presidency of Religious Affairs. In 1926 the mejelle and shari'ah law codes gave way to an adapted Swiss Civil Code and penal codes modelled on German and Italian ones.

Statism meant that the state regulated economic life and entered fields private enterprise would not, and after the Great Depression it took an active part in investment, notably in infrastructure, power stations and iron and steel. Nationalism defined every citizen as a Turk, and reformism treated the changes as irreversible.

The six principles were written into the Turkish constitution as state ideology on 5 February 1937. The Republican People's Party, which Atatürk founded on 9 September 1923, carried them for decades, and later constitutions in 1961 and 1982 kept secularism, nationalism and democracy.

Abroad, observers in Germany, France, Britain and several countries farther east followed the Turkish transformation closely in the 1920s and 1930s. The Bolsheviks saw Kemalists as allies against Western imperialism. Historian Şükrü Hanioğlu calls Kemalism a scientifically sanctioned version of Turkish nationalism, drawing on Enlightenment ideas, positivism and republicanism.
kempten: Kempten is the largest town of the Allgäu, in Swabia, Bavaria. It is one of the oldest urban settlements in Germany. The area was possibly first settled by Celts, and the Greek geographer Strabo mentions a town of the Celtic Estiones named Kambodunon, which is considered the oldest written reference to any German city. No archaeological evidence has yet been found that this Celtic settlement existed.

In 15 BCE Roman troops led by Nero Claudius Drusus and his brother Tiberius conquered and destroyed the existing Celtic settlement. The town, Latinized as Cambodunum, was rebuilt on a classical Roman plan with baths, a forum and temples, first in wood and then in stone after a fire that destroyed almost the whole town in 69. It possibly served as capital of the province of Raetia in the first century before Augsburg took that role. The Alemanni destroyed it in 233, and the settlement moved to the Burghalde hill above the river Iller. In the middle of the 5th century the last Roman troops left and the Alemanni took the town over entirely.

The Franks destroyed the town again in 683, because it had supported an uprising against the Frankish kingdom. Around 700 two Benedictine monks from the Abbey of Saint Gall, Magnus von Füssen and Theodor, founded Kempten Abbey, the first monastery in the Allgäu. It became one of the most privileged of the Frankish Empire with the support of Charlemagne's wife Hildegard. After Magyar raids, Ulrich of Augsburg, who was also abbot, began rebuilding the monastery and the town in 941.

In 1213 Emperor Frederick II made the abbots members of the Reichstag and granted the Abbot of Kempten the title of Duke. In 1289 King Rudolf I granted privileges to the settlement in the valley, making it the Free Imperial City of Kempten. The last property rights of the abbots in the city were sold in 1525, and from then two independent cities of the same name lay side by side. Conflict grew when the Imperial City turned Protestant in 1527, in opposition to the Catholic abbey. Both were destroyed during the Thirty Years' War, by imperial forces and Swedish troops respectively. The abbey and the city came under Bavarian rule in 1802–03, and in 1819 the two cities were united.

Kempten had about 68,000 inhabitants in 2016. Among its sights are St Lorenz Basilica, commissioned in 1652 by the abbot Roman Giel of Gielsberg and acknowledged as the first large church built in Germany after the end of the Thirty Years' War, the Duke-Abbots' Residence, St Mang Church and the Archaeological Park Cambodunum, where excavations in the late 19th century and again in the 1950s uncovered the foundations of the Roman town.
kenneth-kaunda: Kenneth Kaunda was born on 28 April 1924 at Lubwa Mission in Chinsali, Northern Rhodesia, the youngest of eight children. His father, the Reverend David Kaunda, a Church of Scotland missionary and teacher born in Nyasaland, died when Kenneth was a child. His mother, Helen Nyirenda Kaunda, was also a teacher and the first African woman to teach in colonial Northern Rhodesia. He trained at the Munali Training Centre in Lusaka from 1941 to 1943 and became a teacher.

Kaunda entered politics in 1949 and in 1953 became Secretary General of the African National Congress under Harry Nkumbula. Kaunda broke with Nkumbula and founded the Zambian African National Congress in October 1958. It was banned in March 1959 and he served nine months in prison. He was elected president of its successor, the United National Independence Party (UNIP), in January 1960. UNIP won the elections of January 1964, and on 24 October 1964 he became the first president of independent Zambia.

The new state had a very poorly developed school system, with about a hundred university graduates, and Kaunda invested heavily in education; the University of Zambia opened in 1966. In April 1968 the Mulungushi Reforms began to bring foreign-owned companies under national control, and a number of mining firms were nationalised. From 1973 rising oil prices and falling copper prices cut state income and left Zambia in debt to the International Monetary Fund. Kaunda banned all parties except UNIP, and the Choma Declaration and a new constitution made Zambia a one-party state. He promoted an ideology he called Zambian Humanism.

He supported the movements against white minority rule in Rhodesia, South West Africa, Angola and Mozambique, allowing groups such as the African National Congress, ZAPU and SWAPO to operate from Zambia. The TAZARA Railway to Dar es Salaam, completed in 1975, gave Zambia a trade route that did not cross white-ruled territory.

After riots in 1990 and a failed coup attempt, Kaunda yielded to demands for multiparty politics. In the elections of 1991 Frederick Chiluba of the Movement for Multiparty Democracy won 75 percent of the vote to his 24. Kaunda handed power over on 2 November 1991, the second mainland African head of state to leave office peacefully after losing a free multiparty election. He retired from politics in 1998 and later worked against the spread of HIV/AIDS. He died on 17 June 2021, aged 97, and Zambia observed 21 days of national mourning.
kenneth-macalpin: Kenneth MacAlpin is believed to have been born around 810 on Iona. According to the traditional genealogy his father was Alpín mac Echdach, king of Dál Riada, but modern historians are sceptical about Alpín's reign, and the genealogy rests on a manuscript written under Malcolm III in the 11th century. A tradition makes Kenneth's grandmother a Pictish princess, a sister of Constantine I and Óengus II, which under Pictish custom would have given him a claim to the Pictish throne. His brother Donald I succeeded him. Dál Riada was mountainous and infertile, and it had lost its western territories in the Hebrides to Vikings.

The Chronicle of the Kings of Alba says Kenneth defeated the Picts and ruled them for 16 years. Most modern historians accept 843 as the year he became king of the Picts, though the Pictish king lists suggest the Pictish kingdom may have fallen in 849 or 850. Sources do not detail the conquest, and a later legend tells of a Pictish nobleman killed treacherously at a feast at Scone. After it, Scots from Dál Riada migrated in large numbers into Pictish lands, and the Picts' language and institutions quickly disappeared. In 848 or 849, according to the Chronicle, Kenneth moved relics from the abbey on Iona, where Viking raids made life untenable, to Dunkeld, and the Stone of Scone was moved to Scone.

Kenneth invaded Lothian in Northumbria six times and razed Melrose and Dunbar, while Britons from Strathclyde burnt Dunblane and Vikings ravaged the country from Clunie to Dunkeld. He married his daughters to the kings of Strathclyde and Ireland. The Chronicle of Melrose calls him one of the first Scottish lawgivers, but no laws survive.

Kenneth died in 858, most likely on 8 February, at Forteviot, of a tumour according to the Chronicle of the Kings of Alba, and was buried on Iona. His brother Donald I succeeded him by tanistry, and then his sons Causantín and Áed ruled in turn. The Alpínid dynasty, formed in this period, ruled until the beginning of the 11th century. Tradition makes him the founder of Scotland, but the current academic consensus is that he was not the first king of Alba. Like his immediate successors he bore the title king of the Picts, and Donald II was the first to be called king of Alba. Historians argue that his chief achievement was founding a new dynasty.
keoladeo-national-park: The park lies 2 kilometres south-east of Bharatpur and 55 kilometres west of Agra, and covers about 29 square kilometres. It is known locally as Ghana, a mosaic of dry grassland, woodland, swamp and seasonal wetland on the eastern edge of the land that becomes desert. A third of it is wetland with mounds, dykes and open water, which alternately wets and dries and so suits waterfowl. The uplands have tall and short grasses, and pockets of kadam woodland. The park holds 379 species of flowering plants, and the wetland is part of the Indo-Gangetic plain.

The wetland is regulated by people. It also protects Bharatpur's settlements from flash floods and gives pasture to local livestock. Water remains only in some depressions, and tube wells pump water into small hollows to save seeds, spores and other aquatic life, which helps in years of drought.

The area was a private duck-shooting preserve of the Maharaja of Bharatpur, and tradition dates its development as a reserve to 1899. Through the efforts of the ornithologist Salim Ali it became a bird sanctuary, and it was designated a Ramsar site in October 1981. It was established as a national park on 10 March 1982 and made a World Heritage Site in 1985 as a wetland of international importance for migratory waterfowl and the wintering ground of the rare Siberian crane.

Some 2,500 cattle and water buffalo had grazed there until grazing was banned in November 1982. The ban caused resentment and an attempted forced entry; police opened fire and eight people were killed. Without grazing, an amphibious grass blocks the channels, and the Rajasthan government has rejected a proposal to allow limited grazing. A project of 1992 to 1995 by India, Russia, the International Crane Foundation and the Wild Bird Society of Japan tried to build a resident Siberian crane population from captive-bred birds, and did not reach its aim. The last Siberian cranes recorded arrived in the winter of 2001–02.

More than 370 bird species have been recorded, and the park is an important staging ground for waterfowl arriving in the Indian subcontinent and leaving for breeding grounds in the western Palearctic. Common waterfowl include gadwall, shoveler, bar-headed goose, painted stork, spot-billed pelican and sarus crane. It also has 27 mammal species, among them nilgai, chital, sambar and blackbuck, and seven of Rajasthan's ten species of turtle. The park is a World Heritage Site and a Ramsar wetland, and water supply from the Ajan Bund reservoir has been irregular.
keraites: The Keraites first appear in history as the ruling faction of the Zubu, a large confederacy of tribes that dominated Mongolia during the 11th and 12th centuries and often fought the Liao dynasty of north China, which controlled much of Mongolia at the time. Their language is disputed. Names and titles of early leaders, such as Toghrul and the title buiruk ('commander'), are Turkic, and many scholars classify them as a Turkic people. Others, among them Vasily Bartold and Boris Vladimirtsov, hold that they spoke a Mongolic language, and Tao Zongyi listed them about 1366 among the 72 Mongol peoples.

After the Zubu broke up, the Keraites kept their dominance on the steppe. Their khanate had a central faction, which served as the khan's army and was drawn from many tribes, and an outer faction of tribes that pledged obedience but lived on their own pastures. Toghrul reigned from the 1160s to 1203 and became the blood-brother (anda) of Yesugei; Genghis Khan called him khan etseg, 'khan father'. In 1196 the Jin dynasty gave him the title Wang, hence Wang Khan. Fearing the growing power of Temüjin, the future Genghis Khan, he plotted with Jamukha against him.

In 1203 Temüjin defeated the Keraites, and Toghrul was killed by Naiman soldiers who did not recognise him. Temüjin dispersed the survivors among the other Mongol tribes. He married Toghrul's eldest niece Ibaqa, and his son Tolui married another niece, Sorghaghtani Bekhi, who became the mother of Möngke Khan and Kublai Khan.

The Keraites were converted to the Church of the East early in the 11th century. According to accounts by Mari ibn Suleiman and Bar Hebraeus, the khan, lost in a snowstorm about 1007, saw a vision of Saint Sergius of Samarkand and promised to become a Christian. He wrote to Abdisho, Metropolitan of Merv, and the king and 200,000 of his people were baptised. William of Rubruck, who visited Mongolia in 1254–1255, found the faith mixed with shamanism and Manicheism. Some versions of the Prester John legend identify that king with Toghrul.

Remnants of the Keraites lived along the Kara Irtysh in the late 14th century and were dispersed in the 1420s in the Mongol-Oirat wars fought by Uwais Khan. Afterwards they disappear as an identifiable group, though they are proposed as part of the ancestry of Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, Bashkir and Nogai groups.
kerala: Kerala is mainly a strip of coastal plains wedged between the Western Ghats and the Laccadive Sea, 38,863 square kilometres in area, with Karnataka to the northeast and Tamil Nadu to the east. Geographically it falls into three regions: the cool eastern highlands, the central midlands of rolling hills and the western coastal lowlands.

In Hindu tradition the land was won from the sea by the sage Parashurama, the sixth avatar of Vishnu, who threw his axe across the water so that the sea withdrew to where it landed. Archaeology shows Neolithic dolmens in the Marayur region and rock engravings in the Edakkal caves in Wayanad from about 6000 BCE. Sumerian records are said to show Kerala as a spice exporter from at least 3000 BCE, and Babylonians, Assyrians and Egyptians were drawn to the Malabar Coast in the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE, as were Arabs and Phoenicians.

The word Kerala first appears as Keralaputra, son of the Cheras, in an edict of the Maurya emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE. The Cheras were the earliest major dynasty of the region and rose through maritime commerce, but often faced invasion from the Chola and Pandya dynasties. A second Chera kingdom, c. 800 to 1102, was founded by Kulasekhara Varman and governed most of present-day Kerala and parts of Tamil Nadu, with a flourishing of art, literature, trade and the Bhakti movement. Most historians hold that Malayalam descends from a dialect of early middle Tamil and became a distinct language between the 9th and 13th centuries.

Vasco da Gama arrived at Kappad, near Kozhikode, in 1498, and the Zamorin of Kozhikode allowed the Portuguese to trade, which led to a factory and fort. In 1947 the princely states of Travancore and Kochi acceded to India, and on 1 July 1949 they merged as Travancore-Cochin. On 1 November 1956 the Malabar district and the Kasargod taluk were joined to it, and its four southern taluks went to Madras State, forming Kerala under the States Reorganisation Act. The first elections in 1957 produced a Communist-led government under E. M. S. Namboodiripad, among the earliest democratically elected Communist governments in the world.

Kerala is a state of southern India with its capital at Thiruvananthapuram, and 33 million people at the census of 2011. Malayalam is the most widely spoken language and, with English, an official one. Hinduism is practised by more than 54 per cent of the people, followed by Islam and Christianity.
kerch: Kerch lies on the Kerch Peninsula in the east of Crimea, on the Kerch Strait that gives access to the Sea of Azov. The Greek city of Panticapaeum stood on Mount Mithridat near the mouth of the Melek-Chesme river, which was navigable in Bosporan times. Its position at the intersection of trade routes between the steppe and Europe made it grow rapidly, exporting grain and salted fish and also making wine and minting its own coins.

Panticapaeum subdued nearby cities and by 480 BCE had become the capital of the Kingdom of Bosporus. For a short time, under Mithradates VI Eupator, it was the capital of the much larger Kingdom of Pontus. The Huns devastated the city in 375.
