Joan, Countess of Flanders, exempted settlers from property tax to encourage weaving, and the town became a centre of linen production.

After Philip IV of France annexed the County of Flanders in 1300, he ordered a castle built in Kortrijk for a French garrison. Heavy taxes and the harsh response of the French governor Jacques de Châtillon led to open revolt in 1302. The town militia massacred his troops in the Bruges Matins on 18 May, and Flemish forces under Guy of Namur besieged the castle. On 11 July 1302 Count Robert II of Artois chose to fight in the open field, and the Battle of the Golden Spurs ended in an unexpected Flemish victory. The Flemish community commemorates the date as a holiday.

The 15th century was prosperous under the Dukes of Burgundy, until the death of Mary of Burgundy in 1482 brought renewed fighting with France. Under Louis XIV the French occupied the town five times in sixty years and razed its fortifications. The flax industry prospered again after the Napoleonic era, and the Treaty of Kortrijk of 1820 fixed the border between France and Belgium. The city was heavily bombed in 1917, and on 21 July 1944 about 300 Avro Lancasters dropped over 5,000 bombs on the centre.

Kortrijk has about 80,000 inhabitants and a textile industry that still draws on its flax tradition. Much of its medieval architecture survives, including the Broel Towers on the Leie, the late-Gothic city hall and the Church of Our Lady, where the golden spurs taken from the battlefield in 1302 were hung. The belfry and the béguinage are both UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
kosciuszko-uprising: The Great Sejm of 1788 to 1792 adopted a new constitution on 3 May 1791, at a time when Poland's neighbours were occupied with wars. Russia and Prussia opposed it. Magnates who had opposed the reform, among them Franciszek Ksawery Branicki and Stanisław Szczęsny Potocki, formed the Targowica Confederation and asked Catherine the Great to intervene. Russian armies entered the Commonwealth on 18 May 1792, and King Stanisław August Poniatowski capitulated. The Grodno Sejm of 1793 annulled the constitution and accepted the Second Partition, by which Russia took 250,000 square kilometres and Prussia 58,000. Tadeusz Kościuszko, who had not lost a battle in the campaign, resigned his commission and planned an uprising from Leipzig.

On 12 March 1794 General Antoni Madaliński refused an order to demobilise and led his cavalry brigade towards Kraków. Kościuszko, a veteran of the American Revolutionary War, announced the general uprising in Kraków's town square on 24 March and took command of all Polish forces. On 4 April he defeated a Russian corps at Racławice. On 17 April an uprising led by Jan Kiliński drove the Russian garrison out of Warsaw, and on 23 April Jakub Jasiński began one in Vilnius. On 7 May Kościuszko issued the Proclamation of Połaniec, which partly abolished serfdom and gave civil liberty to peasants, though the nobility boycotted it.

Prussia entered the war on 10 May. Kościuszko was defeated at Szczekociny on 6 June, and Warsaw was besieged from 13 July until early September. On 10 October he was wounded and captured at Maciejowice. On 4 November Alexander Suvorov's troops stormed Praga, a suburb of Warsaw, and by one Russian estimate about 20,000 people, soldiers and civilians, were killed. Tomasz Wawrzecki surrendered on 16 November near Radoszyce.

About 150,000 men took up arms during the eight months, and the Polish rebels lost 27,000 men and the Russians 4,080. The following year Austria, Russia and Prussia carried out the Third Partition, annexing the rest of the country. Reforms easing serfdom were revoked, and the Commission of National Education was abolished. In the Russian partition thousands of noble families who had supported the uprising lost their estates. The uprising and the Proclamation of Połaniec are seen as the start of modern political thought and of the leftist movement in Poland.
kosice: Košice lies at an altitude of 255 metres on the river Hornád, at the eastern reaches of the Slovak Ore Mountains. It is about 20 kilometres from the Hungarian border, 80 kilometres from the Ukrainian border and about 400 kilometres east of Bratislava, and a chain of villages connects it to Prešov, 36 kilometres to the north. The first written mention, in 1230, calls it Villa Cassa. The name probably comes from a Slavic personal name, Koš, with the Latin form Cassovia becoming common in the 15th century; another theory derives it from the Old Slovak kosa, a clearing.

The city was part of the Kingdom of Hungary from the year 1000, and researchers hold that its population had a German majority until the mid-16th century. Jews lived in Košice from the 16th century but were not allowed to settle permanently; they could enter for the town fair and had to leave by night, living mostly in nearby Rozunfaca, until the ban was lifted in 1840.

In 1604 Catholics seized the Lutheran church in the city. The Calvinist Stephen Bocskay, in a Protestant insurrection against the Habsburgs backed by the Ottomans, then occupied Košice, where the future George I Rákóczi joined him as a commander. Giorgio Basta failed to recapture it for the Habsburgs. By the Treaty of Vienna in 1606 the rebels gave back the territory including Košice and won religious toleration for the Magyar nobility. Bocskay died in Košice on 29 December 1606 and was buried there. In 1661 the traveller Evliya Çelebi described the inhabitants as Hungarians, Germans and Upper Hungarians; by 1850 Slovaks had a plurality of 46.5 percent.

The Red Army captured the town in January 1945, and it served as a temporary capital of the restored Czechoslovak Republic until the Soviet forces reached Prague. The Košice Government Programme was declared there on 5 April 1945. Ethnic Germans of the area were expelled.

Košice is the second-largest city of Slovakia and the economic and cultural centre of the east, with about 230,000 inhabitants. It is the seat of the Slovak Constitutional Court and, since 1995, of the Archdiocese of Košice. Its preserved historical centre is the largest among Slovak towns and holds the Cathedral of St Elizabeth, Slovakia's largest church. The city is known as the first settlement in Europe granted its own coat of arms. It was European Capital of Culture in 2013.
kosovo: Kosovo covers 10,887 km2 in the centre of Southeast Europe. Most of its borders run along mountains, notably the Accursed Mountains in the west, a continuation of the Dinaric Alps, and the Šar Mountains in the southeast. Between them lie two major plains, the Kosovo Plain in the east and the Metohija Plain in the west. The name comes from Kosovo Polje, Blackbird Field, the karst field where the Battle of Kosovo was fought in 1389. In the Middle Ages the western territory was called Metohija, because large portions of land belonged to Serbian Orthodox monasteries and Mount Athos; Albanians call it Dukagjini.

The earliest evidence of organised settlement belongs to the Neolithic Starčevo and Vinča cultures. In antiquity the area was the core of Dardania, named after the Dardani, a Paleo-Balkan people usually described as Illyrian, though scholars debate whether they were Illyrian or Thracian. Dardania was incorporated into the Roman Empire in the 1st century BCE and became a separate Roman province in the 3rd century CE. Under the Byzantines the region faced Slavic migrations in the 6th and 7th centuries, and control passed between the Byzantines and the First Bulgarian Empire.

In the 13th century Kosovo became integral to the medieval Serbian state and the establishment of the Serbian Patriarchate. Ottoman expansion in the late 14th and 15th centuries brought the fall of the Serbian Empire, and the Battle of Kosovo of 1389, in which a Serbian-led coalition fought the Ottoman Empire, is regarded as one of its defining moments. Various dynasties, chiefly the Branković, governed afterwards. The Ottoman Empire fully conquered Kosovo after the Second Battle of Kosovo and ruled for nearly five centuries until 1912. The Ottoman Vilayet of Kosovo, created in 1877, was the first time the name was applied to a wider area.

Kosovo was a centre of the Albanian Renaissance and saw Albanian revolts in 1910 and 1912. After the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913 it was ceded to the Kingdom of Serbia, and after the Second World War it became an Autonomous Province within Yugoslavia. Tensions between the Albanian and Serb communities culminated in the Kosovo War of 1998 and 1999, after which the Yugoslav Army withdrew and the United Nations Interim Administration Mission in Kosovo was established.

Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia on 17 February 2008. Its recognition is partial, and Serbia does not officially recognise it as a state. The capital and largest city is Pristina, and the euro is the official currency. Four Serbian Orthodox churches and monasteries, including Visoki Dečani, the Patriarchate of Peja, Our Lady of Ljeviš and Gračanica, are inscribed as the World Heritage Site Medieval Monuments in Kosovo.
kosrae: Kosrae, formerly known as Kusaie or Strong's Island, is the easternmost of the Caroline Islands. It is a volcanic island and a state of the Federated States of Micronesia, with a land area of about 110 square kilometres. The main island, traditionally called Ualung, meaning the high island, rises to Mount Finkol at 634 metres. A fringing reef surrounds it, and the largest of the islets within the reef is Lelu Island. The state capital is Tofol.

Archaeological evidence shows that the island was settled at least by the early years of the first millennium CE. The city of Leluh existed from about 1250, in its heyday had about 1,500 people and covered some 27 hectares, and had burial pyramids for the nobility. By the time of first contact with European travellers in 1824, Kosrae had a highly stratified society with matrilineal lineages and clans, in which nobles controlled land worked by commoners and settlements consisted of small groups of close relatives sharing a single cook house.

The Spanish navigator Álvaro de Saavedra made the first recorded Western sighting on 14 September 1529. The island was under nominal Spanish sovereignty from 1668 but was not effectively occupied until 1885, after the Carolines Question between Spain and Germany was settled by the arbitration of Pope Leo XIII. The French corvette La Coquille, under Louis-Isidore Duperrey, visited in June 1824. Congregationalists set up the first mission post in 1852, and virtually the whole island had converted to Christianity by the 1870s. The captain and blackbirder Bully Hayes was shipwrecked there on 15 March 1874 and lived at Utwe for seven months, during which he terrorised the local people, before he was arrested and escaped.

After the Spanish–American War of 1898 Spain sold the Caroline Islands to Germany for 25 million pesetas, and the islands came under Japan during the First World War, as the South Seas Mandate from 1919 to 1947. The Japanese fortified Kosrae in the Second World War, but no battles occurred there, and tunnel bunkers dug into the interior peaks survive. The United States took over administration in 1945 as part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. Kosrae became a separate district in 1977 and joined the Federated States of Micronesia, in which it is the only single-island state. Kosraean is its official language, and English has equal authority.
kostis-palamas: Kostis Palamas was born in Patras on 13 January 1859 (O.S. 1 January), in the same house in which the Italian novelist Matilde Serao was born. He received his primary and secondary education in Mesolonghi. In 1877 he enrolled at the School of Law, Economics and Political Sciences of the University of Athens but soon abandoned his studies. In the 1880s he worked as a journalist, and in 1886 he published his first collection of verses, Songs of My Fatherland.

Palamas was a central figure of the Greek literary generation of the 1880s and, with Georgios Drosinis and Ioannis Polemis, a co-founder of the New Athenian School, also called the Palamian or Second Athenian School. His collections include Hymn to Athena (1889), Eyes of my Soul (1892), The Grave (1898), The King's Flute (1910), Altars (1915) and The Nights of Phemius (1935). He also published a novel, Death of a Youth (1901), and a drama, The Thrice-noble (1903). He was among the most respected literary critics of his day and helped to bring about a reappraisal of Andreas Kalvos, Dionysios Solomos and the Ionian School of poetry.

He wrote the words of the Olympic Hymn, set to music by Spyridon Samaras and first performed at the 1896 Summer Olympics. The hymn was then shelved, as each host city until the 1960 Winter Olympics commissioned an original piece. The version by Samaras and Palamas was declared the official Olympic Anthem in 1958 and has been performed at each celebration of the Games since 1960. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize for Literature on 14 occasions but never received it, and held an administrative post at the University of Athens from 1897 to 1926.

Palamas died on 27 February 1943, during the Axis occupation of Greece. His funeral at the First Cemetery of Athens the next day, attended spontaneously by several thousand people, became a major symbolic event of the Greek resistance. The funerary poem composed and recited by the poet Angelos Sikelianos roused the mourners, and the representatives of the occupying powers who came to lay a wreath were greeted with the Greek national anthem and shouts of Long Live Freedom. Palamas has been informally called the national poet of Greece, and the old administration building of the University of Athens, where his office was, now bears his name.
kostroma: Many scholars believe early Eastern Slavic tribes reached the region between 400 and 600, so the city could be older than its official founding. Like other towns of the eastern Rus, it was sacked by the Mongols in 1238. It then became a small principality under Prince Vasily of Kostroma, a younger brother of Alexander Nevsky. When he inherited the grand ducal title in 1271 he did not leave for Vladimir, and his descendants ruled Kostroma for about another half century, until Ivan I of Moscow bought the town.

As one of the northernmost towns of the Grand Duchy of Moscow, Kostroma was a place of retreat for the grand dukes when enemies besieged Moscow in 1382, 1408 and 1433. Novgorod pirates, the ushkuiniks, looted it in 1375. Its growth in the 16th century followed trade with English and Dutch merchants of the Muscovy Company through the northern port of Archangel.

Boris Godunov had the Ipatiev and Epiphany monasteries rebuilt in stone, in time for the Time of Troubles. The peasant Ivan Susanin became a symbol of the city's resistance to foreign invaders, and the future tsar Mikhail Romanov lived at the Ipatiev monastery, where an embassy from Moscow offered him the Russian crown.

In 1773 a great fire devastated the city, which was rebuilt with streets radiating from a single point near the river. A story says Catherine the Great dropped her fan on the city map and told the architects to follow its design. A railway linked Kostroma with Moscow from 1887.

Kostroma is the administrative centre of Kostroma Oblast and part of the Golden Ring of Russian cities, with 267,481 inhabitants in the 2021 census. The five-domed Epiphany Cathedral, built in 1559 to 1565, was the city's first stone building and holds a 10th-century Byzantine icon, Our Lady of St. Theodore. The Ipatyevsky monastery survives largely intact, with its 16th-century walls and towers and its 17th-century cathedral. The Resurrection church on the Lowlands is the only city church that survives from the 17th century. Much of the 18th-century town plan and its provincial neoclassical buildings remain.
kostrzyn-nad-odra: The town lies in the historic Lubusz Land at the confluence of the Oder and Warta rivers, about 90 kilometres south of Szczecin. Until 1945 the municipal area also included the suburb of Küstrin-Kietz on the west bank of the Oder, which now belongs to Germany as part of the Küstriner Vorland municipality.

The area was held by the Piast dukes and kings of Poland from about 960 until 1261. Duke Mieszko I used it as a staging area before the Battle of Cedynia in 972. In 1223 Duke Władysław Odonic of Greater Poland granted the fortress to the Knights Templar, and the name first appears in 1232, as Cozsterine. In 1261 the Ascanian margraves of Brandenburg seized it for their Neumark, and by 1300 it held Magdeburg town rights and grew through river trade. It passed to the Bohemian Crown in 1373, then to the Teutonic Order, which sold it to Brandenburg after the Thirteen Years' War began in 1454.

The castle built by John of Brandenburg-Küstrin grew into one of the largest fortresses of the region, though its expansion limited the room for the town. The fortress surrendered to the French without a fight in 1806, and the town burnt to the ground in 1814 during the French retreat. About 640 insurgents of the Greater Poland Uprising were held there in 1848. Railways reached it in 1857 and 1875, making it an important rail hub. In the First World War the fortress held a prisoner-of-war camp for Allied officers, regarded as the only German camp of that war from which no one escaped.

In the Second World War the town housed a prisoner-of-war camp and a sub-camp of Sachsenhausen. Air raids and the fighting on the Oder destroyed almost 95 per cent of its buildings, and the Red Army captured it on 11 March 1945. The Potsdam Conference gave it to Poland, the remaining Germans were expelled and Poles resettled the ruins. The remnants of the old town were razed and their bricks used to rebuild other Polish cities. The central area now lies around the railway station, east of the mouth of the Warta.
koszalin: Koszalin lies in north-western Poland, in West Pomerania, 12 kilometres south of the Baltic coast, on the river Dzierżęcinka. Founded in the Middle Ages, it was a seaport until the 17th century and one of the main cities of Central Pomerania, with Kołobrzeg and Słupsk. Archaeological excavations have found traces of settlement from the Funnelbeaker, Globular Amphora and Lusatian cultures and from Roman times and the early Middle Ages.

The area became part of the emerging Polish state under Mieszko I around 967. In 1214 Duke Bogislaw II of Pomerania gave the village of Koszalice to a Norbertine monastery, and settlers, mostly German, were invited in. In 1248 the eastern part of Kołobrzeg Land, with the village, passed to the Diocese of Kammin. On 23 May 1266 Bishop Hermann von Gleichen granted it a charter with Lübeck law, local government and privileges to attract settlers from the west. When the bishops moved their residence to Kołobrzeg in 1276, the diocese was administered from Koszalin, and a Cistercian monastery was founded in 1278.

The city gained direct access to the Baltic in the 14th century and joined the Hanseatic League in 1386, which brought conflicts with the rival seaports of Kołobrzeg and Darłowo. In 1475 a quarrel with Duke Bogislaw X led to the duke's kidnapping and brief imprisonment in the city. The town became mostly German-speaking, and in 1516 a ban on buying from Slavic speakers and on admitting them to craft guilds was enforced. In 1534 it became mostly Lutheran under the influence of Johannes Bugenhagen.

Swedish troops occupied Koszalin in 1637 during the Thirty Years' War, and after the Treaty of Westphalia in 1648 and the Treaty of Stettin in 1653 it went to Brandenburg-Prussia as Cöslin. A fire in 1718 heavily damaged it. It entered the German Empire in 1871, and a railway from Stettin to Danzig reached it by 1878. The Red Army captured the city on 4 March 1945, and under the Potsdam Agreement it became part of Poland. Its German population still there was expelled, and the city was resettled by Poles and Kashubians.

Koszalin is the capital of Koszalin County in West Pomeranian Voivodeship, and was the capital of Koszalin Voivodeship from 1950 to 1998. Its distinctive landmark is the Gothic St Mary's Cathedral from the early 14th century, now the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Koszalin-Kołobrzeg. Pope John Paul II visited in 1991 and consecrated the sanctuary on Chełmska Hill. The city has held an annual festival of film debuts since 1973.
kota-bharu: Kota Bharu means 'new city' or 'new castle' in Malay. It stands in the north-east of Peninsular Malaysia, near the mouth of the Kelantan River, and its position by the river made it a trading centre. Before it took on the role of capital it was known as Kuala Kelantan, and the capital of Kelantan had been divided between two places, Kota Kubang Labu and Kota Pengkalan Datu. The Royal Palace had stood on the site before the town was established.

Sultan Muhammad II of Kelantan established Kota Bharu as the state capital in 1844, and he wanted the new capital built in his honour. In the 19th century Kelantan was a prosperous state with a population of around 30,000 to 50,000, including about a thousand Chinese. It produced gold, tin ore, black pepper, areca nut, rice, rattan, bamboo, agarwood and songket, and Kota Bharu acted as an entrepôt for these goods.

On 8 December 1941 Japanese invasion forces landed at Pantai Sabak, about 10 kilometres from the town. This began the Battle of Kota Bharu, the first battle of the Malayan campaign. Japanese forces captured the town and went on to defeat the British in jungle warfare and capture Singapore.

Kota Bharu was declared the Cultural City on 25 July 1991 by Sultan Ismail Petra, on the strength of its history and its local arts. On 1 October 2005 the Kelantan state government rebranded it the Islamic City under its policy of Developing With Islam, a title that describes the town's character and does not change its legal status as a city.

Kota Bharu is the state capital and royal seat of Kelantan, and the old royal palaces are still occupied by the Sultan and Sultanah. Most of its people are ethnic Kelantanese Malays who speak the Kelantan Malay dialect, and there is a sizeable Chinese community. Kelantanese culture is distinctive within Malaysia and shows some Thai influence from the nearby border. Siti Khadijah Market is its best-known market, and the town had the only Carnegie library in Malaysia, founded in 1938 and opened to the public in 1967.
kota-kinabalu: Kota Kinabalu lies on the north-west coast of Borneo, facing the South China Sea, on a narrow flatland between the Crocker Range to the east and the sea to the west. Mount Kinabalu, which gave the city its name, stands about 50 kilometres to the east-north-east. The name is derived from Aki Nabalu, meaning the revered place of the dead. Six islands lie off the coast, the largest being Gaya Island, where the first British settlement stood. Its climate is tropical rainforest, with high temperatures, heavy rain and humidity all year.

The Kadazandusuns called the area Dondoung. From the 15th century it lay under the influence of the Bruneian Empire. A Dutch map of 1657 labels the place Api Api, a name that later survived as Api-Api, and which the Chinese community still uses in its Hakka form. In 1882 the British North Borneo Chartered Company founded a small settlement at Gaya Bay, already inhabited by the Bajau people, with its first site on Gaya Island. In 1897 the Bajau-Suluk chief Mat Salleh burned it down.

In July 1899 the place opposite Gaya Island was judged a suitable site, and it was named Jesselton after Sir Charles Jessel, vice-chairman of the Company. It became a major trading port and was linked to the North Borneo Railway. Jesselton was largely destroyed in the Second World War. The Japanese occupation provoked several local uprisings, notably the Jesselton Revolt, which the Japanese defeated.

After the war the Company could not pay for reconstruction, and North Borneo passed to the British Crown as a colony. In 1946 the Crown declared Jesselton the colony's capital and began to rebuild it. When Malaysia was formed, North Borneo became Sabah and the town took its present name. It was granted city status on 2 February 2000.

Kota Kinabalu is the capital of Sabah and the seat of its state government, with most federal agencies of the state also based there. Its population was 452,058 at the 2010 census and 500,421 at the 2020 census. Malay, with a Sabahan creole, is the main language, and about a fifth of residents are of Chinese descent, mostly Hakka. The city is a main commercial centre of East Malaysia and a gateway for visitors to Sabah, with Kinabalu Park about 90 kilometres away.
kothen: The first documentary mention of Cothene dates to 1115. By 1194 it was a market town and a seat of the princes of Anhalt, and it received its charter in 1200. The surrounding area is unusually rich in archaeological finds, the earliest signs of human habitation dating from the early Stone Age, about 250,000 years ago. Wolfgang (1492–1566), prince of Anhalt-Köthen, was a Protestant reformer of the principalities of Anhalt, and Ludwig I (1579–1650) was a co-founder of the Fruitbearing Society. Gisela Agnes (1669–1740) acted as regent for her son Leopold from 1704 to 1715.

Prince Leopold of Anhalt-Köthen (1694–1728) employed Johann Sebastian Bach as Kapellmeister, and the Brandenburg concertos and the Well-Tempered Clavier belong to Bach's years there. Funeral services for Leopold were held in the church of St. Jakob on 23 and 24 March 1729, where Bach performed his cantata Klagt, Kinder, klagt es aller Welt, BWV 244a. The composer Carl Friedrich Abel was born in the town in 1723; with Johann Christian Bach he later founded the Bach-Abel Concerts in London, the first subscription concerts in England.

Köthen is the capital of the district of Anhalt-Bitterfeld in Saxony-Anhalt, about 30 km north of Halle, and the seat of the main campus of the Anhalt University of Applied Sciences. Samuel Hahnemann practised there from 1821 to 1834 and published many of his best-known works in those years; in 1855 his disciple Arthur Lutze opened a homoeopathic clinic. The ornithologist Johann Friedrich Naumann, born near the town, worked at the ducal court from about 1810 to 1835.

Schloss Köthen, the palace of the reigning princes, was built mainly between 1597 and 1660 and has a Hall of Mirrors of 1722 where Bach's music is now often performed. A small side wing was bombed in 1944; the rest has been restored, and the palace houses the Naumann Museum of ornithology and a Prehistorical Museum. A Bach Festival has been held in the town every second year since 1967.
kourou: Kourou lies at the mouth of the Kourou River on the Atlantic coast, some 60 kilometres north-west of Cayenne, and is ringed by four hills, Carapa, Pariacabo, Café and Lombard. Little is known of the pre-colonial era, when the area was mostly populated by the Kalina, also called Galibi, before the French arrived in the late 17th century. Rock art can still be seen at Les Roches Gravées nearby. Vicente Yáñez Pinzón sailed past in 1500, and in 1744 La Condamine, returning from the expedition sent to Peru in 1735 to measure a degree of the meridian arc, gave his name to one of the mountains behind the town.

After the Jesuits abandoned their mission, which had baptised a few Galibis in 1710, Kourou remained a small village until the expedition of 1763. In that year, under the Treaty of Paris, Great Britain took control of New France, and France, having lost its largest and richest colony, sent a large expedition to Guiana commanded by Choiseul. Some 10,000 to 12,000 people, mostly French, tempted by stories of an El Dorado, settled at Kourou, where the engineers Mentelle and Tugny had designed the layout of the town. It was unprepared for them.

About 6,000 died within the year of fevers and other illnesses, and the survivors fled to islands free of mosquitoes, which became known as the Salvation Islands. The failure discouraged settlement, and the colony earned the nickname Enfer Vert, or Green Hell.

In 1852 the three main islands off the coast, the Salut group including Devil's Island, became prisons, holding mostly political prisoners and some of France's toughest criminals, and the first prisoners arrived in 1862. Kourou's own prison, devoted mostly to agriculture, was part of the same system. A law of 1938 ended transport of new prisoners from France, and the Kourou Prison closed in 1946.

The Guiana Space Centre was founded a little behind the town by CNES in 1965, and the European Space Agency has used its launch facility since 1975. The 3rd Foreign Infantry Regiment of the French Foreign Legion, whose mission is to protect the centre, has had a base at Kourou since 1973. The Dreyfus Tower, once used to signal to the islands by semaphore, remains where the river meets the ocean.
koutoubia-mosque: Marrakesh was founded around 1070 by the Almoravids as their capital and captured in 1147 by the Almohads under Abd al-Mu'min. The Almohads, who considered the Almoravids heretics, reportedly demolished the city's mosques on the argument that they were not aligned with the proper qibla. The Almoravid grand mosque, the Ben Youssef, was already closely integrated into the urban fabric, so Abd al-Mu'min built a new mosque next to the former Almoravid kasbah, the Ksar el-Hajjar, which became the site of the new Almohad palace.

The commonly accepted chronology, by Henri Terrasse, Henri Basset and Gaston Deverdun, has the first mosque begun in 1147 and prayers held in it by 1157, when a copy of the Qur'an attributed to Uthman was moved there from Córdoba. A study of 2022 by Antonio Almagro and Alfonso Jiménez proposes instead that building began in May 1158 and was finished in the same year, helped by brick and rammed-earth construction. The name comes from the Arabic kutubiyyin, booksellers, since at one time as many as 100 vendors worked in the streets at its base.

Abd al-Mu'min later built a second mosque directly against the south-eastern side of the first, around 1158 on the usual chronology. The reasons are not fully understood. The popular narrative says the first mosque was found to be misaligned with the qibla, though the second is aligned slightly further from the modern direction; other explanations include a growing population or a mosque reserved for the ruling elite. Many scholars think the two coexisted for a time as one large mosque. The second mosque is the structure that stands today, and the first survives as ruins on the esplanade.

The current mosque is roughly 90 metres wide and about 57 to 66 metres long, mainly of brick with some sandstone. It has eight entrances, four on each side, and a private entrance for the imam. The minaret is 77 metres high and is decorated with varying geometric arch motifs, with a spire and metal orbs at the top. Ya'qub al-Mansur possibly finished it around 1195, and it likely inspired the Giralda of Seville and the Hassan Tower of Rabat.

The mosque is the largest in Marrakesh and a symbol of the city. In the 19th century the 'Alawi sultans Muhammad IV and Hasan I restored the upper part of the minaret, and further restoration was carried out in the 20th century and at the end of the 1990s. Winston Churchill painted the minaret after the Casablanca Conference of 1943. The mosque is still active, and non-Muslims are not allowed inside, but the similar Tinmal Mosque south of Marrakesh can be visited as a historic site.
kowloon: Kowloon, formerly spelled Kaulung, is one of the three areas of Hong Kong with Hong Kong Island and the New Territories. It lies directly north of Hong Kong Island across Victoria Harbour, bordered by the Lei Yue Mun strait to the east and by a mountain range including Tate's Cairn and Lion Rock to the north. The Chinese name means Nine Dragons and alludes to eight mountains and a Chinese emperor: Kowloon Peak, Tung Shan, Tate's Cairn, Temple Hill, Unicorn Ridge, Lion Rock, Beacon Hill, Crow's Nest and Emperor Bing of Song. It is an urban area made up of the Kowloon Peninsula and New Kowloon.

The part of Kowloon south of Boundary Street, together with Stonecutters Island, was ceded by Qing China to the United Kingdom under the Convention of Peking of 1860. For many years it stayed largely undeveloped, and the British used it mainly for tiger-hunting expeditions. The part north of Boundary Street, called New Kowloon, was leased to the British for 99 years as part of the New Territories under the Second Convention of Peking of 1898. Within New Kowloon lay the Kowloon Walled City, which was demolished in 1993. The same area was called Kwun Fu Cheung in the Song dynasty.

Large-scale development began in the early 20th century with the Kowloon-Canton Railway and the Kowloon Wharf. Flight paths into Kai Tak Airport limited building heights, so Kowloon kept a much lower skyline than Hong Kong Island. West Kowloon was once the site of a dockyard of the Royal Navy. The census of 1911 recorded 7,306 people, mostly Hakka. After Japan invaded China in 1937, about 750,000 refugees arrived in Kowloon and nearby areas between 1937 and 1939, and after the Second World War slums housing refugees from the newly established People's Republic of China gave way to public housing estates.

By statute Kowloon is only the area south of Boundary Street and Stonecutters Island, but in common use New Kowloon is counted as part of the Kowloon urban area. Its five districts are Kowloon City, Kwun Tong, Sham Shui Po, Wong Tai Sin and Yau Tsim Mong. Cantonese is the usual language of about 86 per cent of residents. Road and rail tunnels connect Kowloon to Hong Kong Island, and no bridges do.
koxinga: Zheng Chenggong, born Zheng Sen, was born on 27 August 1624 at Hirado in Japan, the son of Zheng Zhilong, a Han Chinese merchant from Fujian, and a Japanese woman known by her surname Tagawa. He lived there until the age of seven, then moved to Fujian. He became a xiucai in the imperial examination in 1638 and in 1644 studied at the Guozijian under the scholar Qian Qianyi. In 1645 the Prince of Tang was installed as the Longwu Emperor with the support of Zheng Zhilong, and gave Zheng Sen the name Chenggong and the title Koxinga, meaning lord granted the imperial surname.

The Longwu Emperor was captured by the Qing and executed in October 1646. Zheng Zhilong surrendered on 21 November 1646, against his family's objections, and Koxinga and his uncles succeeded to the leadership of his forces. Operating outside Xiamen, he used naval superiority for amphibious raids in Fujian. By 1650 he led the Zheng family and pledged allegiance to the Yongli Emperor of the Southern Ming, who made him Prince of Yanping in 1655. Talks with the Qing lasted until November 1654 and failed. On 9 May 1656 a Qing fleet attacked Kinmen and, partly through a storm, lost most of its ships. He later besieged Nanjing for almost three weeks from 24 August, but was defeated and slipped back to his ships.

In 1661 Koxinga landed to attack Dutch Formosa, helped by Taiwanese Aboriginal groups who turned against the Dutch. The governor Frederick Coyett surrendered Fort Zeelandia on 1 February 1662, ending 38 years of Dutch rule on Taiwan. During the siege Koxinga executed the missionary Antonius Hambroek and took his teenage daughter as a concubine. He then set about making Taiwan a base for Ming loyalists.

In 1662 he sent the friar Vittorio Riccio to Manila to demand tribute from the Spanish, who refused; the planned attack never took place. Koxinga died in June 1662, aged 37, of an unspecified illness; modern historians suspect malaria. His son Zheng Jing succeeded him as Prince of Yanping, and a dynastic state on Taiwan continued until 1683. Koxinga is worshipped as a god in coastal China, Southeast Asia and Taiwan, where a temple in Tainan honours him and his mother.
kpalime: Kpalimé is a city in the Plateaux Region of Togo, 120 km north of Lomé and 15 km from the border with Ghana. It is the administrative capital of Kloto Prefecture and has a population of 75,084, making it the fourth-biggest town in Togo after Lomé, Sokodé and Kara. It lies near Mount Agou, the highest point in Togo, and Mount Kloto, and is a base for visiting waterfalls, coffee and cocoa plantations and the Misahöhe Forest Reserve. Ewe is the main local language and French, the official language of Togo, is spoken by anyone who has been to school.

Kpalimé was originally Agomé-Kpalimé, one of the villages of the Agomé people, whose origins can probably be traced to Yorubaland. According to the account of the town's origins, King Agokoli of Notsé, a tyrant of the early 18th century, caused many people to flee, and groups of fugitives including the Agomé reached Mount Kloto. After a quarrel over a goat's head, the elders spread to the plain. The fifth group moved to Mokpalipé, meaning crossroads, a name that evolved into Kpalimé. The Agomé-Kpalimé later learned trade from Hausa traders who crossed their territory with caravans from Salaga on the way to Keta. Its chiefs belong to the Apeto dynasty, though the paramount chief of the Agomé is the chief of Agomé-Yo.

In 1890 Jesko von Puttkamer, German Imperial Commissioner for Togoland, founded a field station at Misahohè, 9 km away. Kpalimé soon overtook it as regional capital, and by 1913 had 39 businesses. The Germans opened the Lomé to Kpalimé branch of Togo Railways in 1907 and built the neo-Gothic Cathedral of the Holy Spirit in 1913. British forces moving in from the Gold Coast occupied the town from 1914 to 1920, after which it was ceded to the French following the Treaty of Versailles. It was thus one of the few places in Africa to pass from German to British to French administration. Under the French its status rose from indigenous commune in 1939 to mixed commune in 1951 and commune in 1959.

Kpalimé is Togo's main centre for crafts such as wood sculpture, weaving, wickerwork, batiks and pottery, with 36 artisanal workshops and retail outlets and an artisanal training college. It is the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Kpalimé, established in 1994. The Misahöhe Forest Reserve, covering 5,000 hectares north-west of the town, is the only site in Togo from which many forest bird species have been recorded.
krak-des-chevaliers: According to the Arab historian Ibn Shaddad, in 1031 the Mirdasid emir Shibl ad-Dawla Nasr settled Kurdish tribesmen at the site, then called Ḥiṣn al-Safḥ, to restore the Mirdasids' access to the coast. The garrison gave it the name Ḥiṣn al-Akrād, fortress of the Kurds, which the Crusaders corrupted to Le Crat and then, confusing it with karak, the Syriac word for a walled city, to Le Crac. In 1099 the company of Raymond IV of Toulouse found it deserted, and a permanent Crusader occupation began in 1110 under Tancred. Because of its Hospitaller owners it was called Crac de l'Ospital; Krak des Chevaliers is a romanticised form of the 19th century.

The castle stands on a hill 650 metres high in the Homs Gap, the route between Tripoli and Homs, about 40 kilometres west of Homs. Between 1142 and 1170 the Hospitallers built a stone curtain wall with square towers around a courtyard of vaulted chambers. In the early 13th century they added an outer wall, 9 metres high, with strongly projecting round towers, a design that had been developed at Château Gaillard by Richard the Lionheart. The castle thus became a concentric castle, and the historian Hugh Kennedy called its outer defences the most elaborate and developed anywhere in the Latin east. Its limestone facing is so fine that the mortar is barely noticeable.

The garrison numbered around 2,000 at its peak, which let the Hospitallers exact tribute from a wide area. The inner ward held a chapel, probably rebuilt after an earthquake in 1170, and a hall of the Knights whose Gothic tracery probably dates from the 1230s. Four large round towers housed about 60 knights, and one was designed for the Grand Master.

The first half of the 13th century has been described as the castle's golden age. From the 1250s the fortunes of the Hospitallers declined, and in 1271 the Mamluk Sultanate captured it after a siege of 36 days, supposedly by means of a forged letter, said to come from the Hospitallers' Grand Master, that made the knights surrender. In the Ottoman period it housed a company of janissaries and was the centre of a tax district. T. E. Lawrence called it perhaps the best preserved and most wholly admirable castle in the world.

Interest in Crusader castles revived in the 19th century, and Emmanuel Guillaume-Rey published plans of it in 1871. By then a village of 500 people had been built inside, and its inhabitants were moved out in 1933. Paul Deschamps's survey of 1934 has been called perhaps the finest account of a single medieval castle ever written. Frescoes were found in 1935, 1955 and 1978. Since 2006 the castle and Qal'at Salah El-Din have been UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
krakow: Kraków lies in southern Poland on the Vistula river, about 219 metres above sea level, on the border between several physiographic regions: the Kraków-Częstochowa Upland to the north-west, the Małopolska Upland to the north-east, the Sandomierz Basin to the east and the foothills of the Carpathians to the south. Its name is traditionally derived from Krakus, the founder and ruler of the Vistulans in tradition, though historians dispute the true origin and the name may come from kruk, meaning crow or raven.

Settlement on the site of Wawel Castle goes back to the Stone Age. Kraków began as a fortified settlement of the Vistulans, a Lechitic tribe, around the 8th century. A legend says Krakus built it above a cave occupied by a dragon, Smok Wawelski. It was a notable commercial centre controlled by Moravia and then captured by the Bohemian duke Boleslaus I in 955, and Mieszko I, the first acclaimed ruler of Poland, took it from the Bohemians towards the end of his reign. In 1038 it became the seat of the Piast monarchs, and it remained the centre of administration until the late 16th century, when Sigismund III Vasa moved his court to Warsaw.

The 15th and 16th centuries were Poland's Golden Age, and many works of Renaissance art and architecture were created in Kraków, including the synagogues of Kazimierz. In 1473 Kasper Straube printed the Calendarium Cracoviense there, the first work printed in Poland. In 1794 Tadeusz Kościuszko began an unsuccessful insurrection in the Main Square; it led to the third and final partition of Poland, and Kraków came under Habsburg rule. After the Second Polish Republic emerged in 1918, the city became again a major academic and cultural centre. In the Second World War it became the seat of Nazi Germany's General Government, and its Jewish population was forced into the Kraków Ghetto and sent to extermination camps. The city was spared destruction.

Kraków is the second-largest city in Poland, with 816,614 inhabitants, and was its official capital until 1596. Its Old Town, with the nearby Wieliczka Salt Mine, is among Poland's first World Heritage Sites, declared in 1978. Landmarks include Wawel Cathedral and Wawel Castle, St Mary's Basilica and Rynek Główny, the largest medieval market square in Europe. Jagiellonian University, founded in 1364 as the Studium Generale, is the oldest university in Poland. Karol Wojtyła, archbishop of Kraków, became Pope John Paul II in 1978.
krasnodar: Krasnodar stands on the right bank of the Kuban River, about 1,300 km south of Moscow, with the Black Sea 120 km to the west. The climate is humid subtropical. Winters are cold and damp with unstable snow cover, the July average is 24.1 °C, and about 735 millimetres of rain and snow fall in a year. No mountains shield the city from cold waves, so winter temperatures below −20 °C are not uncommon.

The city began in 1793 as a military camp and then a fortress built by the Black Sea Cossacks to defend the imperial borders and to assert Russian dominion over Circassia, a claim that Ottoman Turkey contested. Its name, Yekaterinodar, meant Catherine's Gift, recognising both Catherine the Great's grant of land in the Kuban to the Cossacks and Saint Catherine of Alexandria, regarded as the city's patron. It received town status in 1867 and by 1888 had about 45,000 people. The 1897 census counted 65,606, of whom 52.9 per cent spoke Russian and 38.3 per cent Ukrainian.

During the Russian Civil War the city changed hands several times between the Red Army and the Volunteer Army. The White general Lavr Kornilov besieged it on 10 April 1918 and was killed a week later when a Bolshevik shell destroyed the farmhouse that served as his headquarters. On 7 December 1920 it was renamed Krasnodar, meaning Gift of the Reds. The city lost over 14 per cent of its population in the Soviet famine of 1932–1933.

German forces occupied Krasnodar from 9 August 1942 to 12 February 1943. The city was heavily damaged, and the Gestapo and mobile SS execution squads killed thousands of Jews, Communists and suspected partisans. From 14 to 17 July 1943 a Soviet tribunal at Krasnodar tried people for collaboration and war crimes and pronounced eight death sentences, carried out in the city square before a crowd of about thirty thousand.

Krasnodar is the largest city and administrative centre of Krasnodar Krai, with a population of 1,154,885 within the city limits. The 2021 census counted one million people there for the first time. The historic centre keeps buildings from the 19th century, and the city has St Catherine's Cathedral and a steel lattice hyperboloid tower built by the engineer Vladimir Shukhov in 1928. It is the home of the Kuban Cossack Choir and of the Kovalenko Krasnodar Regional Art Museum, the oldest public art museum in the North Caucasus.
kremnica: Kremnica lies in the Kremnica Mountains, where abundant gold ore made it one of the major mining towns of the world in the Middle Ages and the modern era. The first evidence of underground mining there dates from the 9th century. After the Mongol invasion of the 13th century, Hungarian kings invited colonists from present-day Germany, including Zipser Germans, whose technology restored the mines. The first written reference to the town dates from 1328, when King Charles I of Hungary granted it royal town privileges; a mint already existed then.

From 1335 the mint produced gold florins and later the Kremnica ducats, used as an international means of payment because their gold was consistently pure. In 1331 the town became the seat of the Chamber Count, who administered all the mines and mints in twelve counties of the kingdom.

At the end of the 14th century Kremnica became the capital of the mining towns of central Upper Hungary. In the 15th century it was the second most important city in the Kingdom of Hungary, and its deputies held second place in the Hungarian Diet, after those of Buda. Gold mining and coin production peaked in the 14th and 15th centuries. The town was one of the main centres of the Reformation in the country and belonged to the Protestant League of Seven Mining Towns.

In the 16th century it was a centre for medals, mostly religious ones, especially by Joachim Deschler. By then miners had to dig deeper and water in the shafts made mining more costly and less profitable. The last gold was extracted in 1970, when all the mines closed. The German population of the town and its surroundings was expelled in 1945 by the Czechoslovak government after the Second World War.

Kremnica is a town in central Slovakia on the brook Kremnický potok, a tributary of the Hron, with 4,586 inhabitants. A castle built between the 13th and 15th centuries towers over the town and is a well-preserved fortification system, with a double wall. At the end of the 15th century the Chamber Count moved to a new house, and his residence in the castle became St Catherine's Church. The town also has a Museum of Coins and Medals, a Baroque plague column on the main square and a 15th-century aqueduct about 20 kilometres long that still supplies hydroelectric power plants. The mint is the oldest still-working mint in the world.
kriegsmarine: Under the 1919 Treaty of Versailles Germany was allowed a minimal navy of 15,000 personnel, six capital ships of no more than 10,000 tons, six cruisers, twelve destroyers and twelve torpedo boats, with no submarines, aircraft carriers or naval aviation. The ships and men were taken over from the Kaiserliche Marine, which was renamed the Reichsmarine. Germany worked from the outset to circumvent the limits, keeping up U-boat design through an office in the Netherlands and developing the G7e torpedo in Sweden. On 15 November 1932 the government decided on a prohibited naval re-armament.

The Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 18 June 1935 allowed Germany a navy equal to 35 per cent of British surface tonnage and 45 per cent of British submarine tonnage, and that year the Reichsmarine became the Kriegsmarine. Its first military action came in the Spanish Civil War, when ships were sent to Spanish waters from July 1936 under the cover of non-intervention while covertly supporting Francisco Franco's Nationalists. After Republican bombers attacked the Deutschland off Ibiza on 29 May 1937, killing 31, the Admiral Scheer shelled Almeria, killing 19 or 20 civilians.

In January 1939 Adolf Hitler approved Plan Z, a programme of about 800 ships for 1939 to 1947, built around six H-class battleships and meant to give parity with the Royal Navy. The outbreak of war in September 1939 shelved it in favour of U-boats, and resources went first to the army and air force. In the first months the Kriegsmarine sank the carrier HMS Courageous and the battleship HMS Royal Oak, and lost the Admiral Graf Spee at the Battle of the River Plate.

Wolfpacks of submarines attacked British convoys in the Battle of the Atlantic, but the tactic was largely abandoned by May 1943 as U-boat losses mounted. After the failure at the Battle of the Barents Sea, Hitler concluded that large warships were useless, and Erich Raeder was replaced as commander-in-chief by Karl Dönitz on 30 January 1943. Dönitz became President of Germany on Hitler's suicide in April 1945.

Hitler was supreme commander, exercising authority through the Oberkommando der Marine. The Luftwaffe held a near-monopoly on military aviation, a source of rivalry with the navy. Kriegsmarine personnel also manned coastal artillery, flak batteries and radar. From mid-1944 surplus personnel were formed into about 40 land regiments and, from January 1945, six divisions. After Germany surrendered, the surviving ships were divided among the victors. At Liepāja in Latvia, in July 1941, its commandants ordered hostages shot and issued anti-Jewish regulations.
kris: The word kris comes from an Old Javanese term meaning dagger. A Chinese source of the 10th century, under the Song dynasty, records that an envoy from She-po, or Java, arrived at court in 992 with gifts that included a small dagger with a hilt of rhino horn and gold. Although the peoples of Southeast Asia already knew stabbing weapons of this type, the kris most probably developed in Java and spread through the archipelago, Malaysia, southern Thailand and the Philippines by diplomacy and trade. A Sundanese manuscript dated to 1518 CE describes the kris as the weapon of kings. Claims of forms older than the Majapahit kris cannot be verified.

A kris has three parts: the blade (bilah or wilah), the hilt (hulu) and the sheath (warangka), each treated as a work of art in carved wood, metal, gold or ivory. Blades are between 38 and 127 cm long and are not normally sharpened, as the weapon is for stabbing. The number of curves, or luk, is always odd, and blades from the Majapahit era are straight, as were more than half of all kris before modern times. The pamor pattern comes from iron with a little nickel, perhaps iron ore from Sulawesi, forged in layers.

The maker was a specialist smith called an empu, a title in Java for those with the skill, and with knowledge of literature, history and the occult as well as spiritual power, since a kris is believed to have a presence of its own. Some blades take years to complete. Heirloom kris, or pusaka, are considered to have good or bad luck, and tales such as that of Empu Gandring's unfinished kris, told in the Pararaton, give some of them supernatural powers.

Although many assume the kris was the main weapon of fighters, warriors carried it as a secondary arm if they lost their main weapon, usually a spear. Commoners wore it daily, especially when travelling, and in peacetime it formed part of ceremonial dress. Men usually wore one, women a smaller one, and heirloom blades were handed down and worn at weddings and other ceremonies. It signalled status, heroism and authority. Javanese, Balinese and Sundanese traditionally wear it at the back, to show that violence is the last resort, whereas elsewhere in the archipelago it is worn at the front or the left hip.

In Bali the kris dance in the Barong performance shows men in trance stabbing themselves unhurt. Kris-making is preserved in the courts of Yogyakarta and Surakarta and in the principalities of Mangkunegaran and Pakualaman, though it nearly came to a standstill before the 1990s and has since revived. In 2005 UNESCO listed the Indonesian kris on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
krishna: The tradition of Krishna appears to have grown from the merging of several independent deities of ancient India, the earliest attested being Vāsudeva, a hero-god of the Vrishni tribe, whose worship is attested from the 5th to 6th centuries BCE in the writings of Pāṇini and from the 2nd century BCE in inscriptions such as the Heliodorus pillar. The Vrishnis were later thought to have merged with the Yadavas, whose hero-god was Krishna, and the two deities became one, who was identified with Vishnu in the Mahabharata. Around 180 BCE the Indo-Greek king Agathocles issued coins whose images are now read as Balarama and Vāsudeva-Krishna. The Mahabharata is the earliest text to describe Krishna as a personality in detail.

Hindus worship Krishna as the eighth avatar of Vishnu and, in Krishnaite traditions, as the Supreme God. His name is a Sanskrit word meaning black, dark or dark blue, and he is usually shown with dark or blue skin. The Mahabharata, the Harivamsa, the Bhagavata Purana and the Vishnu Purana tell his life, and agree on the main story. He is born in a prison at Mathura to Devaki and Vasudeva and raised by Nanda and Yashoda, because Devaki's brother, the tyrant Kamsa, has been told that her eighth child will kill him. As a boy he is a cowherd and a prankster, the butter thief, who lifts Govardhana hill to shelter Vrindavana from rain.

As an adult he kills Kamsa and leads the Yadavas to the city of Dwaraka. In the Kurukshetra War he serves as Arjuna's charioteer on condition that he raise no weapon, and his counsel to Arjuna forms the Bhagavad Gita.

Krishna is a central figure of bhakti, devotional worship, within Vaishnavism, and devotees see lila, divine play, as the central principle of the universe. His birth is observed each year at Krishna Janmashtami, in late August or early September, with fasting, singing, night vigils and temple visits. Mathura and Vrindavan, where there are about 5,500 temples, are major pilgrimage sites, and regional forms include Jagannatha in Odisha, Vithoba in Maharashtra and Guruvayoorappan in Kerala. His stories inspired dance forms such as Bharatanatyam, Kathakali and Odissi, and reliefs at Prambanan in Java, dated to the 9th century, show episodes of his life.
krishna-river: The Krishna River, in full Krishnaveni, is the third-longest river in India after the Ganga and Godavari, and the fourth-largest in water inflow and basin area. It rises in the Western Ghats near Mahabaleshwar in Maharashtra at an elevation of about 1,300 metres, flows past the town of Wai and continues east until it empties into the Bay of Bengal. It passes through Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana and is a major source of irrigation in all four states.

It has 13 major tributaries, among them the Ghataprabha, Malaprabha, Bhima, Tungabhadra and Musi. The Bhima is the longest, at 861 kilometres. The basin covers 258,948 square kilometres, nearly 8 per cent of India's area, and most of it is rolling country, bounded on the west by the unbroken line of the Western Ghats. Its soils include black and red soils, laterite and alluvium, and the Krishna-Godavari delta is known as the Rice Granary of India.

Jain literary sources, including the Kalpasutra and the Nisithacurni, describe the region near the Krishnavena as Abhiradesa, the land of the Abhiras, which points to an early association with that people. Hindus revere the river as sacred and believe that it removes the sins of those who bathe in it. Every twelve years the Krishna Pushkaram fair is held on its banks. The first holy place on the river is Wai, known for the Mahaganpati Mandir and the Kashivishweshwar temple, with seven ghats on the river.

Kudalasangama, where the Krishna meets the Malaprabha, holds the samadhi of Basavanna, the founder of the Lingayat sect. Other holy places include Srisailam, with the Mallikarjuna Jyotirlinga, and the Kanaka Durga Temple at Vijayawada. The three tributaries Panchganga, Warana and Yerla meet the Krishna near Sangli, and Hindus consider these places holy. The Bhilawadi Krishna Ghat is believed to date from 1779.

The basin holds oil and gas in the Krishna-Godavari Basin, coal at Yellandu, iron ore and other minerals. The Krishna Wildlife Sanctuary protects the last surviving mangrove forests in its estuary. Many dams and barrages cross the river, among them the Almatti, Srisailam, Nagarjuna Sagar and Tungabhadra dams and the Prakasam Barrage. Bridges built under British rule, such as the Irwin Bridge at Sangli, still cross it.
krishnadevaraya: Krishnadevaraya was born on 17 January 1471, the son of Tuluva Narasa Nayaka, an army commander, and his queen Nagamamba, and came to the throne after the death of his half-brother Viranarasimha. In 1513 he fought Sultan Quli Qutb Shah of Golconda in person at Pangal, where the Vijayanagara army was defeated and obliged to retreat. His army laid siege to Udayagiri in 1512 and, after a campaign of about a year, took Kondaveedu through a night attack found by his prime minister Timmarusu. The Gajapati king Prataparudra Deva was driven to Cuttack, surrendered and gave his daughter Jaganmohini in marriage to Krishnadevaraya, and the Krishna River became the boundary of the two kingdoms.

He established friendly relations with the Portuguese in Goa in 1510, obtaining guns and Arabian horses and Portuguese help with the capital's water supply. On 19 May 1520 he secured Raichur Fort from Ismail Adil Shah after a difficult siege in which 16,000 Vijayanagara soldiers were killed, helped by a Portuguese contingent under Cristovão de Figueiredo. His reply to the Sultan's envoys was haughty, and he then occupied Bijapur and proclaimed the eldest of three imprisoned Bahmani princes king of the Deccan. At home he abolished taxes such as the marriage fee and made annual tours of the empire. The travellers Paes, Nunez and Barbosa praised the efficiency of his administration.

Krishnadevaraya composed the Telugu poem Amuktamalyada, on which he based his view that a king should rule with an eye to dharma, and several Sanskrit works including Madalasa Charita and Jambavati Kalyana. His reign is regarded as a golden age of Telugu literature, and eight Telugu poets known as the Ashtadiggajas, among them Allasani Peddana and Mukku Timmana, adorned his court. He also patronised Kannada, Sanskrit and Tamil poets; the court language was Kannada. The Madhva saint Vyasatirtha was his rajaguru, though Sri Vaishnavas claim that Venkata Tathacharya held the role.

He rebuilt the Virupaksha Temple and made land grants to Tirumala, Srisailam, Chidambaram and other temples. He visited the Tirumala Venkateswara Temple seven times, and 229 of its roughly 1,250 published inscriptions are attributed to him.

In 1524 Krishnadevaraya made his son Tirumala Raya crown prince; the prince was poisoned soon afterwards, and the king, suspecting Timmarusu, had him blinded. He fell ill while preparing an attack on Belgaum and died on 17 October 1529, succeeded by his brother Achyuta Deva Raya. The Mughal emperor Babur considered him the most powerful ruler in India, and Mukku Timmana praised him as the destroyer of the Turks.
krivichs: The Krivichs, also written Kryvichs, were a tribal union of early East Slavs between the 6th and the 12th centuries. It is suggested that they were originally native to the area around Pskov and that they moved into mostly Finnic areas in the upper reaches of the Volga, the Dnieper and the Dvina, south of the lower Velikaya and into parts of the Neman basin. According to Max Vasmer, their name probably comes from that of their forefather Kriv, an interpretation that stems from East Slavic mythology. The Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus mentions the tribe in De Administrando Imperio under forms such as Κριβιτζοί.

The Krivichs left many archaeological monuments: the remains of agricultural settlements with traces of ironworking, jewellery-making, blacksmith's work and other crafts, long burial mounds of the 6th to 9th centuries with cremated bodies, mounds of rich warriors with weapons, and distinctive jewellery such as bracelet-like temple rings and glass beads made of stretched wire. By the end of the first millennium they had well-developed farming and cattle-breeding.

They settled along the trade route from the Varangians to the Greeks and traded with the Varangians. Their chief tribal centres included Gnezdovo, Izborsk and Polotsk. As a tribe they took part in the military campaigns of Oleg and Igor against the Byzantine Empire.

The name outlived the tribe. In Latvian, Krievs means a Russian and Krievija means Russia, and through the Baltic lands the word became known in Central Europe: a German chronicler from Duisburg wrote in 1314 of the land of Crivitae, and a Polish publication of 1687 called the Polotsk saint Paraxedis the queen of the Kryvians. In Latvian a Belarusian is a Baltkrievs, and Belarus is Baltkrievija. The Belarusian historian Vaclau Lastouski published a magazine called Kryvich in Kaunas from 1923 to 1927. Places called Kryvičy in modern Belarus may be named after the tribe, though this is contested.
krnov: Krnov lies in the historic region of Czech Silesia, on the border with Poland, at the confluence of the Opava and Opavice rivers. It is about 21 kilometres northwest of Opava and 49 kilometres northwest of Ostrava. The town proper lies in the Zlatohorská Highlands, and the western and southern parts of its territory reach into the Nízký Jeseník range. The highest point is the hill Bednářský vrch, at 588 metres. It is a town of the Bruntál District in the Moravian-Silesian Region and has about 22,000 inhabitants.

The first written mention of Krnov dates from 1240, and it was a town by 1269 at the latest, perhaps from 1253. Fortifications were built in the second half of the 13th century, and the Minorites came in 1273 and founded a monastery. Krnov belonged to the Duchy of Troppau until 1377, when the Duchy of Krnov separated and the town became its capital. In 1523 the duchy passed to the Hohenzollern family, who built a castle; the town reached its peak of prosperity and growth under their rule.

The Thirty Years' War brought decline, and after the war the duchy passed to the Liechtenstein family, who began the re-Catholicisation of the duchy. After the War of the Austrian Succession Krnov became a border town, and a fire in 1779 destroyed almost the whole town. Industrialisation in the 19th century, with textile factories and a railway opened in 1872, more than doubled its population in a few decades. In 1910 about 98 percent of its 16,681 people gave German as their native language. From 1938 to 1945 Germany occupied it, and after the war the German population was expelled under the Potsdam Agreement.

The Neo-Renaissance town hall, built in 1901 to 1903, was designed by Leopold Bauer, a native of Krnov. The Church of Saint Martin was first documented in 1281, and the Krnov Synagogue is the only one in the region to survive in its original form. The former cotton mill and the pilgrimage site on the Cvilín hill, with its Church of Our Lady of the Seven Sorrows built in 1722 to 1727, are protected as national cultural monuments. The town is known for the drink Kofola, and its pipe-organ firm Rieger-Kloss was founded in 1873.
kromeriz: Kroměříž lies on both banks of the Morava River in the Zlín Region, about 20 kilometres north-west of Zlín, where the Haná River flows into the Morava on the town's northern edge. Its name comes from the personal name Kroměžir, meaning Kroměžir's property. In the Middle Ages it was a market village at the crossing of the Amber and Salt roads, at a ford across the Morava where a toll was collected.

The first written mention, under the Latin name Cromezir, is in a document written between 1107 and 1125, when the Olomouc bishop Jan II bought the settlement. In the thirteenth century it became the centre of a dominion of the Olomouc bishopric. Raids by Tatars, Cumans and Hungarians in 1241 and 1253 depopulated the settlement. Bishop Bruno von Schauenburg then rebuilt it, founding the market square on the hill above the old settlement, surrounding it with walls, building the Church of Saint Maurice and planting vineyards. The place was first called a town in 1266 and was officially promoted to a town in 1290.

Jews were allowed to settle in the town in 1322, and in the mid-sixteenth century its Jewish community was the largest in Moravia. The bishops lost control of the town during the Hussite Wars in 1423 and regained it in 1455. Bishop Stanislav I Thurzo rebuilt the bishop's residence as a castle in late Gothic and Renaissance style.

Swedish troops under Lennart Torstensson plundered the town in 1643, burning most of its buildings, and a large fire struck in 1656. Bishop Karl II von Liechtenstein-Kastelkorn then rebuilt the town and had the castle completely rebuilt by 1686, founding a mint and ornamental gardens between 1666 and 1675. The Constitutive Imperial Congress sat in Kroměříž in 1848, and in August 1885 the Austrian and Russian emperors met there.

Kroměříž is a town of about 28,000 inhabitants in the Czech Republic and is best known for its Baroque castle and gardens, added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1998. The historic centre is protected as an urban monument reservation. The Castle Gallery holds about 500 paintings, including a late work by Titian, the Flaying of Marsyas. The Church of Saint Maurice retains its early Gothic appearance and holds the grave of Bishop Bruno von Schauenburg.
kronborg: The castle began as a fortress called Krogen, meaning the Hook, built in the early fifteenth century by the Danish king Eric of Pomerania. He insisted that ships entering or leaving the Baltic Sea through the Øresund pay sound dues, and built a strong fortress at the narrowest point of the strait to enforce them. Denmark then held both shores, and with Helsingborg Castle opposite and a guard ship it could control all navigation.

Krogen stood on Ørekrog, a sandy tongue of land, and consisted of a square curtain wall with stone buildings inside. Large parts of its walls survive within the present castle, and Christian III added corner bastions in 1558 and 1559.

After the Northern Seven Years' War ended in 1570, Frederick II extended the bastions to meet the improved power of artillery. The works, led by the Flemish architect Hans Hendrik van Paesschen, were completed in 1577, and the castle then took the name Kronborg, Crown Castle. Its buildings were extended into three wings between 1574 and 1585. From 1578 Anthonis van Obbergen took over as master builder, and the south wing gained a storey and a ballroom measuring 62 by 12 metres, the largest hall in Northern Europe when finished in 1582.

The walls were clad in sandstone from Scania and the roof in copper. James VI of Scotland stayed there in 1590 after marrying Anne of Denmark. A fire on the night of 24 to 25 September 1629 destroyed much of the castle, sparing only the chapel. Christian IV rebuilt the exterior without major changes by 1639, though the interior never fully regained its former glory. During the war of 1658 to 1660 a Swedish army under Carl Gustaf Wrangel besieged and took Kronborg, and the Swedes carried off many art treasures, including the courtyard fountain.

The Crownwork and new ramparts followed in 1688 to 1690. From 1739 the castle also served as a prison, where Queen Caroline Mathilde was held in 1772. It was under military administration from 1785 to 1922, and the army left in 1923.

Kronborg is among the most important Renaissance castles in Northern Europe and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2000. It was opened to the public in 1938 after a thorough renovation. As Elsinore, the anglicised name of the surrounding town of Helsingør, it is the setting of Shakespeare's Hamlet, which was first staged at the castle in 1816 by soldiers of the garrison and has been performed there many times since. A legend also places the sleeping Danish hero Ogier the Dane, or Holger Danske, at Kronborg, waiting until his homeland needs him; a statue of him lies in the casemates.
kronstadt-rebellion: Kronstadt, on Kotlin Island in the Gulf of Finland, was the main base of the Baltic Fleet and defended Petrograd. Its sailors had taken part in the October Revolution and the civil war, and Leon Trotsky had earlier called them the adornment and pride of the revolution. The island held about 50,000 civilians and 26,000 sailors and soldiers, most of them veterans of 1917.

As the Russian Civil War ended, the country was in ruin, and war communism and the forced seizure of peasants' grain deepened the hardship. A January cut of one third in bread rations led to demonstrations in Moscow and strikes in Petrograd, where about 60 percent of the large factories closed for lack of fuel. When the crews of the Petropavlovsk and Sevastopol heard of the repression in Petrograd, they passed a resolution of fifteen demands, including new elections to the soviets by secret ballot, freedom of speech and press for workers, peasants, anarchists and left socialists, and the release of political prisoners.

The rebels called their movement a third revolution, meant to restore power to freely elected soviets. They sought reform of the Bolshevik party, not its end, and rejected help from émigrés. The authorities presented them as agents of the Entente and counter-revolution, and issued an ultimatum on 5 March. Operations began on 7 March, when some 60,000 troops took part. Tukhachevsky's units advanced over the ice in a snowstorm; many soldiers drowned, others defected or refused to advance, and the attack failed.

On 16 March Tukhachevsky's reinforced army of 50,000 prepared to take the island and its 15,000 rebels, beginning with heavy artillery fire. Cadets and Red Army units attacked before dawn, and after heavy fighting on 17 March the last northern forts fell by 1 a.m. The revolt was suppressed on 18 March after it had lasted sixteen days. No power agreed to give the rebels military support, and no aid reached the island.

There were no public trials. Of about 2,000 prisoners, 13 were tried in private as leaders and sentenced to execution two days after the fall of Kronstadt. Hundreds of rebels were killed at Kronstadt and hundreds more shot in Petrograd, and the rest were sent to prisons and forced labour camps, where many died of hunger or disease.

Lenin called the crisis the most critical the Bolsheviks had yet faced. The rebellion did not meet its demands, but it hastened the New Economic Policy, which replaced war communism. Emma Goldman and other supporters of the regime lost their faith in it. Historian Paul Avrich judged that the rebels had little chance of success.
krosno-odrzanskie: Krosno Odrzańskie is a town in Lubusz Voivodeship in western Poland, on the east bank of the Oder at its confluence with the Bóbr. It is the capital of Krosno County. Its position at a point of passage across the Oder made it important on the western border of the Polish kingdom with the Holy Roman Empire from the 11th to the 13th centuries.

The town was first mentioned as Crosno in 1005, when Duke Bolesław I Chrobry of Poland had a fortress built there in his conflict with Emperor Henry II and the West Slavic Veleti confederation. In 1163 it belonged to the Duchy of Silesia, ruled by Bolesław I the Tall, and in 1201 his son Duke Henry I the Bearded gave it a town charter. Henry built a stone castle there, where he died in 1238 and where his widow Hedwig of Andechs took refuge during the first Mongol invasion of Poland in 1241. When the Duchy of Wrocław was divided in 1251, the town became part of the new Duchy of Głogów under Konrad I.

When the last Piast duke of Głogów, Henry XI, died without issue in 1476, his widow Barbara of Brandenburg, daughter of Elector Albert Achilles, inherited the territory. His cousin Duke Jan II the Mad of Żagań devastated the town in opposition, but in 1482 he signed an agreement with Albert Achilles, who kept the area. It remained formally a lien of the Bohemian kingdom until 1538, when King Ferdinand I renounced all rights, confirming its place in the Neumark of Brandenburg. With Brandenburg, Crossen became part of the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701, of the Province of Brandenburg in 1815 and of the German Empire in 1871. A whirlwind devastated the town in May 1886.

The Red Army took the town in 1945, and it became Polish again. Polish communists from Poznań arrived on 2 May to take over its administration, and a second group of 66 members who also meant to rule it caused a conflict that was resolved by June. The adjective Odrzańskie, after the Oder, was added to distinguish it from other settlements of the same name, notably Krosno. From 1975 to 1998 it lay in Zielona Góra Voivodeship. It had 11,319 inhabitants in 2019. People born there include the painter and architect Georg Wenzeslaus von Knobelsdorff and the Mesoamerica scholar Eduard Seler.
kruje: Krujë stands at about 600 metres on the foot of Mount Krujë, between the mountain and the plain of the Ishëm River, 20 kilometres north of Tirana. Its name is related to the Albanian word kroi, meaning 'fountain' or 'water source', and it first appears as Kroai in Byzantine documents of the early 9th century. In ancient times the region was inhabited by the Illyrian tribe of the Albani, and the town lies near the Iron Age site of Zgërdhesh. A middle-sized fortress grew into a town probably between the 6th and the 9th century.

In 1190 Krujë became the capital of the Principality of Arbanon, founded by Progon, the first Albanian state of the Middle Ages. Later it belonged to the Kingdom of Albania, and by 1395 it was under Ottoman vassalage. On 28 November 1443 Skanderbeg took the town by deceiving its governor with a forged letter of the sultan and raised the first Albanian flag there. In 1444 he made it part of the League of Lezhë.

In 1450 a force of 1,500 to 2,000 men under Vrana Konti and Skanderbeg defeated an Ottoman army of about 100,000 led by Sultan Murad II. Ballaban Pasha and Sultan Mehmed II besieged the town without success in 1466 and 1467, with about 150,000 men between them. After Skanderbeg died in 1468 troops of the Republic of Venice joined the garrison. The Ottomans took the town in 1478 after besieging it for over a year.

The town revolted against Ottoman rule in 1906. On 20 September Ottoman troops ambushed the rebel leaders who had come to negotiate, and about 30 people died. Krujë was captured on 14 August 1912 during the revolt that led to the Declaration of Independence. In the Second World War the resistance leader Abaz Kupi, a native of the town, built one of the first permanent resistance forces in Albania there.

Krujë is a town and municipality of north-central Albania. The Roman Catholic bishopric of Krujë was founded in 1167. The Skanderbeg Museum, founded in 1982, stands beside the castle, and the national ethnographic museum, founded in 1989, occupies a villa of the Toptani family built in 1764.
krum: Krum was born around the middle of the 8th century, but his family background and the circumstances of his accession are unknown. It has been speculated that he descended from Khan Kubrat through Kubrat's son Kuber. His name is probably of Turkic origin and may reflect a shortened form of an Old Turkic word for rule, leadership or authority. He became khan sometime between 796 and 803.

Around 805 Krum defeated the Avar Khaganate and advanced north into the Tisza region, which gave Bulgaria a common border with the Frankish Empire. Bulgarian forces defeated a Byzantine army in the Struma valley in 807. In 809 he forced the surrender of Serdica and, despite a guarantee of safe conduct, slaughtered its garrison of 6,000. In 811 the emperor Nikephoros I advanced into Bulgaria, took Pliska on 20 July and burned it. Krum armed as many men as he could, women and peasants included, and on 26 July trapped the retreating Byzantines in the Varbitsa Pass. The army was wiped out and Nikephoros killed. It is said that Krum had the emperor's skull lined with silver and used it as a drinking cup.

In 812 Krum took Develt and Mesembria. At the Battle of Versinikia on 22 June 813 he routed the army of Michael I Rangabe, and then advanced on Constantinople, where he performed a pagan ceremony before the walls, sacrificing people and animals. He ordered a moat and rampart dug from Blachernae to the Golden Gate. Michael was forced to abdicate, the third emperor to lose his throne to Krum in as many years. Leo V the Armenian then tried to ambush Krum during talks; Krum escaped wounded, and in revenge burned churches and monasteries in Eastern Thrace and took Adrianople.

Krum was preparing a great attack on Constantinople, with Slavs, Avars and siege engines, when he died on 13 April 814, most likely of a hemorrhage and stroke. During his reign Bulgarian territory doubled in size, reaching from the middle Danube to the Dnieper. He is remembered for the first known written Bulgarian law code, which gave subsidies to beggars and state protection to the poor and severely punished drinking, slander and robbery. Through these laws he became known as a strict but just ruler who brought Slavs and Bulgars into a centralised state.
krusevac: Kruševac lies in the valley of the West Morava, on the Rasina river, in central Serbia. Its name comes from the Serbian word krušac, meaning river stone, which was widely used in building at the time. Lord Lazar Hrebeljanović founded it in 1371 as a fortified town and used it as his seat.

Lazar built the Lazarica Church, also called the Church of St Stephen, between 1375 and 1378 in the Morava style of architecture. An edict of 1387, in which he confirmed the rights of Venetian merchants on Serbian territory, names the town as his seat. The Serbian army assembled there before the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. According to legend, crows brought news of the defeat to Lazar's wife, Princess Milica, from the tower of her palace, and after the battle she held the town as her seat. Little remains of Lazar's city apart from the fortress, which was declared a Cultural Monument of Exceptional Importance in 1979.
