kuril-islands: The Kuril Islands are a volcanic archipelago of 56 islands and many islets, running north-east from Hokkaido to the Kamchatka Peninsula and separating the Sea of Okhotsk from the North Pacific. They form a Greater Kuril Chain and, at the south-western end, a parallel Lesser Chain. The islands are summits of stratovolcanoes; the chain has around 100 volcanoes, some 40 of them active, and frequent earthquakes. Winters are long, cold and stormy and summers short and foggy. The name Kuril comes from the Ainu word kur, meaning man; Russians later linked it to the verb kurit', to smoke, because of the volcanic plumes.

The Ainu inhabited the islands from early times, although few records predate the 17th century. They traded among themselves for centuries before either Japanese or Russians appeared, and Japanese goods carried by the Menashi Ainu reached Kamchatka. Japanese merchants entered the islands in the 17th century, and by the 18th century the Ainu were subject to the lord of Matsumae. A Tokugawa map of 1644 shows 39 islands north-east of Hokkaido. A Dutch expedition under Maarten Gerritsz Vries explored them in 1643, and Russian Cossacks landed on Shumshu in 1711.

In the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1875 Russia renounced its claims to the Kurils in exchange for Japan renouncing its claims to Sakhalin. Japanese administration then forcibly assimilated the Ainu, who were granted Japanese citizenship but had to adopt Japanese names, while many Japanese moved onto the islands. Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto assembled the strike force for the attack on Pearl Harbor in Hitokappu Bay on Iturup in 1941, and the fleet sailed on 26 November. The Yalta Agreement of February 1945 promised the Kurils and South Sakhalin to the Soviet Union in return for joining the Pacific War.

Soviet forces invaded the North and South Kurils between 18 and 31 August 1945. By 1946 the Soviets had expelled the entire Japanese civilian population, roughly 17,000 people. The Kuril Islands dispute over the four southernmost islands has continued since, and Japan has never accepted the Soviet claim.

The islands are administered by Russia as three districts of Sakhalin Oblast, with a population of roughly 20,000. Japan claims Kunashir, Iturup, Shikotan and the Habomai islets as its Northern Territories, and holds that the other islands are undetermined under international law because the San Francisco Peace Treaty names no owner and the Soviet Union did not sign it. Seabirds nest on the islands in millions, and the surrounding waters are among the most productive in the North Pacific.
kursk: Kursk stands at the confluence of the Kur, Tuskar and Seym rivers and is the administrative centre of Kursk Oblast. Its name comes from the Kur River, a name derived from kurya, meaning channel. The city was first built as a fortress on a hill dominating the plain. Its position on the shortest routes from Moscow to the Crimea and from Moscow to Kiev later made it an important trading town.

Kursk probably emerged as a fortified settlement of the Severians by the 9th century and became part of Kievan Rus' in the late 10th century, as a stronghold of the Kievan princes on the south-eastern border. The Life of Theodosius of the Caves mentions it in 1032, and the Tale of Igor's Campaign praises the Kursk warriors. In the early 12th century it became the seat of a separate appanage principality. Polovtsians raided it, and the Mongols under Batu Khan devastated it; it was rebuilt, but the Golden Horde had again ruined it by the end of the 13th century.

Its revival began with a new fortress built under Feodor I of Russia. Kursk was captured in 1604 by supporters of False Dmitry I and withstood Polish–Lithuanian sieges in 1612, 1616 and 1617 and another in 1634. After the Belgorod Line was built it became one of the largest trade and craft centres of southern Russia, with an annual fair held under the walls of the monastery of Our Lady of Kursk. It received city status in 1779, became the centre of Kursk Governorate in 1797 and by the mid-18th century was among the ten largest Russian cities. A fire in 1781 led to a regular plan in 1782.

German forces occupied Kursk from 4 November 1941 to 8 February 1943. In July 1943 they launched Operation Citadel, their last major offensive against the Soviet Union, and the village of Prokhorovka near Kursk became the centre of one of the largest tank battles in history. Rebuilding began in February 1944, and by 1950 the urban economy was fully restored.

Kursk had 440,052 inhabitants at the 2021 census and is the oldest city of its oblast. Its stone churches include the baroque Sergiev Cathedral and Trinity-Sergius Cathedral, both completed in 1778. The Soviet government developed it as a railway hub on the strength of nearby iron ore deposits.
kurt-eisner: Kurt Eisner was born in Berlin on 14 May 1867 to Emanuel Eisner and Hedwig Levenstein, both Jewish. He studied philosophy and then became a journalist in Marburg. From 1890 to 1895 he was a contributing editor of the Frankfurter Zeitung, and an article attacking Kaiser Wilhelm II earned him nine months in prison. From 1892 to 1917 he was married to the painter Elisabeth Hendrich, with whom he had five children; he later married the editor Elise Belli, and they had two daughters.

He was an open republican as well as a Social Democrat and joined the SPD in 1898, although German Social Democracy, for tactical reasons, held back from republican propaganda. He became editor of Vorwärts after the death of Wilhelm Liebknecht in 1900, but in 1905 a majority of the editorial board, which favoured more orthodox Marxists, called on him to resign.

Afterwards his work was mostly in Bavaria. He was chief editor of the Fränkische Tagespost in Nuremberg from 1907 to 1910 and then a freelance journalist in Munich. In 1917, at the height of the First World War, he joined the Independent Social Democratic Party of Germany. In 1918 he was convicted of treason for inciting a strike of munitions workers, and spent nine months in Stadelheim Prison before the general amnesty of October released him.

He then organised the revolution that overthrew the Wittelsbach monarchy in Bavaria, and became the first republican premier of the People's State of Bavaria. On 23 November 1918 he made public documents from the Bavarian representative in Berlin in July and August 1914, which he thought showed that the war was caused by a small horde of mad Prussian military men together with industrialists, politicians and princes. At the Berne Conference of Socialists he attacked moderate German socialists for refusing to acknowledge Germany's part in causing the war. For that speech and his hostility to Prussia, large sections of the German people came to hate him bitterly.

On 21 February 1919 Anton Graf von Arco auf Valley, a far-right Bavarian nationalist, shot Eisner in the back in Munich as he was on his way to resign before the Bavarian parliament. The elected government fled Munich, and the short-lived Bavarian Soviet Republic followed. Arco-Valley was sentenced to death in January 1920, but the sentence was reduced to life imprisonment, and he was pardoned in 1927.

Eisner was buried in the Munich Ostfriedhof. A monument to the dead of the revolution, commissioned in 1922, held his urn; it was demolished on 22 June 1933 and the urn moved to the New Jewish Cemetery. After World War II the artist Konstantin Frick re-created the monument. A plaque set in the pavement in 1989 marks the place where he was murdered.
kurt-schuschnigg: Kurt Schuschnigg was born on 14 December 1897 in Reiff am Gartsee, now Riva del Garda, in the Tyrolean crown land of Austria-Hungary. In the First World War he was taken prisoner on the Italian Front. He studied law at Freiburg and Innsbruck, and after graduating in 1922 practised as a lawyer in Innsbruck.

He joined the right-wing Christian Social Party and in 1927 was elected to the Nationalrat as its youngest deputy. From January 1932 he was Minister of Justice, and from May 1933 also Minister of Education, under Karl Buresch and then Engelbert Dollfuss. He openly discussed abolishing the parliamentary system, restored the death penalty, and after the socialist February Uprising of 1934 had eight insurgents executed at once.

After the Nazi Otto Planetta assassinated Dollfuss in the July Putsch, Schuschnigg became chancellor of the authoritarian Federal State of Austria on 29 July 1934. He ruled mostly by decree and his policies differed little from those of his predecessor, though his rule was milder. He had to manage a near-bankrupt state while armed paramilitary forces owed loyalty to rival parties and the Austrian Nazis grew stronger. His overriding concern was to preserve Austria's independence.

He sought to balance Germany by aligning with Italy and Hungary, a policy that failed once Mussolini sought Hitler's support. In July 1936 he signed an agreement with Germany that released imprisoned July Putsch insurgents and put the Nazi contact men Edmund Glaise-Horstenau and Guido Schmidt in the cabinet. On 12 February 1938 he met Hitler at the Berghof, where he was presented with what amounted to an ultimatum, including the appointment of Arthur Seyss-Inquart as minister of security, and was coerced into agreeing.

On 24 February he told the Federal Diet that Austria would go thus far and no further. He then proclaimed a plebiscite for 13 March. Hitler demanded its cancellation and then Schuschnigg's resignation. He resigned on 11 March, German troops entered Austria the next day, and he was placed under house arrest.

Schuschnigg was held in solitary confinement and then spent the war in Sachsenhausen and Dachau. In late April 1945 he narrowly escaped an execution order, was freed by Wehrmacht officers in South Tyrol and passed to American troops on 4 May 1945. He emigrated to the United States, where he was professor of political science at Saint Louis University from 1948 to 1967 and became a citizen in 1956.

The Austrian People's Party would not admit him, because it wished to distance itself from the dictatorship. On returning to Austria he downplayed his time of dictatorial power and tried to justify the regime. He died at Mutters, near Innsbruck, in 1977.
kuru-kingdom: The Kuru kingdom was a tribal union of the Bharata and Puru tribes, formed in the Middle Vedic period as a result of their alliance and merger after the Battle of the Ten Kings. With its centre of power in the Kurukshetra region, it was the first recorded state-level society in the Indian subcontinent and dominated roughly from 1200 to 800 BCE. Its first capital was at Āsandīvat, identified with modern Assandh in Haryana. Later literature names Indraprastha, identified with Purana Qila in Delhi, and Hastinapura as the main Kuru cities. The kingdom corresponds with the archaeological Painted Grey Ware culture.

The Atharvaveda praises Parikshit as King of the Kurus, ruler of a prosperous realm, and the Shatapatha Brahmana commemorates his son Janamejaya as a conqueror who performed the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice. These two kings played a decisive part in consolidating the state and developing the srauta rituals. The Kurus later declined after being defeated by the non-Vedic Salva tribe, and the centre of Vedic culture shifted east to the Panchala kingdom. Post-Vedic literature says the capital was moved to Kaushambi after floods destroyed Hastinapur.

By the 6th century BCE the dynasty had divided into Kuru and Vatsa kingdoms. Buddhist sources describe Kuru as a minor state under a chieftain called Koravya, and by the time of the Buddha its small states had been replaced by a Kuru republic.

The clans that formed the kingdom were largely semi-nomadic and pastoral, but as settlement moved into the western Ganges plain, farming of rice and barley became more important. The fourfold varna system replaced the older twofold division of arya and dasa. Kings ruled with a rudimentary administration of a priest, village headman, army chief, emissary, herald and spies, and took tribute from commoners and weaker neighbours. A common council, the Samiti, could elect or dethrone the king, and a smaller assembly of elders, the Sabhā, advised him.

The Kurus arranged the scattered hymns of different clans into the Vedas, forming the bulk of the Rigveda, and developed the srauta rituals. The Mahabharata centres on a conflict between two branches of the Kuru dynasty, possibly around 1000 BCE, though archaeology has not shown whether its specific events have a historical basis.
kuruc: The word kuruc was first used in 1514 for the armed peasants led by György Dózsa. Today's etymologists derive it from the Turkish kurudsch, 'rebel' or 'insurgent'. In 1671 Meni, the beglerbeg pasha of Eger, applied it to the mostly noble refugees from Royal Hungary, and from 1671 to 1711 it was used in Hungarian, Slovak and Turkish texts for the rebels against the Habsburgs. The opposite term, labanc, widespread after 1678, meant the Austrians and their loyalist supporters; it comes from a Hungarian word for 'long hair', referring to the wigs of Austrian soldiers.

After the magnate conspiracy and the rebellion of Francis I Rákóczi, Emperor Leopold I introduced absolutist government in Royal Hungary. The court tried again to suppress Protestants, and in 1673 it set up a governing council under Johann Caspar von Ampringen. Soldiers dismissed from frontier castles, nobles who lost their estates and Protestants fled east and gathered by the Tisza. In 1672 these 'fugitives' (bújdosók) invaded Upper Hungary and took the castles of Diósgyőr, Ónod, Szendrő and Tokaj, but on 26 October 1672 a Habsburg army defeated them at Gyurke. In 1674 a trial of Protestant pastors ended in sentences of death, and the pastors were sold as galley slaves in Naples, which caused public outcry across Europe.

Between 1674 and 1678 the fugitives were led by Count Paul Wesselényi, and in May 1677 France, Poland, Transylvania and the fugitives signed a treaty in Warsaw. In 1678 Mihály Teleki took the lead, and the same year Emeric Thököly declared war on the Habsburgs and his army occupied almost all of Lower and Upper Hungary. The fugitives elected him their leader at Szoboszló in January 1680. In 1681 Leopold I restored the constitution and the Palatine of Hungary.

From then on the history of the kurucs is that of the Thököly Uprising of 1680–85 and Rákóczi's War of Independence of 1703–1711, which had a wider social base and more complex aims than the original movements. Rákóczi himself did not use the word, preferring the French term insurgents or malcontents. After 1711 many former kuruc soldiers joined the Habsburg army, and in the first half of the 18th century 'kuruc' came to mean Hungarian hussars in that service. By the end of the century it was only a historical term. Today it can denote Hungarians who stand for strict national independence, in a positive sense of patriotic or a negative sense of chauvinistic. The South German oath Kruzitürken joins Kuruzen and Türken.
kurukshetra: Kurukshetra is a historical region of India, also called Dharmakshetra, the realm of duty, and the Land of the Bhagavad Gita. The name also refers to the city of Kurukshetra, the administrative headquarters of Kurukshetra district. In the Vedas it is described as a region, not a city, and kshetra means region in Sanskrit. Its boundaries correspond roughly to the central and western parts of present-day Haryana and Punjab, and one account places it between two rivers, the Sarasvati and the Drishadvati.

According to the Puranas, the region is named after King Kuru, ancestor of the Kauravas and Pandavas of the Mahabharata, and the Kurukshetra War of that epic is believed to have taken place here. The Vamana Purana says that Vishnu blessed Kuru with two boons: that the land would be known as holy after his name, and that anyone dying there would go to heaven.

The Kuru kingdom, a union of Vedic Indo-Aryan tribes of the northern Iron Age (c. 1200 to c. 900 BCE), developed into the first recorded state-level society in the Indian subcontinent. It collected its ritual hymns into the Vedas and developed the Srauta rituals, which contributed to the roots of Hinduism. It dominated the middle Vedic period under Parikshit and Janamejaya, but had become something of a backwater by the 5th century BCE. Its traditions supplied the basis of the Mahabharata.

The Mauryan empire conquered Kurukshetra in the late 4th century BCE, after which it became a centre of Buddhism and Hinduism. The Kushans later took the region, and the Gupta empire conquered it in the early 4th century CE, when it saw a cultural and religious revival. The Pushyabhuti dynasty ruled after the Gupta empire, and the town reached its height under King Harsha (c. 590 to 647 CE), when the Chinese scholar Xuanzang visited Thanesar. Civil war followed Harsha's death without a successor.

Tomara A Kashmiri army briefly held the area in 733, and the Tomara dynasty took over from 736. Mahmud of Ghazni sacked it in 1014, and it joined the Delhi Sultanate in 1206. Babur put down a local rebellion in 1526 and made it part of the Mughal Empire. Under Akbar it became a spiritual centre for Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims. Maratha forces controlled it until the British took it in 1805, after the Second Anglo-Maratha War.

Kurukshetra is an important Hindu pilgrimage destination. The 48 kos parikrama is a traditional circuit of about 90 km round the holy city, made on foot to all its sites. Brahma Sarovar, one of Asia's largest man-made ponds, draws many pilgrims to bathe on Somavati Amavasya and at solar eclipses, and Jyotisar is the site where the Bhagavad Gita is said to have been delivered to Arjuna.
kurultai: The word kurultai, also spelled quriltai, literally means 'gathering'. The oldest recorded mention of its root, before the time of Genghis Khan, is the verb Qur in the Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk of the 11th century, where it meant to assemble, to assemble into a formation, or to build. Another hypothesis derives it from the hypothetical Proto-Mongolic verb *kura-, *kurija-, 'to collect, to gather', from which comes khural, 'meeting, assembly'. The same root gives the Mongolian khurim, 'feast', which first referred to large festive gatherings on the steppe.

A kurultai was a medieval political and military council made up of members of a Mongol khan's family, imperial sons-in-law, captains of the army and others. All Great Khans of the Mongol Empire were formally elected at one, and khans of subordinate states such as the Golden Horde were chosen by a similar regional assembly. The Secret History of the Mongols records that in the year of the tiger, 1206, the people gathered at the source of the Onan river, hoisted the white standard with nine tails and gave Chinggis Qa'an the title of Qan.

Chiefs also assigned critical positions and titles at a kurultai and decided the military direction the new khan would follow. Most major campaigns were first planned at such assemblies, and lesser ones met under subordinate leaders and generals. No laws were written down there, but the decisions set policy.

A kurultai needed senior members from across the empire, who were generally also military leaders. Without them its decision was viewed as illegitimate or no action was taken. The deaths of Ögedei in 1241 and Möngke in 1259 drew Mongol leaders and troops away from the outskirts of Vienna and Venice and from Syria, which halted operations against the Austrians and the Mamluks.

The Golden Horde's enthronement was described by the 15th-century German traveller Johann Schiltberger: the khan was seated on white felt and raised in it three times, carried round the tent, seated on a throne, given a golden sword and sworn in. The gathering was also a festival with feasting and traditional games, many of which continue in the modern Mongolian Naadam. Women attended, though they could not vote.
kurume: Kurume lies on the Chikugo Plain in southern Fukuoka Prefecture, about 40 kilometres from the prefectural capital at Fukuoka City. The Chikugo River flows from the north-east to the south-west of the city and marks much of its boundary, and the Minou Mountain Range, with Mount Takatori, Mount Hatsushin and Mount Mino, rises along its southern and south-eastern side. Its climate is humid subtropical, with the most rain in July. In 2005 the surrounding towns of Kitano, Jōjima, Mizuma and Tanushimaru were merged into it, giving the city a long east-west shape.

The area was part of ancient Chikugo Province and was the site of its provincial capital, its kokubun-ji and its ichinomiya. During the Edo period it came under the Kurume Domain, ruled for most of its history by the Arima clan, whose policy of promoting industry developed the castle town around Kurume Castle into a commercial centre. The clan's family temple, Bairin-ji, was founded near the castle. The modern city was established on 1 May 1889, with the creation of the modern system of municipalities.

From 1915 to 1919 over 1,000 German and about 50 Austro-Hungarian prisoners of war, taken after the surrender at Tsingtao, were held in an internment camp at Kurume, the largest in Japan. Exchanges between the prisoners and local people left a lasting mark on the city, and the prisoners' work and skills contributed to the local rubber industry that became the basis of the tyre maker Bridgestone. Kurume was a garrison town for the Imperial Japanese Army and from 1922 a centre of the rubber and chemical industries. On 11 August 1945 an air raid by 53 B-24 bombers killed 212 people and destroyed much of the urban centre.

Kurume is a regional commercial centre. Bridgestone was founded here by Shōjirō Ishibashi (1889–1976), whose family made jika-tabi, the sock-like shoes of farmers, and found that rubber soles protected the wearers from parasitic worms in the rice paddies; the company's original plant remains in the city. Traditional products include kasuri, an indigo-dyed woven cloth, and rantai shikki, lacquered bamboo trays and bowls. The city has many National Historic Sites, among them Kofun burial mounds and the Chikugo Kokufu ruins, and attractions such as Kurume Castle, Kōra taisha, Kurume Suitengū and Zendō-ji, the head temple of the Jōdo sect in Kyushu.
kurunegala: Kurunegala is the capital of the North Western Province and of Kurunegala District. It lies at the junction of several main roads, about 94 km from Colombo, 42 km from Kandy and 51 km from Matale, at an altitude of 116 metres and surrounded by coconut plantations and rubber estates. Eight large rocks encircle and dominate the city, and six of them take their names from the animals they are imagined to resemble, among them Ibbagala, the Tortoise Rock, and Wanduragala, the Monkey Rock. The largest is Ethagala, the Elephant Rock, which reaches 325 metres.

The city is named after that rock: kurune means tusker and gala means rock in Sinhala. Its old name was Hasthishaila-pura, Sanskrit for the City of the Elephant Rock. A folk legend says that in a long-ago drought a witch turned some of the water-consuming animals into stone.

Kurunegala had a citadel in the 13th century, and its rise as a capital followed events at Yapahuwa. The sacred tooth relic was taken from the Yapahuwa kingdom to the Pandyan country by an Aryacakravarti from the Jaffna Kingdom during the rule of Buwaneka Bahu I (1272 to 1284). King Parakrama Bahu III, who ruled from Kurunegala between 1287 and 1293, brought it back.

Kurunegala remained the seat of government for three further kings: Buwanekabahu II (1293 to 1302), Parakramabahu IV (1302 to 1326) and Buwanekabahu III (1326 to 1335), also called Wanni Buwanekabahu, the son of Pandit Parakramabahu II and believed to be the last king to rule from the city. Vijayabahu V ruled from Dambadeniya and Yapahuwa from 1335 to 1341, after which the kingdom shifted to Gampola. Under the Kurunegala kings the economy rested on agriculture, trade and taxes, and the royal income came chiefly from farmers' shares of their harvest and from gems such as pearls and moonstones.

Little survives of the royal complex: a stone entrance, steps, rock pillars and ruined walls of the palace and of the Palace of the Tooth Relic. Nearby are the archaeological cities of Parakramapura, with the remains of a moated palace and monasteries of the 12th century, Dambadeniya and Yapahuwa.

Most of the people of Kurunegala are Sinhalese, with sizeable Moor, Tamil, Burgher and Malay communities. Buddhism is the main religion, alongside Hinduism, Christianity and Islam. The Athkanda Raja Maha Viharaya and the Ibbagala Raja Maha Viharaya are among its Buddhist temples, and the city is the seat of Roman Catholic and Anglican dioceses. A large reservoir built by ancient kings, Kurunegala Lake, lies at the edge of the centre, and a clock tower of 1922 commemorates officers from the Wayamba province killed in the First World War.
kusel: Kusel lies on the Kuselbach in the southwest of Rhineland-Palatinate, in the North Palatine Uplands, about 30 kilometres northwest of Kaiserslautern. The floor of the dale is roughly 220 metres above sea level, and hills close it in on both sides. Lichtenberg Castle stands just beyond the town's limits to the west, and the Remigiusberg and the Potzberg to the east. With about 5,000 inhabitants, Kusel challenges Cochem for the title of Germany's smallest district seat. Until 1865 its name was written Cusel, and its oldest form, Cosla, is a Celtic word for a brook.

Celtic graves of the Iron Age have been found around Kusel, and after the Battle of Tolbiac in 496 the area came under Frankish rule. A Frankish royal estate of the 7th century stood on the ruins of a Roman one, and the Remigiusland around it was given to the Archbishopric of Reims, probably between 575 and 590. In 931 the estate passed to the Abbey of Saint-Remi in Reims. In 1127 monks from Reims founded a Benedictine house on the Remigiusberg. The Counts of Veldenz, who had been hired to protect the Remigiusland, built Lichtenberg Castle about 1214 in rivalry with the owners, and it is now known as Germany's biggest castle ruin.

Charles IV is known to have granted Kusel town rights in 1347. In 1444 it passed to the Duchy of Palatine Zweibrücken, which bought the Remigiusland in 1552 for 8,500 Rhenish guilders. In 1635, during the Thirty Years' War, Croatian troops of the Imperial army under General Matthias Gallas entered by cunning, killed more than half the townsfolk and burned the town. It took 40 years to rebuild it, and it was burned again in the Franco-Dutch War. A fire in 1794 burnt out almost all the old buildings.

Kusel is the seat of the Kusel district and of the Kusel-Altenglan Verbandsgemeinde. The medieval street layout survives in the old town, and the centre has Classicist and Historicist buildings of the 19th century, among them the Classicist Protestant parish church of 1829 to 1831. Cloth-making was the main industry from the mid-19th century until after the Second World War. The tenor Fritz Wunderlich was born in Kusel, and the Fritz-Wunderlich-Halle in its cultural centre bears his name. The Kuseler Herbstmesse, held in early September, is said to be one of the biggest folk festivals of the Western Palatinate.
kushan-empire: Chinese sources describe the Kushans as one of five aristocratic tribes of the Yuezhi. Many scholars believe the Yuezhi were an Indo-European people, and some suggest a Tocharian origin, while others propose an Iranic Saka origin. The Records of the Great Historian and the Book of Han place them in the grasslands of eastern Xinjiang and north-western Gansu, until the Xiongnu beheaded their king and forced them west between 176 and 160 BCE.

Traces of the Kushans in Bactria and Sogdiana date to the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, where they displaced the Sakas and built fortresses on the ruins of Hellenistic cities such as Ai-Khanoum. The earliest documented ruler, Heraios, called himself a tyrant in Greek on his coins. Kujula Kadphises later welded the Yuezhi tribes into a tight confederation.

Kushan rulers are recorded for about three centuries, from around 30 to around 375 CE. Vima Takto expanded the empire into north-western South Asia, and his son Vima Kadphises added conquests in Bactria. Kanishka the Great, the fourth king, ruled a huge territory from his accession. According to the Rabatak inscription it reached south to Ujjain and Kundina and east beyond Pataliputra. His successor Huvishka's rule was a period of retrenchment and consolidation, in which he devoted effort to controlling the city of Mathura.

Vasudeva I was the last of the Great Kushans, and the end of his rule coincides with the Sasanian invasion as far as north-western India. The empire fragmented into semi-independent kingdoms in the 3rd century, which fell to the Sasanians, who established the Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom. In the 4th century the Guptas pressed from the east, and the last Kushan and Kushano-Sasanian kingdoms were overwhelmed by invaders from the north, the Kidarites and later the Hephthalites.

The Kushans initially used Greek for administration, then adopted the Eastern Iranian Bactrian language, written in an adapted Greek script. Their gold, silver and copper coins carried more than thirty gods, drawn from Iranian, Greek and Indian worlds, together with images of kings and the Buddha. Kushan rulers were patrons of Buddhism, and Kanishka is remembered in Buddhist tradition for convening a great council in Kashmir. Between the mid-1st and mid-3rd century, Buddhism, patronised by the Kushans, spread to China and other Asian countries along the Silk Road.

The art of Gandhara, at the crossroads of Kushan power, developed Greco-Buddhist traditions. The Kushans also had diplomatic contacts with Rome, and in the 1st and 2nd centuries they collaborated militarily with the Han general Ban Chao, though in 86 they marched against him and were defeated.
kushinagar: Kushinagar, in Pali Kusinārā and in Sanskrit Kuśinagara, is a town in the Kushinagar district of Uttar Pradesh. Alexander Cunningham held that the name came from the abundance of kusha grass in the region. According to the Mahāparinibbāṇa Sutta (Sutta 16 of the Dīgha Nikāya), the Buddha in his eightieth year travelled with disciples for months from Rājagṛha through Pāṭaliputta, Vesāli, Bhoganagara and Pāvā to Kushinagar. At Pāvā a resident named Cunda invited them to a meal that included sūkaramaddava, and soon afterwards the Buddha fell ill with a painful complaint resembling dysentery. He crossed the Kakkuttha River, now the Khanua, and reached Kushinagar, where he lay down between sala trees on his right side and attained parinirvana. His body was cremated seven days later.

The Sakya clan was to receive the ashes, but six other clans and a king claimed them too. A Brahmin named Drona divided them into eight portions: for Ajātasattu of Magadha, the Licchavis of Vesāli, the Sakyas of Kapilavastu, the Bulis of Allakappa, the Koliyas of Rāmagāma, the brahmin of Veṭhadīpa, the Mallas of Pāvā and the Malla king of Kushinagar. According to Buddhaghosa each portion was placed in a reliquary and buried in a tumulus, later enlarged into stupas; of these only the Ramagrama stupa in Ramgram, Nepal, is said to remain intact.

The ruins were first mentioned in modern literature in 1837 by D. Liston, who noted that they were already a place of worship. Alexander Cunningham excavated the Matha Kuar shrine and the Ramabhar stupa in 1861–1862 and was the first archaeologist to identify the site as the place of the Buddha's parinirvana. In 1876 Archibald Carlleyle uncovered the Mahaparinirvana stupa and a reclining Buddha 6.1 metres long. A Burmese monk, Sayadaw U Chandramani, asked the English Governor of India in 1901 for permission for pilgrims to worship the image. J. Ph. Vogel conducted campaigns between 1904 and 1907. Laurence Waddell suggested in 1896 that the death took place near Rampurva, but archaeology and the sutta both support Kushinagar.

The red sandstone reclining Buddha lies in the Parinirvana Temple, on its right side with its head to the north. The Parinirvana Stupa stands behind it, and the Ramabhar stupa, 1.5 km east, marks the cremation place. The Matha Kuar shrine holds a seated Buddha in blue stone, with an inscription of the 10th or 11th century. Modern temples in Thai and other Buddhist styles also stand there.
kutahya: Kütahya lies on the Porsuk River in western Turkey, at 969 metres above sea level, and is the seat of Kütahya Province. The surrounding region has broad areas of gentle slopes with agricultural land, rising to high mountain ridges to the north and west. Its population is 263,863. Old sources name the ancient city Kotiaeon, Cotiaeum or Koti, and its history is said to reach back to 3000 BCE, although the date of its founding cannot be fixed.

In the Iron Age the area was settled by the Phrygians. In 676 BCE the Cimmerians defeated the Phrygian king Midas III and dominated the region, until Lydian rule replaced theirs in the time of Alyattes. Alexander the Great established control there in 334 BCE, and after his death in 323 BCE the region passed to Antigonos I. In 133 BCE Cotyaeum came under Roman rule and became part of the province of Phrygia Salutaris. Menas, a soldier turned hermit, declared himself a Christian before the prefect Pyrrhus in 304 CE and was tortured and beheaded on a rock outside the city. Under Justinian I the town was fortified with a double line of walls and a citadel.

Kotyaion fell briefly to the Seljuks in 1071 and was sacked by them again some time after 1180. It was later taken by the Germiyanids and by Timur, until the Ottomans conquered it. It was first the centre of Anatolia Eyalet, and the troops of Ibrahim Pasha of Egypt briefly occupied it in 1833. Kütahya was occupied by the Greek Army on 17 July 1921 during the Turkish War of Independence, and the Turkish Army captured it in ruins on 30 August 1922.

Under the Ottomans, many Armenians settled in the town and came to dominate tile-making and pottery. Kütahya became a major centre of the Ottoman ceramic industry, producing tiles and faience for mosques, churches and official buildings across the Middle East. A small ewer now in the British Museum, inscribed in Armenian script with a date of 1510, gave its name to Abraham of Kütahya ware. Arthur Lane proposed in 1957 that this ware was made from 1490 until about 1525, and his chronology has been generally accepted.

During the Armenian genocide of 1915 the Ottoman governor, Faruk Ali Bey, went to great lengths to protect the Armenians of the district from deportation. He was removed in March 1916, and the community suffered under his successor. The ceramicist David Ohannessian, a master of a Kütahya workshop, was deported in early 1916 and later travelled to Jerusalem to help restore the Dome of the Rock, where Armenian ceramics continue today.
kutaisi: Kutaisi lies on the Rioni River, 221 kilometres west of Tbilisi, in the Imereti region of Georgia, and is the capital of Imereti. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. Archaeological evidence indicates that it was the capital of Colchis in the sixth to fifth centuries BCE. It is believed that in the Argonautica, the Greek epic poem about Jason and the Argonauts, Apollonius Rhodius took Kutaisi to be their final destination and the residence of King Aeëtes.

Kutaisi was later the capital of the kingdom of Lazica until a brief Arab occupation. An Arab invasion of western Georgia was repelled in 736 by Abkhazians together with Lazic and Iberian allies. Around 786 Leon II won full independence from the Byzantine Empire and moved his capital to Kutaisi, uniting Lazica and Abasgia in a dynastic union that led to the unification of the Georgian monarchy in the 11th century. From 1008 to 1122 it was the capital of the Kingdom of Georgia, and from the 15th century until 1810 the capital of the Kingdom of Imereti.

During the 17th century the Imeretian kings repeatedly appealed to the Russian Empire for help against the Ottomans, and were ignored. In 1768, under Catherine the Great, troops under General Gottlieb Heinrich Totleben joined King Heraclius II of Georgia, and Totleben helped King Solomon I of Imereti recover Kutaisi on 6 August 1770. The Russian–Turkish wars ended in 1810 with Russia's annexation of the Imeretian kingdom, and Kutaisi became the capital of the Kutaisi Governorate, which covered much of western Georgia.

In March 1879 the Kutaisi Circuit Court tried nine Georgian Jews from Sachkhere who were falsely accused of killing a Christian girl for religious purposes. After ten days and nearly 70 witnesses they were acquitted, as their lawyers showed that the accusation rested largely on false testimony. The trial drew attention across the Russian Empire.

Kutaisi is the third-largest city of Georgia, with 160,971 inhabitants in 2025. The ruined Bagrati Cathedral, built by King Bagrat III in the early 11th century, is its landmark, and the Gelati Monastery a few kilometres east is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Motsameta Monastery is named for the brothers David and Constantine, dukes of Margveti, who were martyred by Arab invaders in the 8th century. The city also holds the Sataplia Cave, with dinosaur footprints, and the Kutaisi Synagogue, built in 1885.
kutna-hora: Kutná Hora, called Kuttenberg in German, lies on the Vrchlice Stream about 52 kilometres east of Prague. Celts of the Hallstatt and La Tène periods lived around the Kaňk hill, where a smelting furnace points to early underground mining. Silver dinars of 985 to 995 were found at Malín, now part of the town. In 1142 monks from Waldsassen Abbey in Bavaria founded Sedlec Abbey, the first Cistercian monastery in Bohemia, and the discovery of silver near Sedlec brought settlers, especially from nearby German-speaking regions.

Silver began to be mined in 1260, and the town is first mentioned in 1289 under its Latin name Mons Cuthna. In 1300 King Wenceslaus II issued the royal mining code Ius regale montanorum, and shortly afterwards Kutná Hora became seat of the central mint of the Czech lands, where Prague groschen were struck. It became the second most important town of the Kingdom of Bohemia after Prague and its main financial centre. On 18 January 1409 King Wenceslaus IV signed the Decree of Kutná Hora there, giving the Czech university nation three votes in elections to the faculty of Prague University.

The Hussite Wars interrupted this growth. Sigismund made the town his base in 1420 for an attack on the Taborites, which led to the Battle of Kutná Hora, and in 1421 the Hussites burned Sedlec Abbey and took the town. The Religious peace of Kutná Hora was concluded there in 1485. Mining was reduced in the 1530s because of flooding in the deepest mines and weaker ore, the main mining zone closed in 1543, and production of the Prague groschen ended in 1547. Swedish raids in 1639 and 1643 caused heavy damage. New attempts at mining in the early 18th century found only thin veins, and the mint closed in 1727.

Kutná Hora has about 22,000 inhabitants. Its centre, including the Sedlec area, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995. The Gothic Church of Saint Barbara was built from 1385 to 1395 to a design by Peter Parler, with the work completed by Johann Parler and continued by other masters in the 15th century. The Italian Court, begun in the Gothic style between 1260 and 1300, housed the royal mint until 1727. At Sedlec the ossuary at the Church of All Saints is decorated with the bones of an estimated 40,000 people who died in plague epidemics and the Hussite Wars.
kuttab: In Arabic the word kuttab is used only of elementary schools. The same institution is called a maktab, or in Morocco an m'siid. In Persian it was the maktabkhana, a name also used in Azerbaijani, Ottoman Turkish and Uzbek, and in Bosnian it is the mejtef or mekteb. The word kuttab shares its root, k-t-b, with kitab, "book". In the medieval Islamic world an elementary school was known as a maktab, a term that dates back to at least the tenth century. Like the madrasas, which provided higher education, a maktab was often attached to a mosque.

The writer Ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna, devoted a chapter of one of his books to the maktab in the 11th century, "The Role of the Teacher in the Training and Upbringing of Children", as a guide for its teachers. He argued that children learn better in classes than from private tutors, citing the value of competition and emulation among pupils and of group discussion. He proposed that children enter at six and remain until fourteen, studying the Qur'an, Islamic metaphysics, language, literature, ethics and manual skills. After fourteen, pupils were to choose a subject of interest, such as medicine, geometry, trade or a craft, with the age of leaving kept flexible.

In the 16th century the jurist Ibn Hajar al-Haytami answered a petition from a retired judge who ran an elementary school for orphans. His fatwa outlined a structure of maktab education meant to prevent any physical or economic exploitation of the enrolled orphans. Kuttabs were often built as parts of religious and charitable complexes sponsored by rulers or local elites. In Cairo they were commonly set in a room above a sabil, a kiosk giving water to the public, in both Mamluk and Ottoman Egyptian architecture. Ottoman külliyes in Istanbul, including the Fatih Mosque and Süleymaniye complexes, contained a mekteb, and the Saadi dynasty included an m'sid in complexes at Marrakesh such as the Bab Doukkala Mosque and the Mouassine Mosque.

The caliphate had the highest literacy rate of the Middle Ages, comparable to that of classical Athens, and the maktab and madrasa played a fundamental role in it. The kuttab came to represent an old-fashioned method of education in countries where most people are Muslim, in which a sheikh teaches students seated on the ground before him. Until modern schools developed in the 20th century it remained the prevalent means of mass education in much of the Islamic world.
kuwana: Kuwana lies in northern Mie Prefecture, at the mouth of the Kiso Three Rivers, which divide Mie and Aichi Prefectures. It has long been a regional centre of fishing, industry, business and culture. The climate is humid subtropical, with warm summers and cool winters.

In the late Heian and Muromachi periods the area was known as Juraku-no-tsu and was a major seaport, controlled by a guild of merchants. The poet Socho described it in 1515 as a major city with over a thousand houses, temples and inns. In the Sengoku period Oda Nobunaga's forces destroyed the Ikkō-ikki in the Sieges of Nagashima of 1571, 1573 and 1574. Under Toyotomi Hideyoshi, Ujiie Yukihiro received a domain of 22,000 koku in 1595, but he sided with the pro-Toyotomi armies at Sekigahara and was dispossessed by Tokugawa Ieyasu.

Under the Tokugawa, Kuwana was the castle town of a domain of 150,000 koku and the forty-second post station of the Tōkaidō. The crossing of Ise Bay from Miya-juku took a whole day, so Kuwana was a necessary stop, to the benefit of its inns and restaurants, which were especially known for clams. The last Kyoto shoshidai, Matsudaira Sadaaki, ruled the domain and fought in the Boshin War. Allied air raids on 17 and 24 July 1945 destroyed some 90 per cent of the urban area, and the Isewan Typhoon damaged it again in 1959.

Kuwana had an estimated 141,045 inhabitants in March 2021. Its traditional industries include metal casting, notably manhole covers, Banko ware ceramics and woodworking, and the farming of hamaguri clams. It is also a bed town for nearby Nagoya and Yokkaichi. Tado Shrine and Nabana no Sato are among its places of interest.
kuyavia: Kuyavia lies on the left bank of the Vistula, east of the Noteć River and Lake Gopło, and is traditionally divided into a north-western part around Bydgoszcz, a central part around Inowrocław or Kruszwica, and a south-eastern part around Włocławek or Brześć Kujawski. It borders Gdańsk Pomerania, Chełmno Land, Greater Poland, Łęczyca Land, Masovia and Dobrzyń Land. The post-glacial lowlands lie 100–130 metres above sea level and hold about 600 lakes larger than one square kilometre, with layers of rock-salt and potassium below the glacial deposits. Their black fertile soils earned Kuyavia the name of the granary of Poland.

Linear Pottery culture existed in the area, and the earliest solid evidence of cheese-making, dated to 5,500 BCE, was found there. The beginnings of a state are connected with the West Slavic Goplans, whose main centre was Kruszwica on the northern shore of Lake Gopło. In the 10th century their territory was conquered by the Polans, and after the death of Mieszko I in 992 it formed part of the early Duchy of Poland. The name Cuiavia first appears in the 1136 Bull of Gniezno issued by Pope Innocent II, which confirmed the bishopric at Włocławek as a suffragan of the Archdiocese of Gniezno.

After the 1138 Testament of Bolesław III Wrymouth, Kuyavia passed to the Duchy of Masovia. In 1233 Duke Konrad I of Masovia created the Duchy of Kuyavia for his son Casimir I, and after Casimir's death in 1267 it was divided into the duchies of Inowrocław and Brześć Kujawski. Władysław I the Elbow-high began to reunite the Polish lands, the Kuyavian line of the Piast dynasty became extinct in 1388, and the territories were fully reintegrated under Casimir III the Great. A Polish victory at the Battle of Koronowo was fought in the region on 10 October 1410.

After the unification of the Polish lands, the region was divided into the Brześć Kujawski and Inowrocław voivodeships, which lasted until 1795. Swedish troops plundered Bydgoszcz, Inowrocław and Włocławek in the late 17th century. In the partitions of Poland Prussia took the region in two stages, in 1772 and 1793, and in 1815 Kuyavia was divided between the Kingdom of Poland and the Kingdom of Prussia. Poland regained the region after the First World War, and it was occupied by Nazi Germany from 1939 to 1945.

Bydgoszcz has been the main economic centre of Kuyavia since the Polish Golden Age, and Włocławek and Bydgoszcz each have their own bishoprics. In 1999 almost the whole of Kuyavia was joined to the Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship.
kuzma-minin: Kuzma Minich Zakhariev-Sukhoruky, known as Kuzma Minin, was born around the 1570s, a native of Balakhna. He became a prosperous butcher in Nizhny Novgorod and a trusted and respected member of the merchants' guild. His family life was modest in record: he had a single son, Nefed, and a wife, Tatiana Semenovna. His standing among the townspeople explains why, when a popular patriotic movement formed there to organise volunteer corps, the merchants chose him to oversee the public funds that they donated.

The movement arose during the Polish intervention in Russia of 1605-1618, which coincided with the Time of Troubles. Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky together formed the popular uprising in Nizhny Novgorod against the occupation by the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Minin handled the money used to raise and equip the Second Volunteer Army, which Pozharsky led. The army was credited with clearing the Moscow Kremlin of Polish forces on 1 November 1612, ending the occupation after the Battle of Moscow.

Minin distinguished himself as a skilled commander. Under the newly elected tsar Michael Romanov he was made a nobleman and a member of the boyar duma. He died on 21 May 1616 and was buried in the Archangel Cathedral of Nizhny Novgorod.

A royal decree of 5 July 1616 confirmed his family in possession of an estate in the Nizhny Novgorod district, consisting of the town of Bogorodskoye with its villages. His son Nefed lived mostly in Moscow, where he worked as a government clerk, and died in 1632, after which the lands reverted to the crown and then passed to Prince Jacob Kudenekovich Cherkassky. Tatiana Minina remained in Nizhny Novgorod and appears to have taken monastic vows late in life, probably at the Resurrection Convent in the city's Kremlin.

Minin and Pozharsky became national heroes in Russian culture, and a central square of Nizhny Novgorod is named after them. Later historians such as Ivan Zabelin and Mikhail Pogodin regarded Minin generally with respect.
kwame-nkrumah: Kwame Nkrumah was born Francis Nwia Kofi Nkrumah on 21 September 1909 at Nkroful, a small village in the Nzema area of the southwest Gold Coast, close to the frontier with the French colony of the Ivory Coast. He was his mother's only child. His father, a goldsmith, worked at Half Assini, and Nkrumah went to the elementary school run there by a Catholic mission. After ten years in the United States he returned to London in May 1945 and enrolled at the London School of Economics, then at University College London, where his supervisor A. J. Ayer thought he lacked an analytical mind, and he did not complete his law studies at Gray's Inn.

The Gold Coast constitution of 1946 gave Africans a majority on the legislative council for the first time, and the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC), the colony's first true political party, was founded in August 1947. It hired Nkrumah to run it, and he sailed home from Liverpool in November 1947. In April 1949 his supporters pressed him to leave the UGCC, and on 12 June 1949 he announced the Convention People's Party (CPP), choosing the word convention, he said, to carry the masses with us. He became prime minister in 1952 and worked closely with the British governor, Arden-Clarke, who told the civil service to support the new government.

Ghana became independent on 6 March 1957, the first British African colony to gain majority-rule independence, and the celebrations in Accra drew over 100 reporters and photographers. His government was socialist and nationalist and funded industrial and energy projects. Accra hosted a series of pan-African meetings: the First Conference of Independent States in April 1958 and the All-African Peoples' Conference in December 1958, with representatives of 62 nationalist organisations.

Unrest followed independence, and in December 1957 an act banned regional or tribal political parties; opposition parties then formed the United Party under Kofi Abrefa Busia. After an alleged assassination plot and worsening economic conditions Nkrumah's government became more authoritarian, and in 1964 a constitutional amendment made Ghana a one-party state with Nkrumah as president for life. While he was on a state visit to China in February 1966, the National Liberation Council, led by Joseph Arthur Ankrah, overthrew him in a coup. He lived the rest of his life in Conakry, Guinea, and died in Bucharest on 27 April 1972. He is remembered as a leading advocate of pan-Africanism and a founding member of the Organisation of African Unity.
kwando-river: The Cuando rises on the slopes of Mount Tembo on the central plateau of Angola and flows south-east along the Zambian border in a maze of channels, in a swampy corridor 5 to 10 km wide. Its flow varies enormously: in the rainy season it floods and may be several kilometres wide, while in the dry season it may disappear into marshes. It continues across the neck of the Caprivi Strip of Namibia and then forms the border between Namibia and Botswana, entering the Linyanti Swamp on the northern border of Botswana. Below the swamp it is called the Linyanti and, farther east after Lake Liambesi, the Chobe, which joins the Zambezi just above the former Kazungula Ferry, now replaced by the Kazungula Bridge.

About 10,000 years ago the Cuando merged with the Okavango River and the two flowed south to Lake Makgadikgadi, now a seasonal wetland. The land there was uplifted, so the Cuando meets higher ground, breaks into channels and swamps dotted with alluvial islands and nearly vanishes into the Kalahari sands, as the Okavango does. Instead it turned east and was captured by the Zambezi.

In years of good flood, water from the Okavango also escapes east along the Magwekwana River, or Selinda Spillway, into the Linyanti Swamp, so that it enters the Zambezi basin. On the north side of the Chobe, at the edge of the Caprivi Swamps, lies the ruined capital of the Kololo people, who conquered Barotseland in the 19th century. So much water is lost to evaporation in the swamps that the river adds little to the Zambezi except when it floods excessively.
kwango-river: The Kwango, or Cuango, is the largest left-bank tributary of the Kasai River in the Congo basin. It begins in the highlands of Alto Chicapa in Angola's Lunda Sul Province, flows north-west across the border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and joins the Kasai near the town of Bandundo, after which its water reaches the Congo. The river is 1,100 km long, of which 855 km lie in Angola, and drains a catchment of 263,500 square kilometres. Its right-bank tributaries are the Wamba and Kwilu rivers.

It has falls and rapids: the lower reaches are navigable for 307 km from the mouth to the Kingushi rapids, and the middle stretches are partly navigable for about 300 km between Kingushi and the Franz Josef waterfalls. In the 19th century the explorer David Livingstone wrote the name as Quango.

The Rund Kingdom, which grew into the Lunda Empire, held territory from the Kwango to the Luapula River. Its rulers took part in the slave trade, and the Lunda expansion in the valley fostered a common political and cultural heritage while also promoting slave trading, which accounts for the low population densities between the Kwango and Kwilu rivers. The Portuguese colonised the valley and usurped the Kingdom of Kasanje. The river was the subject of a Portuguese treaty signed in Lisbon on 25 May 1891 and a declaration of 24 March 1894.

The valley is inhabited by the Yaka, Suku, Mbala and Pende, whose crafts include mask carvings and figurines in geometric patterns. Palm oil and rubber were historically produced there, and the basin holds large resources of diamonds, especially in Angola's Lunda Norte Province.
kwantung-army: In 1895 Qing China granted the Kwantung Leased Territory on the Liaodong Peninsula to Japan in the Treaty of Shimonoseki, but the Triple Intervention led the Qing to withdraw the lease within weeks. It was leased to Russia in 1898. After the Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905 the lease passed to Japan, which also gained influence along the South Manchurian Railway. The Kwantung Garrison was established in 1906 to defend the territory, with an infantry division, a heavy siege artillery battalion and six independent garrison battalions guarding the railway, 14,000 men in all, headquartered at Port Arthur. In 1919 civilian and military administration were separated and the Kwantung Army command was created.

In the 1920s and 1930s the army was a stronghold of the radical Imperial Way Faction, many of whose leaders advocated overthrowing the civilian government at home and a more aggressive policy on the Asian mainland. Although it was nominally subordinate to Imperial General Headquarters, its leaders often acted against orders from Tokyo without consequence. Junior officers plotted the assassination of the Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin in 1928. The leadership then engineered the Mukden Incident and the invasion of Manchuria in 1931 against the express orders of Tokyo, which was presented with a fait accompli. The insubordination was rewarded rather than punished, and in 1932 the army was the main force behind the founding of Manchukuo, whose administration it controlled.

The army fought border conflicts with the Soviet Union, stalemating at Lake Khasan in 1938 and losing at Nomonhan in 1939 with heavy casualties, after which its more insubordinate elements were purged. By 1941 it had grown to 700,000 troops, but as the war turned its best units and equipment were sent south. In 1945 it had 713,000 personnel, many of them poorly trained, and was swiftly defeated when the Soviet Union invaded Manchuria on 9 August. General Otozō Yamada ordered a surrender on 16 August, a day after Emperor Hirohito's announcement, and over 500,000 Japanese prisoners were sent to Soviet labour camps.

The Kwantung Army sponsored Unit 731, which carried out biological warfare and human experimentation on civilians and prisoners of war under Dr. Shirō Ishii. Ishii and the unit's members received immunity from prosecution before the Tokyo tribunal in exchange for data on germ warfare. Twelve members of the unit were sentenced at the Khabarovsk War Crime Trials, and former Kwantung Army generals, among them Seishirō Itagaki and Kenji Doihara, were sentenced to death at Tokyo. Its alumni included Hideki Tōjō.
kwara-state: Kwara State lies in north central Nigeria. It borders Kogi State to the east, Niger State to the north, mostly across the Niger River and Lake Jebba, and Ekiti, Osun and Oyo states to the south. Its western border forms part of the international border with Benin. The state is split between the West Sudanian savanna in the east and the Guinean forest–savanna mosaic in the rest. In the far north-west lies the Borgu section of the Kainji National Park, and a small part of the Old Oyo National Park lies in the far south-west.

In the pre-colonial period most of the area was part of the Oyo Empire. Parts of the west belonged to the Borgu kingdoms, peopled by the Bariba, Boko and Bissa, and to the Nupe Kingdom, which existed from 1531 to 1835. The Fulani jihad later annexed part of the area and placed it under the Gwandu sphere of the Sokoto Caliphate. British expeditions occupied the area in the 1890s and 1900s and made it part of the Northern Nigeria Protectorate, which merged into British Nigeria in 1914.

After independence in 1960 the area was part of the Northern Region. On 27 May 1967 the military government of General Yakubu Gowon divided the four regions of the federation into twelve states, and Kwara was created from the former Ilorin and Kabba provinces. It was first named the West Central State and renamed Kwara, a Hausa name for the River Niger, in 1976. It has since lost territory: the Idah and Dekina area went to the new Benue State on 13 February 1976, and on 27 August 1991 five local government areas were cut off to form part of Kogi State while Borgu was merged with Niger State.

The capital is Ilorin, and the state has sixteen local government areas. Principal groups include the Yoruba, Nupe, Bariba and Fulani, and Christianity, Islam and traditional religions all have followers. Agriculture is the main source of the economy, with cotton, cocoa, coffee, kola nut and palm produce among the cash crops. Attractions include the Esie Museum, the Owu waterfalls and Sobi Hill, the largest landform in Ilorin.
kwazulu-natal: KwaZulu-Natal lies in the south-east of South Africa, with a long shoreline on the Indian Ocean, and covers about 92,100 square kilometres, roughly the size of Portugal. It has three geographic areas: a lowland coast that is very narrow in the south and wider in the north, the undulating plateau of the Natal Midlands, and two mountain areas, the western Drakensberg, a basalt wall rising over 3,000 metres beside Lesotho, and the Lebombo Mountains in the north. The Tugela, the largest river, flows across the centre of the province.

On Christmas Day 1497 the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama saw the coast and named it Natal, the Portuguese word for Christmas. The Nguni branch of the Bantu had occupied the area from the early 1300s. The first European settlers, mostly British, established Port Natal as a trading post and made almost no attempt to develop the interior, whose inhabitants had been decimated by the Zulu king Shaka. Afrikaner Voortrekkers entered through the Drakensberg passes in 1837, defeated the Zulus at the Battle of Blood River in 1838 and established the Republic of Natal, which lasted from 1839 until Britain annexed it in 1843.

From 1860 the British brought increasing numbers of Indians, mainly Tamils, to work the coastal sugar plantations. The colony acquired Zululand, north of the Tugela, after the Zulu War of 1879, and the lands north of the Buffalo River in 1902. In the South African War of 1899 to 1902 Boer forces besieged Ladysmith, and for three months the line between the two armies followed the Tugela. The colony became a province of the Union of South Africa in 1910.

In 1994, after the end of apartheid, the KwaZulu homeland, whose name means Place of the Zulu, was reincorporated into Natal and the province was renamed KwaZulu-Natal. It is the only South African province with the name of its dominant ethnic group in its name.

Pietermaritzburg is the seat of the provincial government and Durban the largest city, which has the busiest port in Africa by most measures. At the 2022 census the province had 12,423,907 inhabitants, the second-most populous in South Africa, and about 82 percent gave Zulu as their first language. It is home to the Zulu monarch, whose constitutional powers are limited. The iSimangaliso Wetland Park and the uKhahlamba Drakensberg Park are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and Hluhluwe–Imfolozi Park is where the southern white rhinoceros was saved from extinction.
kweneng-district: Kweneng is one of the districts of Botswana. It is the only district without a foreign border, and it adjoins the Central, Kgatleng, South-East, Southern, Kgalagadi and Ghanzi districts. Most of Botswana is tableland that slopes from east to west, and the district lies at an average elevation of around 915 m. The vegetation is savannah, with tall grasses, bushes and trees. Annual precipitation is around 25 cm, most of it falling in the summer season from November to May, and most rivers are seasonal, the Metsimotlhabe being the most prominent and prone to flash floods.

Kweneng is the recent historical homeland of the Bakwena people, the first group in Botswana to be converted to Christianity by the missionary David Livingstone. Landmarks such as Livingstone's Cave allude to that history, and the Kgosi Sechele I Museum is one of the district's major attractions. The rock paintings at Manyana village are another.

Botswana gained independence from the British in 1966 and adapted the colonial administration framework to form its district administration. The policies were modified during 1970–74 to address some basic issues. The district is run by a district administration and a district council, which are responsible for local administration; the council's major activities are tribal administration, remote area development and local governance, and its executive powers are vested in a commissioner appointed by the central government.

The seat of the district's government is Molepolole, a village that was counted in 2011 as the most populous in Botswana. The district's population was 304,549 in the 2011 census, up from 230,335 in 2001. Kweneng has two census districts, Kweneng East and Kweneng West, and agriculture is the major profession in Kweneng East.
kwidzyn: Kwidzyn lies on the Liwa River, about 5 kilometres east of the Vistula and some 70 kilometres south of Gdańsk, in the region of Powiśle. A Pomesanian settlement called Kwedis existed there in the 11th century. The Teutonic Order then built a castle and founded the town of Marienwerder, which was peopled with artisans and traders from towns in the northern parts of the Holy Roman Empire.

In 1243 the Bishopric of Pomesania received the town and castle from the Order as fiefs, and the settlement became the seat of the bishops of Pomesania. The knight Werner von Orseln, murdered at Marienburg in 1330, was among the first to be buried in the new cathedral. Saint Dorothea of Montau lived in the town from 1391 until her death in 1394, and the pilgrims to her shrine helped its economy. The Prussian Confederation, which opposed Teutonic rule, was founded there on 14 March 1440. In 1454 King Casimir IV Jagiellon of Poland incorporated the region at its request, and the Thirteen Years' War began. After the Order's defeat the town became part of Poland in 1466, held as a fief by the Order.

The Teutonic state became a secular Lutheran duchy in 1525, and in 1618 the ducal rights passed to the Brandenburg branch of the House of Hohenzollern. Brandenburg severed its ties with the Polish crown in 1657 and made its realm the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701. In 1772 the district of Marienwerder joined the new Prussian Province of West Prussia. The town had 12,983 inhabitants in 1910, of whom 12,408 were German-speaking and 346 Polish-speaking.

After the First World War the town lay in an area that voted in a plebiscite supervised by the League of Nations. In Marienwerder 7,811 votes were cast to remain in East Prussia and Germany and 362 for Poland, and Polish sources report electoral fraud. In January 1945 the civilians were ordered to evacuate, and most left. The Red Army captured the town on 30 January 1945 and burned and pillaged its centre. Settlers from Poland and Lithuania later repopulated it, and it returned to Poland under the Potsdam Agreement.

Kwidzyn is the capital of Kwidzyn County in the Pomeranian Voivodeship and has 36,731 inhabitants. Its main landmark is the 14th-century Brick Gothic castle, seat of the Pomesanian Cathedral Chapter, which now houses a museum and is a Historic Monument of Poland. The adjacent co-cathedral of Saint John the Evangelist, built between 1343 and 1384, contains the tombs of three Grand Masters of the Teutonic Knights.
kyiv: Kyiv lies on both banks of the Dnieper River, which flows southward through the city toward the Black Sea. The older and higher western part sits on wooded hills with ravines and small rivers, and these gave the city toponyms such as Podil (lower), Pechersk (caves) and uzviz (a steep street). The city expanded onto the low left bank to the east only in the 20th century. Its name is traditionally derived from Kyi, one of four founders named in tradition, though the linguist Jaroslav Rudnyckyj reads it as meaning palisaded settlement.

The first people in the region lived there in the late Paleolithic. Roman coins of the 2nd to 4th centuries suggest trade with the eastern provinces of the Roman Empire. Scholars debate when the city was founded. The traditional date is 482 CE, so the city marked its 1,500th anniversary in 1982, while archaeology points to the sixth or seventh century, and some researchers date it as late as the late 9th century. In the Primary Chronicle the brothers Kyi, Shchek and Khoryv and their sister Lybid are the founders.

A Slavic settlement on the trade route between Scandinavia and Constantinople, it was a tributary of the Khazars until its capture by the Varangians in the mid-9th century. Under Varangian rule it became a capital of Kievan Rus', the first East Slavic state. The Siege of Kiev in 1240 left it in ruins, and it lost most of its influence for centuries. It grew into a centre of Eastern Orthodox learning in the 16th century, and the Mohyla Academy was founded as a theological school in 1632.

The city prospered during the Industrial Revolution of the Russian Empire in the late 19th century. In 1918 the Ukrainian People's Republic declared independence and made Kyiv its capital. After the Ukrainian-Soviet and Polish-Soviet wars it became part of the Ukrainian SSR, whose capital it became in 1934. It suffered significant destruction in World War II and recovered as the third-largest city of the Soviet Union. It became the capital of independent Ukraine in 1991.

Kyiv is the capital and most populous city of Ukraine, with 2,952,301 inhabitants in January 2022. It has a special legal status as a city that is also treated as a region of the country. It remains a centre of Eastern Orthodox Christianity, and the Saint Sophia Cathedral and the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, the Monastery of the Caves, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Taras Shevchenko University, founded in 1834, is the oldest university in continuous operation there.
kyiv-pechersk-lavra: Anthony, a monk of Mount Athos who came from Liubech in the Principality of Chernigov, returned to Rus' as a missionary of the monastic tradition and settled in Kyiv. He chose a cave on the Berestov Mount above the Dnipro, and a community of disciples soon gathered. Prince Iziaslav I of Kyiv gave the whole mount to the monks, who founded a monastery built by architects from Constantinople. The caves are narrow underground corridors with living quarters and chapels. Anthony's first cave became the Far Caves, and in 1057 he moved to the Near Caves.

Supported by princes and boyars, the monastery became the most important centre of religion and culture in Rus'. Its monks produced the Primary Chronicle and the Kyiv Caves Patericon. It was plundered by the Cumans in 1096 and sacked by Prince Andrey Bogolyubsky in 1169, and Mongol invaders under Batu Khan attacked it in 1240. Prince Simeon Olelkovich rebuilt it in 1470, and Tatars burned it again in 1482.

In the second half of the 16th century the Patriarch of Constantinople granted it the rights of stauropegion, and it began to bear the name Lavra. In the 17th century, under the archimandrites Eliseus Pletenetsky, Zacharias Kopystensky and Peter Mohyla, it stood at the heart of Ukrainian national identity. Pletenetsky founded its printing house in the 1620s, and a school founded in 1631 later formed the Kyiv Mohyla Academy. After the Moscow Patriarchate annexed the Metropolis of Kyiv in 1685, the Lavra was gradually subjected to Russian imperial authority. A fire in 1718 destroyed its library and archive.

Soviet authorities confiscated valuables in 1921 and 1922 and turned the monastery into a museum. On 3 November 1941 the main Dormition Cathedral, built in the 11th century, was blown up. Monastic life was revived in 1988, the 1000th anniversary of the Christianization of Kievan Rus', and the rebuilt cathedral was reopened on 24 August 2000.

The Lavra was inscribed with Saint Sophia Cathedral as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1990. Its Great Lavra Belltower, designed by Johann Gottfried Schädel and built in 1731 to 1745, is 96.5 metres high. More than a hundred people are buried in the Lavra, among them the chronicler Nestor, the Lithuanian Grand Duke Švitrigaila and Pyotr Stolypin. The caves still hold the bodies of saints.
kyrgyz-people: The Kyrgyz speak the Kyrgyz language, which is the official language of Kyrgyzstan. The name has several explanations. It is often derived from the Turkic word kyrk, forty, so that Kyrgyz would mean a collection of forty tribes. Chinese sources transcribed the name in many ways, among them Gekun and Jiankun, in records going back to the Records of the Grand Historian, compiled between 109 and 91 BCE.

The Yenisei Kyrgyz, whose home lay in western Mongolia and the Yenisei valley, were of particular importance in forming the modern Kyrgyz. In 840 a revolt led by the Yenisei Kyrgyz brought down the Uyghur Khaganate. The Kyrgyz then moved as far as the Tian Shan range and held that territory for about 200 years.

In the 12th century Mongol expansion shrank Kyrgyz power to the Altai and Sayan Mountains, and with the rise of the Mongol Empire in the 13th century the Kyrgyz migrated south. In 1207 Genghis Khan's eldest son Jochi occupied Kyrgyzstan without resistance, and the state remained a Mongol vassal until the late 14th century. Various Turkic peoples ruled the Kyrgyz until 1685, when they came under the Oirats, or Dzungars, until 1757. Many tribes that had fled the Dzungars then returned to what is now Kyrgyzstan. By the 16th century people bearing the name lived in South Siberia, Xinjiang, the Tian Shan and Kazakhstan.

European writers of the 18th and 19th centuries used the form Kirghiz for both the Kyrgyz and the more numerous Kazakhs, calling the Kyrgyz proper Kara-Kirghiz, the Black Kirghiz. After the suppression of the 1916 rebellion against Russian rule in Central Asia, many Kyrgyz migrated to China and Afghanistan.

The Kyrgyz are predominantly Sunni Muslims of the Hanafi school. Arab traders brought Islam along the Silk Road in the 7th and 8th centuries, but a Persian text of the 10th century still described the Kyrgyz as people who venerate fire and burn their dead. Conversion began in the mid-17th century, with Sufi missionaries playing an important part, and by the 19th century the Kyrgyz were considered devout Muslims.

Kyrgyz communities live outside Kyrgyzstan. More than 145,000 Kyrgyz in China are one of the country's officially recognised ethnic groups, living mainly in the Kizilsu Kyrgyz Autonomous Prefecture in Xinjiang.
kyrie: Kyrie is a transliteration of the Greek Κύριε, the vocative of Κύριος, and gives its name to the prayer also called the Kyrie eleison. The Greek ἐλέησόν με κύριε, have mercy on me, Lord, is the Septuagint's translation of a phrase often found in the Psalms. In the gospel of Matthew the cry occurs three times: from the Canaanite woman who calls on Jesus as Son of David, from a man pleading for his son, and from two blind men. In the parable of the Publican and the Pharisee, the tax collector prays for mercy as a sinner. In the biblical text the phrase always has an explicit object, such as me, us or my son.

In Eastern Christianity, including the Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, Assyrian and Eastern Catholic Churches, Kýrie, eléison is among the most repeated phrases. It is the usual response in litanies, said singly or three times, and some petitions call for twelve or even forty repetitions. It is the origin of the Jesus Prayer, a foundation of personal prayer for Eastern Christians. The Coptic liturgy uses it in both Coptic and Greek.

In Rome the liturgy was first said in Greek. Josef Jungmann suggests that the Kyrie of the Roman Mass is a vestige of an opening litany like those of some Eastern churches, kept after Latin became normal. The Roman Rite also uses the variant Christe, eléison, from the Greek Χριστέ, ἐλέησον, meaning Christ, have mercy.

As early as the sixth century Pope Gregory the Great noted that East and West sang the Kyrie differently. In the East it was sung in unison by those present, while in the West the clergy sang and the people responded, and the West sang Christe, eléison as many times as Kýrie, eléison. In the Tridentine Mass it is sung or said three times, followed by a threefold Christe, eléison and another threefold Kýrie, eléison; the nine invocations are said to unite the petitions of the faithful with those of the nine choirs of angels. It is also the standard opening of litanies in the Roman Rite, such as the Litany of the Saints.

The Kyrie is the first sung prayer of the Mass ordinary and is usually part of any musical setting of the Mass. Since 1549 Anglicans have normally sung or said it in English, and in the 1552 Book of Common Prayer it was inserted into a recitation of the Ten Commandments. The Lutheran Mass places it after the Prayer of Thanksgiving, and Methodism also uses it.
kythira: Kythira lies opposite the south-eastern tip of the Peloponnese, between the Greek mainland and Crete, and is traditionally listed as one of the seven main Ionian Islands although it is distant from the main group. From ancient times until the mid-19th century it was a crossroads of merchants, sailors and conquerors, and its architecture blends traditional, Aegean and Venetian elements. It has a land area of 279.593 square kilometres and rugged terrain with steep cliffs and deep bays. It is close to the Hellenic arc plate boundary zone and so prone to earthquakes.

There are archaeological remains from the Helladic period, contemporary with the Minoans, and evidence of Kythiran trade as far as Egypt and Mesopotamia. The island had a Phoenician colony in the early archaic age, and the sea-snail that yields Tyrian purple is native to it. The archaic Greek city stood at Scandea, with a temple of Aphrodite Ourania, who may represent a Phoenician cult of Astarte. Sparta took the island from Argos early in the sixth century BCE. Athens occupied it three times when at war with Sparta, in 456 BCE, from 424 to 410 BCE and from 393 to 387 or 386 BCE, using it to support trade and to raid Laconia.

Christianity is attested from the fourth century CE, and according to legend Saint Elessa came from Laconia to convert the island. Archaeological evidence suggests the island was abandoned about 700 CE. After the Byzantine reconquest of Crete in 962 Saint Theodore of Cythera led a resettlement, found only wandering bands of hunters, and established a great monastery at Paliochora, around which a town grew, largely populated from Laconia. After the Fourth Crusade Venice took the island, kept a coast patrol on Kythira and Antikythera to protect its route to Constantinople, and called it Cerigo. Kythirans still recall the destruction and looting of Paliochora by Barbarossa, and Barbary pirates raided the island.

In 1797 Napoleon ended the Venetian Republic and Kythira was among the islands incorporated in the French department of Mer-Égée. In 1799 the Ionian Islands became the Septinsular Republic, and in 1809 the British set up the United States of the Ionian Islands, a protectorate they ruled for nearly half a century before ceding it to King George I of Greece.

Kythira belongs to the Islands regional unit of the Attica region, and the municipality, merged in the 2011 reform with Antikythera, covers 300.023 square kilometres. The chief town, Chora, holds the Historical Archives of Kythira, the second largest in the Ionian Islands after Corfu. In Greek mythology the island was sacred to Aphrodite, said to have been born from sea foam near it, and the adjective Cytherean derives from its name.
kyushu: Kyushu is the most southerly of Japan's four main islands, with a land area of 36,782 km2. It is mountainous, and its highest point is Mount Kujū at 1,791 m. Mount Aso, at 1,591 m, is the largest active volcano in Japan, and tectonic activity also shows in many hot springs, the best known of them at Beppu on the east shore and around Aso in the centre. The Kanmon Straits separate the island from Honshu. Because it is the island nearest the Asian continent, it has historically been the gateway to Japan. Parts of Kyushu, particularly Miyazaki and Kagoshima prefectures, have a subtropical climate, and the main crops are rice, tea, tobacco, sweet potatoes and soy.

Kyushu has been called Kyūkoku, the Nine Countries, Chinzei, meaning West of the Pacified Area, and Tsukushi-no-shima. The historical region of Saikaidō, the West Sea Circuit, covered the island and its surroundings, and the present name Kyūshū, nine provinces, comes from the nine ancient provinces on it: Chikuzen, Chikugo, Hizen, Higo, Buzen, Bungo, Hyūga, Ōsumi and Satsuma. In the Taihō Code reforms of the 8th century, Dazaifu was established as a special administrative term for the region. One theory holds that in ancient times Kyushu was home to its own independent dynasty, with a southern-influenced culture and tradition distinct from that of Honshu.

Kyushu holds about 10 percent of Japan's population, concentrated along the northwest in Fukuoka and Kitakyushu, with corridors running to Sasebo, Nagasaki, Kumamoto and Kagoshima. It has maintained the strongest economic and cultural ties with Okinawa from ancient times, and traces of Okinawan scales, cuisine and language appear throughout. The gottan, a traditional stringed instrument, is regarded as a midpoint between the shamisen of mainland Japan and the Okinawan sanshin.
