Porcelain from Arita, Imari, Satsuma and Karatsu is well known, and the Tanegashima Space Center is Japan's largest rocket-launch complex. The island has World Heritage Sites including Yakushima, the Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, and the Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region.
kyustendil: Kyustendil lies in the far west of Bulgaria, in the southern part of the Kyustendil Valley near the borders with Serbia and North Macedonia. It is 90 kilometres southwest of Sofia and 130 kilometres northeast of Skopje, and it is the capital of Kyustendil Province. The modern name comes from Kösten, the Turkified name of the 14th-century Serbian magnate Constantine Dragaš, with the Turkish il, meaning shire or bath.

A Thracian settlement was founded on the site in the 5th to 4th centuries BCE, known for its asclepion, a shrine to the god of medicine Asclepius. As Pautalia it was a town in the district of Dentheletica, and its coins show a river-god Strymon, since it stands at the sources of the Strymon. Later Pautalia belonged to the province of Dacia Mediterranea and was its third largest city. Its Roman fortress of the 2nd to 4th century covered over 29 hectares, with a granite wall 2.5 metres wide. Its only recorded residential bishop, Evangelius, was summoned to Constantinople in 516.

The town appears under the Slavic name Velbazhd in a charter of Basil II in 1019. It passed to the Second Bulgarian Empire after Kaloyan conquered the area between 1201 and 1203, and in 1282 the Serbian king Stefan Milutin defeated the Byzantine Empire and took it. In 1330 the Serbs defeated the Bulgarians nearby, keeping the region for Serbia. Under Dejan and his sons, Jovan and Konstantin Dragaš, it formed part of a province in eastern Macedonia, and in 1373 the Ottoman army compelled Jovan to accept Ottoman vassalage. The town was annexed in 1395.

Under Ottoman rule it was a sanjak centre and later a kaza centre until 1878. Its people took an active part in the Bulgarian National Revival, and the town was freed from Ottoman rule on 29 January 1878.

The Regional History Museum shows many Thracian and Roman objects, above all a collection of coins, and excavations have revealed an early Christian, late Roman bishop's palace. Many mosques stood in the town under Ottoman rule, but only two remain. Kyustendil is the centre of an Orthodox eparchy, and it is also a Latin Catholic titular see.
kyzylorda: A settlement is said to have existed here under Seljuk, the founder of the Seljuk dynasty. The modern city began in 1817 as a Kokand fortress known as Ak-Mechet, the white mosque. In 1853, during the Russian conquest of Turkestan, Russian troops under General Vasily Perovsky took the fort. They established a new one, Fort-Perovsky, named after the general, and around it the town of Perovsk developed in Russian Turkestan. It was granted city status in 1867.

Soviet power was first established in the city in October 1917, and in 1922 the name Ak-Mechet was restored. In 1925 the city was renamed Kzyl-Orda, a name meaning a red city, from the Turkic word for red, used here with its Soviet ideological sense, and a Turkic and Mongolian word for city. In the same year the capital of the Kazakh ASSR was moved to it from Orynbor. The Kyzylorda State Archive, founded in 1928, holds documents from the period when the city was the Kazakh capital. The Kyzylorda State University was founded in 1937, and in 1938 the city became the capital of the newly established Kyzylorda Region.

Kyzylorda is the capital of Kyzylorda Region in south-central Kazakhstan and has a population of 242,462 according to the 2020 count. The spelling Kyzylorda, based on the Kazakh form, has been used since the late 20th century, after the dissolution of the Soviet Union and Kazakhstan's independence in 1991. The city is known for rice production, with two rice mills, and has developed as a supply centre for the oilfields of the nearby Turgay Basin. Its climate is a cold desert one, with hot summers, cold winters and low rainfall.

Kyzylorda State University, named after Korkyt ata, was established in 1950 and is the leading centre of education in the Aral region. Places of interest in the region include the vanished Aral Sea, the Baikonur cosmodrome, archaeological excavations at Sauran and Shyganak and the memorial complex of Korkyt Ata.
